### **About This Document Document**

Called for by the U.S. Coral Reef Task Force's (USCRTF)

--- SENTENCE 4 ---
*National Action Plan to Conserve Coral Reefs*, this is the first biennial report on the condition of coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5 ---
It is the scientific baseline for subsequent reports on the health of U.S. coral reef ecosystems that are to be used by NOAA and others to evaluate the efficacy of coral reef conservation and management practices.

--- SENTENCE 6 ---
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Ocean Service led the development of this report.

--- SENTENCE 7 ---
It was authored by 38 experts and supported by 79 contributors from government agencies and non-governmental organizations across the nation and internationally.

--- SENTENCE 8 ---
Over 100 Task Force members and other notable scientists have reviewed this document.

--- SENTENCE 9 ---
This document was prepared and printed under the auspices of NOAA's National Ocean Service in cooperation with federal and non-federal (State, Territory, and Commonwealth) members and staff of the USCRTF, and other eminent coral reef scientists and managers.

### **Authorizations, Appropriations, Agency Actions Actions**

**Coral Reef Conservation Act of 2000 Act of 2000 –**

--- SENTENCE 38 ---
The Coral Reef Conservation Act ( Public Law 106-562, U.S.C. 6401 *et seq*., December 2000) authorizes \$16 million annually from 2000-2004 to the Secretary of Commerce to help preserve, sustain, and restore the condition of coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 39 ---
The Act authorizes 1) the establishment a new Coral Reef Conservation Program to providing matching grants for projects that conserve coral reefs, and 2) funding for a National Program to conduct a variety of coral reef activities such as mapping, assessment, monitoring, research, restoration, public outreach, and removing abandoned fishing gear, marine debris, and grounded vessels.

--- SENTENCE 40 ---
The Act also requires the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to develop a National Coral Reef Action Strategy, and authorizes establishing a Coral Reef Conservation Fund to build public-private partnerships for coral reef conservation.

--- SENTENCE 41 ---
See http://www.coralreef.noaa.gov/ for more information.

--- SENTENCE 42 ---
**2000-02 Agency Activities Activities –**

--- SENTENCE 43 ---
A variety of government (Federal, State, Territory, Commonwealth) and non-governmental partners are engaged in activities that help conserve, protect, and manage coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 44 ---
Some activities have increased since 2000.

--- SENTENCE 45 ---
For example, beginning in 2000 the Department of Commerce and the Department of the Interior received new funding specifically related to coral reef conservation.

--- SENTENCE 46 ---
Other entities have continued or shifted resources to begin addressing coral reef related issues on land and at sea.

--- SENTENCE 47 ---
For more information please contact the United States Coral Reef Task Force http:// coralreef.gov/.

**Coral Reef Presidential Order Order –**

--- SENTENCE 48 ---
As part of the National Ocean Conference in June 1998, President Clinton signed the Coral Reef Protection Executive Order (13089) to conserve and protect the health, biodiversity, heritage, and ecological, social, and economic values of U.S. coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 49 ---
The Executive Order tasks Federal agencies with a number of actions including reviewing and increasing efforts to protect coral reef ecosystems, working with State and Territorial resource trustees and other partners.

--- SENTENCE 50 ---
The Order created an interagency U.S. Coral Reef Task Force (USCRTF) to oversee implementation of the Order.

--- SENTENCE 51 ---
For more information see http://coralreef.gov/.

**United States Coral Reef Task Force Coral Reef Task Force –** Established by Executive Order 13089 in 1998, the USCRTF is co-chaired by the Secretary of the Interior and Secretary of Commerce.

--- SENTENCE 52 ---
It is composed of the heads of 11 Federal agencies, the Governors of 7 states and territories, and the Presidents of the Freely Associated States (Palau, Marshal Islands, and Micronesia).

--- SENTENCE 53 ---
Working with many government and non-government partners, the USCRTF adopted the *National Action Plan to Conserve Coral Reefs* (National Action Plan) in March 2000, the first national blueprint for U.S. action to address the loss and degradation of coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 54 ---
The National Action Plan outlines thirteen major goals to address key threats to reefs.

--- SENTENCE 55 ---
For more information on the Task Force please see http://coralreef.gov.

!

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Kapuna (Hawaiian elder and expert fisherman)

--- SENTENCE 61 ---
Buzzy Agard started fishing the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands in the early 1950s.

--- SENTENCE 62 ---
When he first arrived, he spotted a school of large moi (threadfins, an early Hawaiian food fish) and harvested them.

--- SENTENCE 63 ---
He tells that there were "no more the next day, the next week, or ten years later."

--- SENTENCE 64 ---
He said he learned that "the reefs are fragile and need to be managed with care.

--- SENTENCE 65 ---
"

The United States has jurisdiction over majestic coral reefs covering an estimated 7,607 mi<sup>2</sup> in the tropical-subtropical belt around the equator.

--- SENTENCE 66 ---
Many of these reef systems support diverse, brightly colored marine life surrounded by emerald seas (Fig. 1); others have been affected by environmental and human-related impacts and need restoration.

--- SENTENCE 67 ---
In the Western Atlantic and Caribbean, shallow-water<sup>1</sup> coral reefs are found off Florida<sup>2</sup>, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI), and in the Navassa Island National Wildlife Refuge near Haiti.

--- SENTENCE 68 ---
In the Gulf of Mexico, reef banks are found on the continental shelf 100 miles south of the Texas/Louisana Border.

--- SENTENCE 69 ---
In the Pacific, coral reefs occur off the Hawaiian Archipelago, American Samoa, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern

Mariana Islands (CNMI), Wake Atoll, and another six remote National Wildlife Refuges<sup>3</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 70 ---
In addition, the Freely Associated States (the countries of the Republic of Palau, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Federated States of Micronesia), included in this report, have some of the richest coral reefs in the world, covering an estimated 4,479-31,470 mi<sup>2</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 71 ---
In response to growing concerns about the condition of reefs, the United States Coral Reef Task Force<sup>4</sup> (USCRTF) called for a nationally-coordinated mapping and monitoring program to help track and evaluate the condition of U.S. coral reefs and report to

the Nation every two years.

--- SENTENCE 72 ---
This report is the first effort to collect consistent, comparable scientific information to assess the status of coral reef health.

--- SENTENCE 73 ---
This first biennial report on the condition of coral reef ecosystems – *The State of Coral Reef Ecosystems of the United States and the Freely Associated States: 2002* was led by NOAA's National Ocean Service.

--- SENTENCE 74 ---
Thirty-eight experts authored the report with information from another 79 contributors.

--- SENTENCE 75 ---
It includes the latest data from published literature as well as unpublished information from coral reef managers and scientists.

--- SENTENCE 76 ---
Information from recent USCRTF mapping, research, monitoring, and conservation initiatives are also included.

--- SENTENCE 77 ---
It has been peer-reviewed by over 100 coral reef ecosystem experts.

--- SENTENCE 78 ---
Coral reefs are called the

(Photo: Mike White).

--- SENTENCE 79 ---
"rainforests of the sea" due to their high biodiversity and threatened status

This report assesses the condition of reef resources, ranks the relative importance of environmental pressures that have degraded reefs, highlights significant actions taken by USCRTF agencies to conserve coral reef ecosystems, and provides recommendations from coral reef managers to fill information gaps.

--- SENTENCE 80 ---
It forms a baseline against which future assessments will be compared, allowing scientists to track and ultimately predict changes in reef conditions.

#### Global Climate Change and Coral Bleaching<sup>6</sup> —

The ultimate long-term environmental threat to coral reef ecosystems is global climate change that many believe is linked to the dramatic increase of coral bleaching in the past decade.

--- SENTENCE 92 ---
Bleaching varies regionally, locally within a reef<sup>7</sup>, and among species.

--- SENTENCE 93 ---
It also coincides with elevated water temperatures associated with El Niño and La Niña events.

--- SENTENCE 94 ---
Although most U.S. reefs escaped major damage from the largest coral bleaching event on record (1997-1998), reefs off Florida, Palau, and Palmyra were devastated (Fig. 2).

--- SENTENCE 95 ---
During this bleaching event, an estimated 16% of the reef corals were destroyed world-wide.

--- SENTENCE 96 ---
– Historically, the broad array of reef

fishing activities has great cultural, economic, and recreational value.

--- SENTENCE 97 ---
This report calculates that U.S. commercial reef fisheries today are worth over \$137.1 million to fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 98 ---
The gross value estimated for commercial fisheries in the Freely Associated States is another \$109.8

Figure 3.

--- SENTENCE 99 ---
The Nassau grouper is a candidate for protection under the Endangered Species Act (Photo: NOAA's NMFS).

!

--- SENTENCE 100 ---
According to coral reef managers, the greatest human-related impacts on the broadest scale are over-harvesting of reef resources and fishing-associated habitat destruction.

--- SENTENCE 101 ---
Overfishing threatens Florida, Puerto Rico, the USVI, the Main Hawaiian Islands, American Samoa, and to a lesser degree reefs around other populated islands.

--- SENTENCE 102 ---
In the South Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and

Caribbean, NOAA identified 23 reef fish as overfished and concluded there was too little data to determine the status of another 232 species.

--- SENTENCE 103 ---
As a result, four species of Western Atlantic grouper have been added to the list of candidate species under the Endangered Species Act (Fig. 3).

--- SENTENCE 104 ---
Managers from Florida, Puerto Rico, USVI, Hawai'i, and the offshore coral banks in the Gulf of Mexico are particularly concerned that certain types of fishing gear, particularly fish and lobster traps and large gill nets, may physically damage and degrade reef habitat.

--- SENTENCE 105 ---
**Diseases** – Over the last few decades, there has been a worldwide increase in reports of new diseases.

--- SENTENCE 106 ---
Disease appears to be more prevalent near human population centers.

--- SENTENCE 107 ---
While there is no direct correlation, long-term, low-level stress from poor water quality, elevated water temperatures, overfishing, and other factors may make reef organisms more susceptible to disease.

--- SENTENCE 108 ---
The Caribbean region has much higher incidences of disease, where outbreaks of a number of diseases have contributed to mass mortalities of corals, fish, sea fans, sea urchins, sponges, sea-

grasses, and other organisms.

--- SENTENCE 109 ---
One of the worst of these, a disease killed over 90% of the mature long-spined sea urchins throughout much of the Caribbean in the early 1980s.

--- SENTENCE 110 ---
Since then, these urchins have recovered to only about 10% of their original numbers on reefs off Florida, Puerto Rico, and the USVI.

--- SENTENCE 111 ---
As used throughout this report, the terms **overfishing** and **overfished** are generally the same as defined for U.S. federal fisheries – a rate or level of fishing mortality that jeopardizes the capacity of a fishery to produce the maximum sustainable yield on a continuing basis (Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, Pub.

--- SENTENCE 112 ---
Law 94-265, 16 U.S.C.1801 Sec. 2).

--- SENTENCE 113 ---
the many coral diseases to emerge over the last 20 years, white-band disease is one of the most virulent, killing up to 90-95% of the elkhorn and staghorn corals off St. Croix, Puerto Rico, and southeastern Florida by the 1990s.

--- SENTENCE 114 ---
With the exception of cancerous tumors infecting green sea turtles8 off the Main Hawaiian Islands, disease in the Pacific Islands is low to moderate.

--- SENTENCE 115 ---
**Tropical Storms Tropical Storms –** With eight hurricanes in the past 20 years nearly destroying staghorn and elkhorn coral populations, USVI managers consider tropical storms a major threat (Fig. 4).

--- SENTENCE 116 ---
Elsewhere, reef corals have more resilience.

--- SENTENCE 117 ---
On many Pacific islands, normal heavy wave action removes relatively fragile vertical branches of corals.

--- SENTENCE 118 ---
As a result, throughout the region, low-growing encrust-

ing and massive growth forms of coral prevail.

Because they lie in the Western Pacific Monsoon Trough, Guam and the CNMI have these low-profile reefs.

--- SENTENCE 119 ---
About half the typhoons that develop in the Pacific pass near or directly hit these islands, yet the extensive living reef structure that protects them sustains surprisingly little damage

even when a super typhoon passes directly overhead.

--- SENTENCE 120 ---
**Coastal Development and Runoff Development Runoff –** Tropical climates, colorful reefs, and clear waters draw permanent residents and tourists to seashores.

--- SENTENCE 121 ---
To sustain the influx, additional housing, hotels, and other coastal development (e.g., roads, airports, hospitals, schools) are needed, all of which result in runoff and sedimentation during and after construction.

--- SENTENCE 122 ---
Runoff and sedimentation from coastal development have degraded coral reef ecosystems off southeastern Florida and the Keys, Puerto Rico, the USVI, most of the Main Hawaiian Islands, Guam, and the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 123 ---
Runoff and sedimentation also occur in rural areas where forests have been removed for agriculture.

--- SENTENCE 124 ---
Near-shore reefs off high Pacific islands in American Samoa, the CNMI, and Palau experience runoff and sedimentation during tropical storms.

--- SENTENCE 125 ---
Although less widespread than overfishing, runoff and sedimentation are of considerable concern to managers in all jurisdictions.

--- SENTENCE 126 ---
**Coastal Pollution Pollution –** Managers from eight jurisdictions consider coastal pollution a major threat to their coastal coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 127 ---
Toxic chemicals and excessive nutrient enrichment are mostly limited to relatively small areas within canals, harbors and marinas, and near sewage disposal sites.

--- SENTENCE 128 ---
There are polluted 'hot spots' near reefs off Florida, Puerto Rico, the USVI, some islands within the Hawaiian Archipelago, American Samoa, Guam, and the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 129 ---
High levels of toxic chem-

> icals have been found in the tissues of reef wildlife off urbanized areas and several of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 130 ---

--- SENTENCE 131 ---
The trade in live reef fish, chunks of coral, and invertebrates for aquariums has grown rapidly over the last decade, raising concerns among scientists and managers, particularly those in Hawai'i (Fig. 5).

--- SENTENCE 132 ---
The United

States is the largest importer of ornamental coral reef species, responsible for around 70-95% of the global trade in coral and 'live rock' and nearly half

<sup>6</sup>**Bleaching** is a condition whereby the algae (called zooxanthellae) living in the epidermal tissue of most reef corals are expelled after prolonged exposure to certain environmental conditions (e.g., elevated temperatures).

--- SENTENCE 134 ---
The color of the coral primarily comes from the zooxanthellae, so the coral whitens when they are expelled, leaving only the white carbonate color of the coral skeleton.

--- SENTENCE 135 ---
This condition can be temporary if the zooxanthellae return within a few days, if not, then coral mortalities can be high.

--- SENTENCE 140 ---
Most of the ornamental fish and invertebrates originating from U.S. waters come from Hawai'i and Florida, with smaller numbers originating in Puerto Rico, the USVI, and Guam.

--- SENTENCE 141 ---
Since 1999, these jurisdictions have taken action with new studies, regulations, **marine protected areas**<sup>9</sup> (MPAs), **no-take zones**, and landmark legal settlements.

--- SENTENCE 142 ---
**Alien**<sup>10</sup>**Species Species –** Only recently have alien species been recognized as a threat to ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 143 ---
Nonnative organisms are introduced to near-shore reefs from ship hull fouling and ballast water, aquarium releases, as well as purposeful introductions for science and aquaculture.

--- SENTENCE 144 ---
Besides the organisms, each may have diseases or parasites that can devastate native species.

--- SENTENCE 145 ---
Although their impacts are not well studied, coastal **invasive** species are a major concern in the Hawaiian Islands with its many rare and endangered species.

--- SENTENCE 146 ---
**Boats, Ships, and Groundings Ships, Groundings –** Boat traffic threatens reef structure and associated wildlife.

--- SENTENCE 147 ---
Groundings, anchor damage, and propellers speeding through shallow waterways are some of the most destructive chronic human factors (Fig. 6).

--- SENTENCE 148 ---
They cause significant localized damage to shallow-water coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 149 ---
The increasing number of large ship and small boat groundings is a major threat off Florida, the USVI, and the Main Hawaiian Islands, and of moderate concern along other populated coasts.

--- SENTENCE 150 ---
**Tourism and Recreation Tourism and Recreation –**

--- SENTENCE 151 ---
The economic value of coral reefs is significant.

--- SENTENCE 152 ---
But growth within the

tourist industry has serious ecological ramifications for coral reef ecosystems off Florida, Puerto Rico, USVI, the Main Hawaiian Islands, Guam, and Palau.

--- SENTENCE 153 ---
This report calculated that annually 45 million visitors come to seaside and live-aboard accommodations to dive, fish, and otherwise enjoy U.S. coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 154 ---
Reef-related tourism generates an estimated \$17.5 billion annually in local income and sales for U.S. States, Commonwealths, and Territories.

--- SENTENCE 155 ---
An additional 113,000 tourists visit the Freely Associated States, spending over \$84.8 million annually.

--- SENTENCE 156 ---
With so many tourists visiting coral reefs, damage is inevitable (Fig. 7).

--- SENTENCE 157 ---
Managers from eight jurisdictions consider the impacts from tourism and associated recreational activities a medium-to-high concern for near-shore coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 158 ---
**Marine Debris**<sup>11</sup>**–** Transported by ocean currents over long distances, marine debris snags, smothers, and breaks coral colonies, and kills marine wildlife (e.g., endangered Hawaiian monk seals, sea turtles, and island sea birds, Fig.

--- SENTENCE 159 ---
8) through either entanglement or ingestion.

--- SENTENCE 160 ---
Marine debris is a matter of high concern for the coral reef managers from the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia.

--- SENTENCE 161 ---
Since 1999, multi-agency clean-up activities have removed over 150 tons of debris from Hawaiian Island beaches and nearshore reefs, but much still remains.

#### **Other Physical Impacts to Coral Reefs Other Reefs –**

There are other human-related impacts to reef structure of concern to managers.

--- SENTENCE 172 ---
Although no longer legal in U.S. waters, dynamiting reefs to collect fish remains a problem in the Indo-Pacific region.

--- SENTENCE 173 ---
Live munitions aboard some sunken World War II relics have been found and used by fishermen to harvest reef fish.

--- SENTENCE 174 ---
Other wrecks may be a danger to recreational divers and local fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 175 ---
For safety reasons, the U.S. Navy recently detonated live depth charges found on a WWII Subchaser that had wrecked on a now popular CNMI reef.

--- SENTENCE 176 ---
Between 1946 and 1958, the United States used Enewetak and Bikini Atolls in the Marshall Islands to test 67 nuclear devices.

--- SENTENCE 177 ---
The craters of many of these blasts can still be seen and the effects on reef structure are evident in shallow waters.

--- SENTENCE 178 ---
Where national security training exercises and live-fire activities have been conducted (Vieques, Puerto Rico; Farallon de Medinilla, CNMI; Kaho'olawe and Kaula Rock, Main Hawaiian Islands), managers are concerned about impacts of bombing and unexploded ordnance on reefs.

#### **National Assessments of Coral Reef Coral Reef Ecosystems Ecosystems**

Every U.S. reef system has sustained impacts from environmental and human disturbance, but all jurisdictions still have some reefs in good to

excellent health.

--- SENTENCE 179 ---
Many scientists consider reef systems in Florida and the U.S. Caribbean to be in the poorest condition, mostly because they are close to dense populations and have been repeatedly hit by a series of hurricanes, diseases, and various chronic human-induced impacts.

--- SENTENCE 180 ---
Pacific reefs, even around urbanized islands, are in significantly better condition.

--- SENTENCE 181 ---
This is due in large part to the fact that many lie off isolated islands and atolls and are surrounded by deep water with prevailing strong currents, upwelling, high waves, and tropical storms that flush the reefs with clean, cool water.

!

--- SENTENCE 182 ---
Seabirds feeding among plastic debris (Photo: NOAA Library).

--- SENTENCE 183 ---
Currently, there is relatively little quantitative information available assessing temporal and spatial trends in coral reef condition.

--- SENTENCE 184 ---
Most coral reefs have yet to be mapped and their resources characterized.

--- SENTENCE 185 ---
Little comparable data are available on coral reef function, structure, and condition.

--- SENTENCE 186 ---
Prior to 2000, the comprehensive mapping and long-term monitoring needed to prepare a national assessment were only available for a few locations12.

--- SENTENCE 187 ---
Since FY0213, with considerable support from the U.S. Congress, NOAA started a major mapping initiative and has provided substantial grants to island agencies to build local capacity for long-term monitoring using comparable sampling methods and protocols.

--- SENTENCE 188 ---
The authors of this report have committed to participating in a nationallycoordinated Coral Reef Monitoring Network to develop criteria, indicators, and metrics for a 'report card' to track changes in the condition of coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 189 ---
It will also allow them to

--- SENTENCE 197 ---
The following regional summaries are largely qualitative reports by the managers and scientists who are most familiar with the reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 199 ---
**Florida Florida –** Florida's coral reefs are extensive.

--- SENTENCE 200 ---
They have the greatest number of tourists/visitors of any U.S. jurisdiction, and consequently have substantial human impacts, particularly along the southeastern coast and in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 201 ---
In general, reef health is declining in southeastern Florida and the Keys, as evidenced by species fluctuations, decreases in coral coverage, and disease.

--- SENTENCE 202 ---
Over the past 20 years, coral bleaching has increased in both frequency and duration, often with high mortality.

--- SENTENCE 203 ---
Particularly massive bleaching events in 1990 and 1997-1998 were responsible for the 80-90% mortality of blade fire corals on shallow-water reefs (Fig. 9).

--- SENTENCE 204 ---
Monitoring in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary showed both coral reef abundance and diversity were declining – coral cover decreased 37% over the past five years.

--- SENTENCE 205 ---
This was preceded by even more dramatic declines in the 1980s and early 1990s.

--- SENTENCE 206 ---
On the other hand, deeper reefs off the Tortugas Ecological Reserve and the Florida Middle Grounds are in excellent condition.

--- SENTENCE 207 ---
In the Keys, 23 of 35 species of groupers, snappers, wrasses, and grunts are overfished, while five fish species from the Florida Keys are considered at risk of extinction.

--- SENTENCE 208 ---
Nearby Florida Bay has

another six at-risk fish species.

--- SENTENCE 209 ---
In Biscayne National Park, 26 of 34 fish species are considered overfished.

--- SENTENCE 210 ---
There is evidence that Sanctuary-designated fully protected zones have already replenished stocks for several over-harvested species.

--- SENTENCE 211 ---
On these reefs, average size and abundance of large groupers, snappers, and spiny lobsters have increased in the past few years.

--- SENTENCE 212 ---
Turbidity, contaminants, and nutrient enrichment can periodically be high and vary geographically14.

--- SENTENCE 213 ---
Toxic contaminant 'hot spots' have been found in the sediments of both Biscayne and Florida Bays.

--- SENTENCE 214 ---
The recreational fishing fleet in South Florida has grown at a near exponential rate since 1964 (a 444% increase in recreational boats from 1964 to 1998) with no limit on the number of boats allowed to fish.

--- SENTENCE 215 ---
**Puerto Rico Rico –** Due to its rapidly growing population and thriving tourism, human pressures on Puerto Rican coral reefs are some of the most severe in the Caribbean.

--- SENTENCE 216 ---
Accelerated urban and industrial coastal development over the last four decades, with the corresponding coastal development, sewage discharge, and sediment runoff during and after construction, have all degraded the condition of nearby reefs.

--- SENTENCE 217 ---
Staghorn and elkhorn coral populations have declined in most locations over the last 25 years from hurricane damage, white-band disease, and coral-eating mollusks.

--- SENTENCE 218 ---
Fishery resources show the classic signs of overfishing – reduced total landings, declining catch-per-unit-effort, smaller fish taken, and recruitment failures.

--- SENTENCE 219 ---
Reef fisheries have plummeted during the last two decades; between 1979 and 1990 they dropped 69%.

--- SENTENCE 220 ---
Shallow-water coral reefs off La Parguera on the main island of Puerto Rico and off the islands of Desecheo and Vieques have the highest abundance and cover of living corals in the Commonwealth, but even those have been stressed significantly.

--- SENTENCE 221 ---
**U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI) (USVI) –** Over the past 20 years, near-shore coral reefs off the USVI have suffered a series of natural disasters and been exposed to increasing chronic impacts from island residents and tourists (Fig. 10).

--- SENTENCE 222 ---
Compounding the devastation from being hit by eight hurricanes with

<sup>14</sup>

--- SENTENCE 223 ---

--- SENTENCE 224 ---

--- SENTENCE 225 ---
On some reefs, living elkhorn coral cover has fallen from 85% to 5%.

--- SENTENCE 226 ---
Major coral bleaching events occurred in 1987, 1990, and 1998, but generally mortality was not high.

--- SENTENCE 227 ---
Macroscopic algae, covering about 5% of the bottom before Hurricane Hugo, are now periodically very abundant, averaging over 30% cover in some months.

--- SENTENCE 228 ---
This is probably the result of decreased algal grazing after the loss of long-spined sea urchins in the early 1980s and the overfishing of **herbivorous fishes**15.

--- SENTENCE 229 ---
Dredging, sand extraction, pier construction, and sewage effluent have all impacted USVI reefs, especially those off St. Thomas and St. Croix.

--- SENTENCE 230 ---
Overfishing is a serious problem throughout the USVI and has had a profound effect on finfish and invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 231 ---
After depleting the desirable species of groupers16, fishers began targeting smaller species.

--- SENTENCE 232 ---
In general, fisheries are close to collapse, even within marine protected areas.

--- SENTENCE 233 ---
**Flower Garden Banks Garden Banks –**

--- SENTENCE 234 ---
The coral reefs in the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary are in excellent condition, largely because 1) the banks are located well offshore, 2) they generally lie deeper (the reef platform is around 55-100+ ft from the surface), and 3) they are far from human settlement.

--- SENTENCE 235 ---
Coral cover on the bank platform averages 47% and has not significantly changed since monitoring began in 1972 (Fig. 11).

--- SENTENCE 236 ---
Disease is relatively low, as is coral bleaching; neither has resulted in significant mortality.

**The Main Hawaiian Islands (MHI) (MHI) –** With a few exceptions and despite changes in coastal land use, near-shore reefs around the eight MHI remain in relatively good condition.

--- SENTENCE 243 ---
Coral reefs suffer from degradation related to human population growth, urbanization, and development.

--- SENTENCE 244 ---
Major sources are ocean outfalls, urbanization, massive coastal recreational development (hotels, golf courses, etc.), and marine invasive species, especially macroalgae and the red mangrove.

--- SENTENCE 245 ---
Previously, ranching, plantation agriculture, and military construction impacted reef condition.

--- SENTENCE 246 ---
There are strong indications of overfishing of the majority of fish and invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 247 ---
Recently there has been concern regarding the expanding live marine ornamental trade for home aquaria.

--- SENTENCE 248 ---
Fishing pressure in heavily populated areas appears to exceed the capacity of these resources to renew themselves.

--- SENTENCE 249 ---
The abundance of reef fishes in areas where fishing is allowed is substantially lower than in areas where it is prohibited.

--- SENTENCE 250 ---
There are numerous no-take marine protected areas off MHI shores; some of the larger ones have been shown to be effective in replenishing local fish stocks, but the rest may be too small to serve as ecosystem refuges (Fig. 12).

--- SENTENCE 255 ---

--- SENTENCE 261 ---

--- SENTENCE 262 ---
The major anthropogenic impact on NWHI reefs is marine debris, mostly nets, plastics, and other trash transported by currents from fleets fishing in distant waters (Fig. 13).

--- SENTENCE 263 ---
The existing Hawaiian Islands and Midway National Wildlife Refuges and now the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve, make these reefs the most highly protected.

--- SENTENCE 264 ---
Furthermore, the State of Hawai'i is presently evaluating its option of developing State fishery management areas in the NWHI.

American Samoa – Coral reefs off American Samoa are recovering from natural disasters – a crown-of-thorns starfish invasion (1979, Fig. 14), three hurricanes (1986, 1990, 1991), and a period of warm weather that caused massive coral bleaching (1994).

--- SENTENCE 267 ---
Added to this are chronic human-induced impacts in populated areas like Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 268 ---
Coral recovery from the natural disturbances has been excellent through 2001.

--- SENTENCE 269 ---
Information is limited, but with a few exceptions, the algae found around the islands are indicative of a low nutrient environment<sup>19</sup> and/or heavy grazing by herbivores.

--- SENTENCE 270 ---
Harvested species such as giant clams and parrotfish are overfished; there is heavy pressure on surgeonfish, and there are fewer and smaller groupers, snappers, and jacks.

--- SENTENCE 271 ---
The endangered hawksbill turtle is in serious decline from illegal harvest and loss of nesting habitat.

--- SENTENCE 272 ---
Fish are contaminated with heavy metals in some areas, particularly in Pago Pago Harbor.

#### **Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana of Mariana**

**Islands Islands –** Generally, the CNMI reef ecosystems are in excellent to good condition.

--- SENTENCE 292 ---
Reefs adjacent to the populated southern islands of Saipan, Tinian, and Rota receive most of human impacts from development, population growth, fishing, and tourism.

--- SENTENCE 293 ---
Although coral reef species were devastated by a major crown-of-thorns starfish outbreak in the late 1960s, most of the affected reefs appear to have

recovered.

--- SENTENCE 294 ---
CNMI coral reefs were spared the impacts of the 1998 coral bleaching event; however, bleaching is now a major concern.

--- SENTENCE 295 ---
Based on qualitative assessments, CNMI's populated southern reefs are all overfished at some level; fish populations on the mostly unpopulated northern reefs are generally in excellent condition.

--- SENTENCE 296 ---
**U.S. Remote Insular**<sup>24</sup> **Reefs –**

--- SENTENCE 297 ---
These reefs off remote and largely uninhabited atolls and islands remain relatively pristine.

--- SENTENCE 298 ---
They have experienced few human-induced pressures outside of longdistance fishing.

--- SENTENCE 299 ---
Disease is low; except for Palmyra Atoll, the same is true for coral bleaching.

>

--- SENTENCE 300 ---
Since the late 1800s, there has been little fishing pressure on any of these reefs.

--- SENTENCE 301 ---
Shallow-water reef fish communities exhibit high density and have substantial populations of large snappers, groupers, and herbivores.

--- SENTENCE 302 ---
#### **Republic of the Marshall Islands of the Marshall Islands –**

The RMI coral reef ecosystems are generally in good to excellent condition.

--- SENTENCE 303 ---
Even the reefs used for the 67 nuclear tests have recovered well, though perhaps not as completely as some scientists have reported.

--- SENTENCE 304 ---
There is little data on the diversity of reef organisms and only recently there have been assessments of general reef condition.

--- SENTENCE 305 ---
With their low elevation (average elevation of 7 ft), the entire Marshall Island chain is in danger of being submerged with even moderate sea level rise from global climate change.

--- SENTENCE 306 ---
**Federated States of Micronesia Federated of Micronesia –** Reef condition throughout the FSM is generally good to excellent.

--- SENTENCE 307 ---
Most of the reefs around the low islands are quite healthy.

Reefs around the populated islands of Pohnpei, Chuuk, Kosrae, and Yap vary in condition, but are generally good with live coral cover ranging from 20-70%.

--- SENTENCE 309 ---
The primary human impacts come from fishing pressure and ship groundings.

--- SENTENCE 310 ---

**Temporal Trends Trends –**

--- SENTENCE 328 ---
In places where there has been credible long-term monitoring, there are alarming temporal trends.

--- SENTENCE 329 ---

**Spatial Trends –** Seven tables in the main report present what is known about the condition of coral reef ecosystems in the 13 jurisdictions.

**Expand and Strengthen Marine Protected Protected Areas (MPAs) (MPAs) –

--- SENTENCE 377 ---
** There is an urgent need to protect the most important reef habitats from further decline by strengthening and expanding a network of coral reef marine protected areas (MPAs) and notake reserves.

--- SENTENCE 378 ---
The goal was to protect at least 5% of all U.S. coral reefs and associated habitat types in each major island group and Florida with notake provisions by 2002, at least 10% by 2005, and at least 20% by 2010.

--- SENTENCE 379 ---
Until all coral reef ecosystem habitats have been mapped, the percentage of these reefs currently protected cannot be accurately calculated.

--- SENTENCE 380 ---
Significant new MPAs and no-take reserves have been established over the past several years off Florida, Puerto Rico, USVI, Hawai'i, CNMI, and in the Navassa, Palmyra Atoll, and Kingman Reef National Wildlife Refuges (see Table 10 for a full listing by area and percentage, Fig. 19).

--- SENTENCE 381 ---
But there is still a long way to go.

--- SENTENCE 382 ---
Currently, there is full no-take protection for 1,329 mi2 of U.S. coral reef ecosystems; in Palau, another 25.2 mi2 of reefs have full protection.

--- SENTENCE 383 ---
Three jurisdictions currently exceed the 2010 goal: the U.S. Remote Wildlife Refuges (30.3%), Guam (approximately 28%, and the Northwestern Hawaiian Island National Wildlife Refuge (21.4%).

--- SENTENCE 384 ---
With the exception of the USVI, elsewhere no-take protection is only 5% or less of the total reef ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 385 ---
Much has been done over the past few years by USCRTF agencies to strengthen MPAs, but current MPAs and new no-take areas cannot be effective without enforcement.

--- SENTENCE 386 ---
This critical need is recognized by all jurisdictional managers as well as the many authors and collaborators who helped prepare this report.

#### **Recommendations and Conclusions Conclusions**

Critical information is needed to conserve and protect U.S. coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 447 ---
Basic mapping has yet to be done for over 85% of all U.S. reefs.

--- SENTENCE 448 ---
As a result, data in this report referring to the area covered by coral reefs, including the percent under no-take provisions, are mostly estimates from a variety of sources.

--- SENTENCE 449 ---
The figures vary widely mostly because of inadequate and inaccurate base maps and charts.

--- SENTENCE 450 ---
Aside from ongoing mapping efforts, many reef areas need basic assessment and biotic inventories.

--- SENTENCE 451 ---
Comparable long-term monitoring needs to be sponsored and integrated across regions.

--- SENTENCE 452 ---
Managers of reefs with recognized high threats need more resources to mitigate impacts from degraded water and substrate quality, overfishing, invasive species, or other anthropogenic stresses.

--- SENTENCE 453 ---
They must be prepared to take bold conservation measures to reverse present trends.

--- SENTENCE 454 ---
To track changes in ecosystem health and evaluate the effectiveness of conservation measures, grants

to State and Territorial agencies need to be continued for the next 5-10 years.

--- SENTENCE 455 ---
Public awareness and education and efforts need to continue at a high level to encourage a new ethic of sustained use of coral reef ecosystems.

####

--- SENTENCE 456 ---
This report finds that:

- • U.S. coral reef areas are extensive.
- • Healthy reef ecosystems are critical for local and regional economies.
- • All jurisdictions still have some reefs in good to excellent health (Fig. 24).

--- SENTENCE 457 ---
These need conservation.
- • All shallow reefs near urbanized coasts are degraded to some extent.

--- SENTENCE 458 ---
These need restoration.
- • Areas next to densely populated shorelines generally have poorer water quality than those far from human habitation.

--- SENTENCE 459 ---
Where water quality is fair to poor, reef ecosystems are degraded.

--- SENTENCE 460 ---
Water quality needs to be improved in those areas, and measures taken to maintain the water quality of areas where reef condition is now deemed good to excellent.
- • Coastal development, runoff, and sedimentation have impacted reefs around most high islands.

--- SENTENCE 461 ---
This needs to be minimized.
- • Fishing pressure has been a primary factor impacting reef ecosystems for decades.

--- SENTENCE 462 ---
There is evidence that overfishing has changed ecosystem structure and function.

--- SENTENCE 463 ---
Different and effective methods of management need to be implemented.
- • Remote reefs with little coastal development, good water quality, and low fishing pressure are in excellent health, as characterized by many large fish and generally high species diversityy.

--- SENTENCE 464 ---
These need to be studied and preserved.
- • Marine refuges with no-take provisions produce more and larger fish.

--- SENTENCE 465 ---
With enough time, they can conserve reef communities and longlived species, producing trophy-sized apex predators.

--- SENTENCE 466 ---
More no-take areas need to be implemented within MPAs to reach the USCRTF goal of 20% protection.
- • Some existing marine protected areas are not protecting reefs.

--- SENTENCE 467 ---
Regulations within these need to be strengthened and adequately enforced.
- •

--- SENTENCE 468 ---
It needs to be expanded and made more effective.

NATIONAL SUMMARY: BACKGROUND BACKGROUND Donna D. Turgeon and Rebecca G. Asch Turgeon and Rebecca Asch Donna D. AschDonna D. Turgeon and Rebecca G. Asch Donna D. and Rebecca G. Asch**

This is the first in a series of biennial reports on the *State of Coral Reef Ecosystems of the United States and the Pacific Freely Associated States*.

--- SENTENCE 474 ---
The National Ocean Service led the development, but it is the product of the 38 coauthors, and they are responsible for its content.

--- SENTENCE 475 ---
It is the result of a nationally-coordinated effort by the USCRTF to assess the condition of coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 476 ---
The working group was comprised of the USCRTF Governors' Points of Contact, members from all of the USCRTF working groups, and the managers and scientists from participating Federal agencies and U.S. States, Commonwealths, and Territories, and the Pacific Freely Associated States27 .

--- SENTENCE 477 ---
Coral reefs are the most diverse, productive, and economically important habitats found in tropical and semitropical oceans.

--- SENTENCE 478 ---
But little specific scientific information is known about the function, structure, and condition of these ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 479 ---
Most have yet to be mapped and their biotic resources inventoried.

--- SENTENCE 480 ---
This report is the beginning of gathering consistent, comparable scientific information on all the reefs in the United States and the Freely Associated States, so the condition of these resources can be reliably assessed and conserved.

--- SENTENCE 481 ---
Coral reefs discussed in this report are found along the Western Atlantic and the continental shelf of the northern Gulf of Mexico, and around Caribbean

and Pacific islands (Fig. 25).

--- SENTENCE 482 ---
Western Atlantic and Caribbean shallow-water coral reefs are off the State of Florida, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the Territory of the U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI), and the Navassa Island National Wildlife Refuge.

--- SENTENCE 483 ---
Deeper reefs in the Northern Gulf of Mexico and the Western Atlantic are also covered.

--- SENTENCE 484 ---
Shallow-water reefs off the U.S. Pacific islands are extensive and include the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, the Territories of American Samoa and Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), and seven remote, unincorporated Pacific island areas28.

--- SENTENCE 485 ---
Also included in this report are Indo-Pacific reefs around the Freely Associated States.

--- SENTENCE 486 ---
These are among the most biologically diverse coral reef ecosystems in the world.

--- SENTENCE 487 ---
With their habitat complexity and species richness, coral reefs protect coastlines from storms and are a source of food and recreation for millions of people.

--- SENTENCE 488 ---
Many near-shore coral reef ecosystems are inextricably linked to coastal human populations, water-based activities, and economics.

--- SENTENCE 489 ---
In general, coral reefs provide livelihoods for hundreds of thousands of people in all U.S. affiliated areas.

--- SENTENCE 490 ---
However, human activity is rapidly degrading many near-shore reefs.

--- SENTENCE 491 ---
If coral reef ecosystems are to continue to support abundant, diverse wildlife,

> as well as the humans that appreciate and depend on them, then they need to be conserved.

--- SENTENCE 492 ---
The mapping, assessment, monitoring, and other conservation activities presented in this report are the beginning of a comprehensive management strategy to conserve reef resources and to report biennially on the effectiveness of those conservation measures.

--- SENTENCE 493 ---

The rest of this Background discusses topics the managers of coral reefs consider important for the context of statements they make on the condition of corals and other aspects of this valuable aquatic ecosystem.

#### Coral Reefs

Although deep-sea coral reefs with three-dimensional structure exist in cooler waters, the familiar reefs are in the shallow, clear turquoise-blue waters of tropical and subtropical seas.

--- SENTENCE 501 ---
Reefs generally sit on continental shelves and submerged bases of volcanoes in depths ranging from emergent on low

tides to around 150 ft. Shallow-water coral reef development is optimum where sea temperatures are warmest, between 30°N and 30°S, which roughly coincides with the 20°C (68°F) **isotherm** (lines drawn on a map that connect points of equal temperature).

--- SENTENCE 502 ---
Most corals cannot survive temperatures much below 60-65°F (16-18°C) even for a few weeks.

--- SENTENCE 503 ---
Coral reefs are the largest biological structures on earth, with millions of coral colonies, each made up of thousands of tiny interconnected corals.

--- SENTENCE 504 ---
There are three general types of reefs, with many gradations and variations (Fig. 26)<sup>6</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 505 ---
Fringing reefs

grow seaward from the rocky shores of islands and continents.

--- SENTENCE 506 ---
Barrier reefs are parallel to shorelines of continents and islands and are separated from land by shallow lagoons.

--- SENTENCE 507 ---
Barrier reefs off oceanic islands originate from fringing reefs in a process that is similar to the formation of atolls.

--- SENTENCE 508 ---
Atolls are ring- or horseshoe-shaped coral reefs and coral islets surrounding a lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 509 ---
An atoll lagoon is formed when the volcano that is the reef's foundation sinks into the ocean, leaving only the upward-growing reef near sea level.

--- SENTENCE 510 ---
Atoll and barrier reef lagoons are usually connected to the open sea by breaks or passes through the reef, and may hold clusters of isolated patch reefs (small reefs that were

gradually separated from associated land masses because of island subsidence or rising sea levels).

--- SENTENCE 511 ---
In addition to shallow reefs, certain corals can also form reef-like structures or **banks** in deeper waters.

--- SENTENCE 512 ---
These structures may play similar roles to shallow reefs, but they have been little studied and are generally not included in this report.

--- SENTENCE 513 ---
The United States and over 100 other countries claim sovereignty over coral reefs (Birkeland 1997a).

--- SENTENCE 514 ---
Spalding *et al.* (2001) estimated the area covered by shallow coral reefs (less than 200 ft.) worldwide to be 109,800 mi² (284,300 km²).

--- SENTENCE 515 ---
Their estimate of shallow reefs comprises less than 1.2% of the continental shelf area and only 0.9% of the world's oceans.

--- SENTENCE 516 ---
Reefs in sovereign U.S. waters cover an estimated 7,607 mi² (19,702.4 km², Fig.

!

--- SENTENCE 517 ---
The numbers were computed using informmation from Hunter 1995, FMRI/NOAA 1998, Ault *et al.* 2001, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission 2001, Kendall *et al.* 2001, S. Gittings pers.

--- SENTENCE 518 ---
comm., and S. White pers.

--- SENTENCE 519 ---
Estimates for the reefs off the Freely Associated States range from 4,479-31,470 mi2 (11,600 81,500 km2 , Holthus *et al.* 1993, Maragos and Holthus 1999, Spalding *et al.* 2001).

####

--- SENTENCE 520 ---
**Reef Ecosystems Reef Ecosystems**

**Ecosystems** are composed of biological communities and habitats.

--- SENTENCE 521 ---
**Biological communities** are interacting populations of individual species.

--- SENTENCE 522 ---
Coral reef ecosystems include the species residing in these habitat types.

--- SENTENCE 523 ---
They also include aquatic residents of associated sand, macroalgae, seagrass, and mangrove habitats.

--- SENTENCE 524 ---
Species have specialized roles (**niches)** within habitats.

--- SENTENCE 525 ---
Basically, organisms can be grouped into three general categories – **planktonic** (floating), **benthic** (bottom dwelling), or **nectonic** (swimming).

!

--- SENTENCE 526 ---
Crustose coralline algae (Photo: James Maragos).

--- SENTENCE 527 ---
An ecosystem includes all the energy, material/ nutrient cycling, and behavioral interactions, linking organisms in a community together and with their environment (Smith 1992).

--- SENTENCE 528 ---
Monitoring components of coral reef ecosystems are key to both understanding their structure and function and wisely managing reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 529 ---
This includes biological factors such as species abundance, size, distributions, diversity, and human-use patterns, along with non-biological factors such as coastal development, sedimentation, and pollution.

#### **Corals and Reef Communities Communities**

Corals are ancient animals that evolved into the modern reef-building forms over the last 25 million years (Allen and Steene 1996).

--- SENTENCE 530 ---
Coral polyp (Photo: James McVey).

initially appeared as solitary forms in fossils more than 400 million years ago.

--- SENTENCE 531 ---
The primary building blocks of a reef are polyps of **stony** coral species (also called **scleractinian** or **hermatypic** corals).

--- SENTENCE 532 ---
Each **polyp** is generally **sessile** (attached to the substrate), with a small cylindrical body and prey-capturing tentacles surrounding the opening or mouth (Fig 28).

--- SENTENCE 533 ---
The polyps of stony corals deposit a calcium carbonate skeletal cup around themselves.

--- SENTENCE 534 ---
A coral reef is comprised of millions of these calcified polyps making up individual coral heads.

--- SENTENCE 535 ---
Coral heads are often cemented together by **coralline** (coral-like, calcareous) algae (Fig. 29).

--- SENTENCE 536 ---
**Symbiotic**30 photosynthetic, single-celled algae, called **zooxanthellae** live in the tissues of each stony coral polyp.

--- SENTENCE 537 ---
Reef-building corals cannot live without them.

--- SENTENCE 538 ---
They depend on these microscopic plants for part of their nutrition, so are limited by their symbiont requirements to the maximum depth light penetrates in clear, oceanic waters (around 150 ft).

--- SENTENCE 539 ---
This symbiosis enhances the growth rate and calcium deposition of shallow-water stony corals and contributes toward coral reefs being the most diverse marine ecosystems on earth.

--- SENTENCE 540 ---
Organisms within coral reef communities can be divided into four main groups.31 First, the **epibenthos** (sessile organisms, the living substrate) provides the complex structure of the reef itself.

--- SENTENCE 541 ---
These are the coralline and fleshy algae, hard and soft corals, and sponges.

--- SENTENCE 542 ---
Second, **plankton** (tiny floating plants and animals, most are microscopic) provides food for the reef **filter feeders**32.

--- SENTENCE 543 ---
Third, the **suprabenthos** are the larger mobile animals that swim over and around the reef.

--- SENTENCE 544 ---
These are the

--- SENTENCE 557 ---
Based on that, Reaka-Kudla (1997) estimated the 'true number of species on global coral reefs is at least 950,000.'

--- SENTENCE 558 ---
Using another broad assumption, including the premise that only 10% of the organisms on coral reefs have been described, Spalding *et al.*  (2001) estimated a global total of 1-3 million species inhabit coral reefs and associated habitats.

--- SENTENCE 559 ---
Sand, algae, seagrass, and mangrove habitats are integral parts of the reef ecosystem, providing critical nursery areas and essential habitat for reef invertebrates and fish (Fig. 31).

--- SENTENCE 560 ---
Marine organisms rely on the different habitats of the coral ecosystem at different life stages, and the loss or degradation of any of those habitats can have serious effects on the reef.

--- SENTENCE 561 ---
Corals, most fishes, and other reef organisms have planktonic larval stages.

--- SENTENCE 562 ---
Floating with ocean currents, these larvae link different ecosystems, often over large distances.

--- SENTENCE 563 ---
Therefore, the health of a reef partly depends on the condition of ecosystems 'upstream' from which reefs derive **recruits** (juvenile and adult organisms that settle out of the plankton or migrate into the reef community).

--- SENTENCE 564 ---
A number of reef-associated species have been **herbivores** (those that feed on plants), **coral** listed as threatened or endangered under the U.S. **livores** (those that feed on corals), **carnivores** Endangered Species Act (Fig. 32).

--- SENTENCE 565 ---
These include (those that eat other animals), and **detritivores** all the sea turtles35, and the Hawaiian monk seal (those that feed on dead and decaying matter).

#### Cultural Value of Reef Ecosystems

Coral reefs are a significant part of a country's natural heritage.

--- SENTENCE 586 ---
Some of the largest individual coral colonies found on reefs today were thriving centuries before human colonization.

--- SENTENCE 587 ---
Rivaling old growth forests, well-developed reefs reflect thousands of years of growth and development.

--- SENTENCE 588 ---
For centuries, coral reefs have provided sustenance and shoreline protection to indigenous peoples.

--- SENTENCE 589 ---
Uses of reef resources are woven into the social and cultural fabric of coastal communities.

--- SENTENCE 590 ---
A 'hukilau' is a traditional Hawaiian fish gathering method (Photo: Jeff Alexander).

!

--- SENTENCE 591 ---
[](_page_29_Picture_10.jpeg)

provide three general types of fishing opportunities: **artisanal** (small village-based fisheries for personal or community consumption), **recreational** (fishing for sport or pleasure), and **commercial** (fishing for commerce through sale, barter, or trade).

--- SENTENCE 592 ---
Native peoples of the Pacific Islands have a strong cultural and economic dependence on coral reefs and marine resources.

--- SENTENCE 593 ---
Each island or island group had its own language, customs, local government, and a reef tenure system controlled at the village level.

--- SENTENCE 594 ---
One example of reef tenure systems still operating in Pacific Island rural regions is the traditional harvest system in Hawai'i<sup>38</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 595 ---
Prior to the 1800s, there were social and cultural controls on fishing with a strictly enforced code of conduct (Fig. 33).

--- SENTENCE 596 ---
Harvest management was not based on the amount of fish, but on identifying the specific times and places where fishing could occur.

--- SENTENCE 597 ---
This kept the fishers from disturbing the

basic processes and habitats of important food resources (Friedlander *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 598 ---
In 1994, the Hawai'i Legislature created a process for designating community-based subsistence fishing areas.

--- SENTENCE 599 ---
These are being created on Moloka'i, Kaua'i, and Hawai'i.

--- SENTENCE 600 ---
One community, residing in the Ho'olehua Hawaiian Homesteads on the northwest coast of Moloka'i, depends on food from the ocean for much of their diet.

## Economic Value of Reef Ecosystems

Coral reefs are an integral component of local and regional economies.

--- SENTENCE 625 ---
Reefs provide protection from storm wave action, reducing erosion, property damage, and loss of life.

--- SENTENCE 626 ---
Tourists at Sanibel Island Beach, Florida (Photo: South Florida Water Management District).

!

--- SENTENCE 627 ---
[](_page_30_Picture_8.jpeg)

protect highly productive coastal wetland and mangrove habitats, as well as coastal communities, ports, and harbors.

--- SENTENCE 628 ---
Costanza *et al.* (1997) estimated reef habitats globally provide \$375 billion each year to humans from living resources (fish and other food) and ecological services (tourism and coastal protection).

--- SENTENCE 629 ---
Cesar (1996) calculated the cost

over a 25-year period of destroying 1 km<sup>2</sup> (about 247 acres) of reef ranged between \$0.6-2.5 million when the value of fishery, tourism, and protection was considered.

--- SENTENCE 630 ---
The environment and the economy are inextricably linked, making the management and protection of coral reef resources critical.

--- SENTENCE 631 ---
Coral reefs support a burgeoning coastal population and are a Mecca for tourists, adding millions of seasonal and temporary visitors (Table 1).

--- SENTENCE 632 ---
The U.S. Census (2002) reported over 10.5 million people resided in U.S. coastal counties and islands adjacent to shallow coral reef ecosystems in 2000, with another 203,000 residents living on the islands of the Pacific Freely Associated States.

--- SENTENCE 633 ---
Each year, 45 million visitors<sup>39</sup> are drawn to U.S. seaside and live-aboard accommodations to fish, dive, and otherwise enjoy coral

reefs (Fig. 34).

--- SENTENCE 634 ---
Another 113,000 tourists visit the tropical isles of the Pacific Freely Associated States.

--- SENTENCE 635 ---
The only region where a survey and market analysis of reef use has been done is the four-county area of South Florida<sup>40</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 636 ---
When the seasonal and temporary visitors are considered, the region's 5.09 million residents are increased to a functional daily population<sup>41</sup> between 5.56-5.92 million, depending on the season (Johns et al. 2001).

--- SENTENCE 637 ---
According to those authors, South Florida residents and visitors spent 18.1 million person-days fishing and diving around natural coral reefs as well as viewing them from glassbottom boats.

--- SENTENCE 638 ---
They used these

and monetary compensation for past use of several atolls for nuclear weapons testing.

--- SENTENCE 656 ---
Bioprospecting (the harvest of biological organisms for medical and other applications) wildlife found on coral reefs offers economic promise.

--- SENTENCE 657 ---
Already, biochemicals produced by many reef species are being used in health care products (e.g., sun blocks), medical procedures (e.g., bone grafts), and pharmaceuticals for treating viral infections and other medical conditions.

--- SENTENCE 658 ---
Ongoing medical research indicates that other biochemicals extracted from reef-associated species may offer treatments for leukemia, skin cancer, and other diseases (Birkeland 1997a).

--- SENTENCE 659 ---
There are concerns among coral reef managers that it may be a new threat to U.S. coral reef ecosystems, so they caution that bioprospecting must be carefully managed.

U.S. coral reefs share many problems with reefs around the world.

--- SENTENCE 661 ---
Coastal residents and the influx of tourists place increasing demands on these complex and fragile ecosystems.

## NATIONAL SUMMARY: ENVIRONMENTAL PRESSURES

In general, there are two types of environmental pressures on reefs (or any ecosystem) – natural forces and human impacts.

--- SENTENCE 708 ---
Natural forces have shaped the distribution of coral reefs over the ages.

--- SENTENCE 709 ---
A broad range of temperature and sea-level changes occur over hundreds and thousands of years.

--- SENTENCE 710 ---
Diseases, storms, and predation are more intense but have shorter-term impacts.

--- SENTENCE 711 ---
On top of natural forces, human-induced pressures come from a myriad of activities (A. Bentivoglio pers.

--- SENTENCE 712 ---
These include the following.

- Coastal development with the resulting runoff and sedimentation
- Chemical water pollution (toxic contaminants and nutrient enrichment)
- Over-harvesting of fishery resources and destruction of reefs and associated habitats
- Direct harvest of coral colonies and live reef fish
- Ship and boat groundings and anchor damage
- Tourism and recreation

- Alien invasive species
- Marine debris

Every coral reef ecosystem under U.S. jurisdiction has suffered from human disturbance to some degree.

--- SENTENCE 713 ---
Because they are close to population centers, portions of reefs off Florida, Puerto Rico, the USVI, the Main Hawaiian Islands, Guam, and the CNMI have been degraded by multiple environmental and human-induced stresses.

--- SENTENCE 714 ---
In contrast, the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary, Navassa Island, the remote Pacific Island refuges, and the NWHI, have few human-induced pressures and remain relatively pristine.

#### **Global Climate Change and Coral and Coral and Coral Bleaching BleachingBleaching**

All coral reef managers considered global climate change a major, yet largely unmanageable threat to the survival of coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 762 ---
Managers from Florida, the RMI, and Palau, however, consider global climate warming and coral

bleaching a major threat to their local reefs.

--- SENTENCE 763 ---
Those from Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, CNMI, the Federated States of Micronesia, and the U.S. remote insular reefs considered these factors a medium threat (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 764 ---
According to the Third Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC 2001), the 1990s was the

warmest decade of the century and 1998 the warmest year on record (1861-2000).

--- SENTENCE 765 ---
In the 1990s, concentrations of greenhouse gases and aerosols reached the highest recorded levels since the preindustrial era.

--- SENTENCE 766 ---
In its conclusions, the Panel blamed human activities for increasing atmospheric concentrations of key greenhouse gases53, primarily from the combustion of fossil fuels, agriculture, and coastal development.

--- SENTENCE 767 ---
This *Third Assessment Report* presents the scientific consensus for changes over the next century.

--- SENTENCE 768 ---
CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere are projected to range between 540-970 ppm in 2100, more than doubling the

- pre-industrial age average of 280 ppm and well above the 2000 average of 368 ppm.
- • Globally averaged, sea surface temperatures are projected to increase 2.5-10.4o F (1.4-5.8o C) between 1990 and 2100.
- • Globally averaged, annual precipitation is projected to increase during the 21st century; regionally, both increases and decreases of 5 20% are projected.
- • Global mean sea level is projected to rise by 0.3-2.9 ft between the years of 1990 and 2100, with regional variation.

--- SENTENCE 769 ---
With confidence, the IPCC (2001) predicts ecological productivity and biodiversity will be affected by climate change and sea-level rise, increasing the risk of extinction for some vulnerable species.

--- SENTENCE 770 ---
Changes in sea level from long-term climate

change, have direct implications for coral reefs, as well as human populations that inhabit islands or shores with little elevation (Fig.

--- SENTENCE 771 ---
There could be severe social and economic effects, as resources critical to island and coastal populations would also be at risk (beaches, freshwater, fisheries, atolls, and wildlife habitat).

--- SENTENCE 772 ---
Using historical evidence,

Shinn (1988) showed changes in reef communities as a result of sea level rise and flooding of shallow inshore bays off southeastern Florida (Florida Key West to Palm Beach).

--- SENTENCE 773 ---
Increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases are expected to change the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme events.

--- SENTENCE 774 ---
There will be more hot days, more heat waves, more heavy precipitation, and fewer cold days.

--- SENTENCE 775 ---
Besides inundating low-lying coastal areas from the melting polar ice, potential climate change impacts include increased sedimentation of coral reefs caused by drought followed by heavy rains.

--- SENTENCE 776 ---
The rising sea level could eliminate deeper reefs because the sunlight needed for photosynthesis would be too low.

#### **Diseases DiseasesDiseases**

Where diseases have wreaked havoc – Florida, Puerto Rico, and the USVI – the coral reef managers consider disease a prime threat to reef health (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 802 ---
Over the past two decades, there has been a worldwide increase in reports of disease affecting coral reef organisms.

--- SENTENCE 803 ---
In the Western Atlantic, disease outbreaks have contributed to die-offs of seagrasses, corals, sea fans, sea urchins, sponges, fish, and other organisms.

--- SENTENCE 804 ---
Disease has modified the structure and composition of reefs by removing common and locally abundant species.

--- SENTENCE 805 ---
Indirect evidence suggests that disease outbreaks in marine environments are becoming more frequent (Harvell *et al.*  1999).

--- SENTENCE 806 ---
Diseases are reported from Pacific reefs, but the incidence is lower than in the Caribbean (Work and Rameyer 2001).

--- SENTENCE 807 ---
Coral disease appears to be more prevalent near population centers.

--- SENTENCE 808 ---
Changing environmental conditions from climate variability coupled with human impacts may weaken corals, making them more vulnerable to disease (Green and Bruckner 2000).

--- SENTENCE 809 ---
Coral diseases have been recorded by 54 different nations, with most records (66%) from the wider Caribbean, including reefs in Florida, Puerto Rico, and USVI (Green and Bruckner 2000).

--- SENTENCE 810 ---
Of 29 diseases reported in the literature, about 80% of the reports are for white-band disease, black-band disease, and white plague.

!

--- SENTENCE 811 ---
Black-band disease devours a knobby brain coral over a one-week period (Photo: Andrew Bruckner).

--- SENTENCE 812 ---

--- SENTENCE 813 ---
Black-band disease, first identified in 1972, occurs at low levels on most Western Atlantic reefs and may increase seasonally during warm periods (Fig. 45).

--- SENTENCE 814 ---
Although black-band disease occurs worldwide, severe outbreaks have only been reported from the Caribbean, including U.S. reefs (Antonius 1973, Edmunds 1991, Kuta and

Richardson 1997, Bruckner 1999).

--- SENTENCE 815 ---
White plague disease was first reported in the Florida Keys (Dustan 1977).

--- SENTENCE 816 ---
A new, more virulent form (plague type II) emerged in the mid 1990s, and since then outbreaks have occurred in the Florida Keys, southwestern Puerto Rico, Culebra Island, and parts of the USVI (Bruckner and Bruckner 1997, Richardson 1998, Hernandez 2001, Miller *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 817 ---
Particularly severe outbreaks were also observed in the spring and summer of 2001, impacting the important massive reef-building corals55.

--- SENTENCE 818 ---
White plague may have severe impacts on reef ecosystems, as this disease affects a large number of coral species and kills tissue at rates up to 0.8 inches2 a day (2 cm2 /day).

--- SENTENCE 819 ---
In a growing list of new coral diseases and other syndromes, yellow-blotch disease is of particular concern.

--- SENTENCE 820 ---
This disease selectively infects slowgrowing, massive corals, some of the most important reef-builders found on Caribbean reefs today.

--- SENTENCE 821 ---
Once infected, the disease slowly kills the colony over several years (Green and Bruckner 2000).

--- SENTENCE 822 ---
In addition to scleractinian coral diseases, scientists have recently identified diseases and **pathogens** (disease-causing organisms) in colonial **anemones** and **soft corals** (soft-bodied sessile organisms that are in the same class as stony corals).

--- SENTENCE 823 ---

--- SENTENCE 827 ---
An invertebrate disease decimated the long-spined sea urchin (*Diadema antillarum*) in the early 1980s (Fig. 46).

--- SENTENCE 828 ---
In the Caribbean Sea and Western Atlantic, populations of mature urchins were reduced to around 3% of their original size (Lessios *et al.*  1984, Vicente and Goenaga 1984, Lessios 1988, Ritchie *et al.* 2000).

--- SENTENCE 829 ---
Long-spined sea urchin populations have been slow to recover, possibly because remaining individuals are too far apart to ensure successful fertilization of gametes that are broadcast into the water (Levitan 1991).

--- SENTENCE 830 ---
In some locations, particularly the shallow reef crests and fore-reefs, urchin numbers remain especially low, only about 1% of the pre-1983 levels.

--- SENTENCE 831 ---
Ecological impacts on the reefs from the die-off of the urchins have been profound.

--- SENTENCE 832 ---
Urchins are herbivores, eating **macroalgae** (large attached algae or seaweed).

--- SENTENCE 833 ---
After the die-off, there was a dramatic increase of algal cover, since grazing on the algae was much reduced.

--- SENTENCE 834 ---
Some areas recovered better from this than others.

--- SENTENCE 835 ---
In the Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary, algal populations returned to prior levels within two years, perhaps due to an increase in other herbivores (Gittings and Bright 1986).

--- SENTENCE 836 ---
But the rest of the Caribbean has yet to recover.

--- SENTENCE 837 ---
For most U.S. reef ecosystems, the shift in coral-algal balance was further exacerbated by a die-off of elkhorn and staghorn corals.

--- SENTENCE 838 ---
Once the coral died from other causes, algae took over.

Long-spined sea urchin (Photo: Emma Hickerson).

--- SENTENCE 841 ---
(2001) postulated the shift from a healthy coral to a fleshy macroalgae-dominated system results from a combination of factors that make the system vulnerable to events triggering the shift.

--- SENTENCE 842 ---
These factors include increased nutrient loading from land-based runoff and discharges and intensive fishing which reduces the numbers of large fish and subsequently the smaller herbivorous species (Aronson and Precht 2000, Scheffer *et al.*  2001).

--- SENTENCE 843 ---
Once herbivorous fish became rare, the reefs rapidly became overgrown by fleshy brown algae.

--- SENTENCE 844 ---
Scheffer *et al.* (2001) commented that this change will be difficult to reverse for two reasons: 1) mature algae are less palatable to herbivores and 2) algae-covered substrates prevent settlement of coral larvae.

#### **Tropical Storms Storms**

With eight major hurricanes in the past 20 years nearly exterminating shallow-water *Acropora* coral populations, USVI managers consider tropical storms a major threat to their reef systems; another five managers from U.S. regions consider tropical storms a medium-level concern (Table 2, Fig. 47).

--- SENTENCE 845 ---
If global climate change is underway and hurricanes occur with more frequency, then all the nation's managers have concerns that reefs would not have sufficient recovery time.

--- SENTENCE 846 ---
Reefs grow in areas subject to hurricanes and typhoons.

--- SENTENCE 847 ---
In general, reefs have great structural resilience and recover from storms.

--- SENTENCE 848 ---
There is also good evidence that that such disturbances help keep reef diversity high (Rogers 1993, J. Ogden pers.

--- SENTENCE 849 ---
For example, sand and rubble keys and coral islets on atolls are notorious for forming and eroding during tropical storms, as fragments break loose and are deposited toward land or in

**ENVIRONMENTAL PRESSURES ENVIRONMENTAL PRESSURES**

!

--- SENTENCE 850 ---
The shape of coral rock terraces in Guam reflect the dominance of encrusting and low profile growth forms (Photo: Ben Mieremet).

--- SENTENCE 851 ---
lagoons (Maragos *et al.* 1973).

--- SENTENCE 852 ---
Hurricanes may also be beneficial because they fragment fast-growing branching corals that monopolize the substrate, freeing space for the slower-growing, massive species.

--- SENTENCE 853 ---
In the Caribbean and American Samoa, hurricanes make landfall on average every 15-20 years.

--- SENTENCE 854 ---
But the CNMI and Guam are hit by about half the typhoons that develop in the Pacific because they lie in the Western Pacific monsoon trough.

--- SENTENCE 855 ---
Guam has felt the impact of 52 major typhoons in the last 48 years.

--- SENTENCE 856 ---
When typhoons pass nearby, the reefs receive the full impact of heavy wave action.

--- SENTENCE 857 ---
Contrary to what might be expected, typhoons in this region affect reefs to a lesser extent (Randall and Eldredge 1977) than hurricanes in the Caribbean (Tilmant *et al.* 1994) because the normal heavy wave action in the Pacific regularly removes the relatively fragile vertical branches.

--- SENTENCE 858 ---
By doing this, the reef structure favors the encrusting or massive growth forms (Fig. 48).

--- SENTENCE 859 ---
Typhoons, hurricanes, or cyclones have less impact on low-growing encrusting corals than they do on high-profile forms.

--- SENTENCE 860 ---
Areas such as American Samoa and Palau, where storms are less frequent, have the higher-growing forms (Hubbard 1997).

#### Coastal Development and Runoff

Reef managers from nine regions consider coastal development, runoff, and sedimentation major threats to their coral reef ecosystems (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 861 ---
These areas include coral reefs off large continental population centers and close-to-shore

reefs off urbanized islands (Fig 49).

--- SENTENCE 862 ---
Near-shore reefs off high islands with relatively low human habitation<sup>56</sup> also experience substantial runoff and sedimentation during tropical storms.

--- SENTENCE 863 ---
In the United States, over 10.5 million people live in coastal counties and on islands near coral reefs, particularly in Florida, Puerto Rico, and much of the Main Hawaiian Islands.

--- SENTENCE 864 ---
The Pacific Freely Associated States has another 203,000 island residents.

--- SENTENCE 865 ---
Infrastructure development is necessary to support coastal residents and the expanding reef tourism industry.

--- SENTENCE 866 ---
This includes a myriad of activities: filling in wetlands to increase land area, dredging sand to replenish beaches, building causeways and bridges over existing reef habitats, dredging channels, erecting marinas and other support facilities along tidal shorelines, and destroying upland vegetation.

--- SENTENCE 867 ---
The impact of increasing human population on reef condition can be both acute and chronic.

--- SENTENCE 868 ---
Reefs and related habitats suffer acute physical damage during construction, when such activities such as dredging to maintain deep-water draft for ships, erecting shoreside docks, and building marinas near or over coral reefs are in progress.

--- SENTENCE 869 ---
The resulting runoff, plumes of sediment, and **turbid** (discolored, opaque) water from these activities can destroy a much broader area of reef habitat.

--- SENTENCE 870 ---
After coastal development is completed, the structures that were built and the activities related

Wide variations in salinity that damage near-shore reefs could become more commonplace if global climate brings more storms and flooding.

Beaches erode from storms and natural wave action.

Dredging to replace sand on bathing beaches is a most destructive activity.

Silt from dredging activities buries corals and suffocates sensitive reef organisms.

Replenishment degrades water quality during the operation.

Not only costly, it affects everything within the areas where the sand is taken from as well as where it is deposited, and must be repeated every 5-10 years.

--- SENTENCE 897 ---

#### Coastal Pollution

Optimum coral reef development is strongly correlated with clean, clear waters.

--- SENTENCE 901 ---
Reef managers from eight jurisdictions consider coastal pollution (e.g., excess nutrients, toxic contaminants, and for the Marshall Islands, radiation) a high threat to their coastal ecosystems (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 902 ---
The USEPA estimates that 60% of water pollution comes from **non-point sources** of contamination (input from a general area rather than a single point like a discharge pipe) such as storm-water runoff from urban areas and agriculture (Eichenberg 1999).

--- SENTENCE 903 ---
More than 75% of the pollutants entering oceans are from non-point, land-based sources (YOTO 1998).

--- SENTENCE 904 ---

--- SENTENCE 905 ---
All of these changed the structure of adjacent reefs (Woodbury 1946, Dawson 1959, Maragos 1993).

--- SENTENCE 906 ---
At Chuuk, Peleliu, Enewetak, and Kwajalein, for example.

At Majuro, Enewetak, Bikini, Tarawa, and Johnston islands.
