--- SENTENCE 1926 ---
Many jurisdictions monitor coastal near-shore waters for dissolved oxygen, turbidity, fecal coliform, enterococcus, oil and grease, selected toxic metals, ammonia, nitrate/nitrite, and pH (e.g., American Samoa, Guam, CNMI).

--- SENTENCE 1927 ---
As an example of the longevity and breadth of EPA prescribed monitoring, the Puerto Rico Environmental Quality Board has been monitoring physical, chemical, and bacteriological parameters at 88 stations along its coastal zone since 1982.

--- SENTENCE 1928 ---
Because this monitoring follows prescribed methodologies, the data should be comparable and useful in determining temporal trends in water quality.

--- SENTENCE 1929 ---
This testing, however, is for parameters affecting human health, some of which may be more useful than others for determining coral reef health.

--- SENTENCE 1930 ---
A few jurisdictions go beyond this set of parameters.

--- SENTENCE 1931 ---
They also monitor for toxic metals and organic chemicals104.

--- SENTENCE 1932 ---
With NOAA and the EPA, the FKNMS has been monitoring an array of water quality contaminants at fixed stations.

--- SENTENCE 1933 ---
To track changes in water quality affecting coral reefs

nationally, the Coral Reef Program is encouraging the addition of certain key water quality indicators to its National Coral Reef Monitoring Network.

--- SENTENCE 1934 ---
Because the water quality data for some of the jurisdictions covered in this report were qualitative or not available, spatial and temporal trends for water quality cannot be assessed nationally.

--- SENTENCE 1935 ---
Managers from the FKNMS, Puerto Rico, and American Samoa, however, indicated that within their coral reef ecosystems, water quality had been deteriorating over the past decade.

--- SENTENCE 1936 ---
Not surprisingly, managers of reefs distant from human populations (the FGBNMS, the NWHI, and the U.S. remote insular reefs) all indicated that their reef systems had excellent water quality.

--- SENTENCE 1937 ---
The remainder had varying degrees of water quality problems within their jurisdiction.

--- SENTENCE 1938 ---
The quantity and quality of reef organisms depends on water quality.

--- SENTENCE 1939 ---
Areas next to densely populated shorelines generally have poorer water quality than areas far from human habitation.

--- SENTENCE 1940 ---
The impact on the diversity and abundance of organisms in those degraded areas is generally lower, correlating directly with water quality and habitat condition.

**Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) and No-Take Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) and No-Take Reserves ReservesReserves –** As of 2002, there were 120 (35 Federal and 85 State/Territorial) MPAs in the United States and 15 MPAs in the Pacific Freely Associated States (Table 10).

--- SENTENCE 1954 ---
These provide variable levels of protection to the reefs, ranging from open harvest access to full enforcement of no-take provisions.

--- SENTENCE 1955 ---
Coral reef MPAs include National Marine Sanctuaries; National Parks, Seashores, Monuments, and Wildlife Refuges; and National Estuarine Research Reserves and Estuary Program areas.

--- SENTENCE 1956 ---
There are also State, Territory, and Commonwealth Parks,

Fishery Management Plans have also designated MPAs for habitat protection, rebuilding fish stocks, and for critical habitats of threatened or endangered species.

--- SENTENCE 1957 ---
Conservation Areas, and Reserves.

--- SENTENCE 1958 ---
U.S. marine areas protected by no-take provisions cover 1,329 mi2 (3,442 km2 ), while another 25.2 mi2 (65.3 km2 ) of no-take reserves protect Palauan reefs.

--- SENTENCE 1959 ---
Realistically, the percentage protected by notake provisions within most jurisdictions most likely will change when the coral reefs are entirely mapped.

--- SENTENCE 1960 ---
For this report, it was deemed impossible to calculate the total reef area protected by no-take provisions across all jurisdictions because over 85% of reef-associated benthic habitats have yet to be mapped105.

--- SENTENCE 1961 ---
The authors of this report concluded that state-of-the-art shallow-water mapping needs to be completed before this could be done with confidence.

--- SENTENCE 1962 ---
A synthesis of more than 100 studies of reserves worldwide shows protection from fishing leads to increased biomass, abundance, average size, and species diversity (Halpern in press).

--- SENTENCE 1963 ---
Because marine reserves contain more and larger fish, protected populations can produce more offspring.

--- SENTENCE 1964 ---
(2001) demonstrated that reserves serve as sheltered nurseries.

--- SENTENCE 1965 ---
Large fish move to waters adjacent to the reserve through density-dependent spillover of juveniles and adults106.

#### **Coral Reef Governance and Management Reef Governance and Management –**

Federal, State, Territorial, and Commonwealth agencies are responsible for the conservation of living marine resources, including fisheries, marine mammals, and endangered and threatened species within the **Exclusive Economic Zone**<sup>110</sup>

--- SENTENCE 1986 ---
Legislation provides the authority for managing coral reef ecosystems (Appendix IV).

--- SENTENCE 1987 ---
These include Fishery Management Plans, management of MPAs, and protection of reef species and resources of concern111.

--- SENTENCE 1988 ---
Fishery Management Plans written by

--- SENTENCE 1989 ---
Fisheries Management Councils govern commercial fishing throughout the EEZ, regulating harvests by annual catch quotas, closed seasons, gear restrictions, and minimum catch sizes.

--- SENTENCE 1990 ---
Most governments collect **landing data** (data collected at the dock or from creel surveys) on the kinds of fish, invertebrates,

and plants taken that can be used to track trends and evaluate the effectiveness of regulations.

--- SENTENCE 1991 ---
In most regions, the management of coral reef resources112 is jointly undertaken by local and Federal agencies.

--- SENTENCE 1992 ---
Within three miles from shore, local agencies generally manage fisheries and other uses of coastal resources.

--- SENTENCE 1993 ---
A variety of legislation gives NOAA the authority to manage living marine resources in U.S. Federal waters113.

--- SENTENCE 1994 ---
Federal fisheries regulations are implemented by the Secretary of Commerce and enforced by NOAA's National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).

--- SENTENCE 1995 ---
**Fisheries Management Plans Plans –** Four of eight Regional Fishery Management Councils have developed federal Fishery Management Plans (FMPs) for reef fisheries resources and proposed implementing regulations.

--- SENTENCE 1996 ---
They are as follows.

--- SENTENCE 1997 ---
Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council – NOAA manages a number of fisheries associated with coral reefs based on FMPs, including Coral and Coral Reefs, Red Drum, Reef Fish Resources, Spiny Lobster, and Stone Crab.

--- SENTENCE 1998 ---
This Management Council also identified the Madison-Swanson and Steamboat Lumps Marine Protected Areas on the West Florida Shelf as potential reserves.

--- SENTENCE 1999 ---
NOAA designated them as such and since has been assessing their resources and fisheries contribution.

--- SENTENCE 2000 ---
South Atlantic Fishery Management Council **–**  Coral reef associated fisheries managed under FMPs in the South Atlantic include Atlantic Coast

> Red Drum; Coral, Coral Reefs, and Live/Hard Bottom Habitats of the South Atlantic Region; Golden Crab; Snapper-Grouper Fisheries; and Spiny Lobster.

--- SENTENCE 2001 ---
This Council proposed the notake zones for the new Tortugas Ecological Reserve.

--- SENTENCE 2002 ---
> Caribbean Fishery Management Council **–** Reef-associated fisheries of Puerto Rico and the USVI managed under FMPs

developed by the Caribbean Fishery Management Council in-clude Corals and Reef-Associated Plants and In-vertebrates; Queen Conch; Reef Fish; and Spiny Lobster.

Western Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Council **–** Three FMPs developed by this Council include coral reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 2003 ---
The Bottomfish FMP regulates fishing primarily for snappers, groupers, and jacks (Fig. 101) in the EEZ around the Territory of American Samoa, Territory of Guam, State of Hawai'i (including the NWHI), the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and U.S.

--- SENTENCE 2021 ---
**Regulations and Enforcement Enforcement –** Regulations have been developed for most commercially

important fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 2022 ---
Those applicable to coral reef ecosystems vary among jurisdictions and cover quotas on catch, closed seasons, closed areas, gear restrictions, and minimum catch sizes.

--- SENTENCE 2023 ---
Other regulations protect coral reef resources by regulating oil exploration and mining, setting up no-anchor zones, regulating coastal construction, and imposing water quality and pollution controls.

--- SENTENCE 2024 ---
All of the nearly 100 jurisdictional managers and experts developing this report agreed enforcement was not adequate to protect coral reef ecosystem resources.

--- SENTENCE 2025 ---
This is an especially difficult task for the larger and more remote reef systems with jurisdictions that lack the ships and staffing to adequately patrol their MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 2026 ---
To support the need to better protect reefs, the USCRTF has called for better enforcement of laws, established new guidance to protect coral reefs, and provided funding and technical assistance to states and territories to build **management capacity**114 .

--- SENTENCE 2029 ---

--- SENTENCE 2030 ---
NOAA, through grants to island jurisdictions, has funded a variety of management activities since 2000 that include hiring full-time, permanent technical staff, purchasing equipment, and conducting various workshops.

SUMMARY: AGENCY RESPONSES AGENCY RESPONSES AGENCY RESPONSES**

(Identifying environmental pressures and gathering the comprehensive data for the National Assessments (the discussions in the previous sections) were mandated by the USCRTF National Action Plan.

--- SENTENCE 2033 ---
USCRTF agencies and their partners have worked together to make the National Action Plan a reality (USCRTF 2000).

--- SENTENCE 2034 ---
In less than two years, significant progress has been made on the two fundamental themes and action items (USCRTF 2002).

--- SENTENCE 2035 ---
The two themes and action items identified by the USCRTF are discussed in the remainder of this section.

--- SENTENCE 2036 ---
**Theme 1: Understand Coral Reef Ecosystems Theme Ecosystems –** 

Understanding coral reef systems is necessary to 1) discern the conservation measures needed and 2) evaluate potential impacts of actions on the condition of the coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2037 ---
This includes comprehensive mapping, assessment, and monitoring of coral reef health (Fig. 102); supporting strategic research on regional threats to coral reef health and the underlying ecological processes upon which they depend; and incorporating the human dimension into conservation and management strategies.

--- SENTENCE 2038 ---
**Theme 2: Quickly Reduce the Adverse Im Theme 2: Quickly Reduce the Adverse Impacts of Human Activities Activities –** Reducing impacts requires an expanded and strengthened network of Federal, State, and territorial coral reef MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 2039 ---
Along with this, it is necessary to reduce the adverse impacts of extractive uses, habitat destruction and pollution; restore damaged reefs; strengthen international activities, ameliorate the impacts of international trade in coral reef spe-

cies; improve governmental accountability and coordination; and create an informed and engaged public.

--- SENTENCE 2040 ---
Many of these actions require effective monitoring of reef health, tracking biotic changes, and evaluating impacts of conservation measures on affected components of the managed ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2041 ---
In FY00 and FY01, DoI and NOAA provided over \$2 million in grants to help the U.S. islands96 improve coral reef management and conservation.

--- SENTENCE 2042 ---
This included monitoring, education, and designation of marine protected areas.

--- SENTENCE 2043 ---
Additionally, in FY00 NOAA provided \$7.8 million, and in FY01 \$27 million to agencies with coral reef management responsibilities for other initiatives for conserving coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2044 ---
In FY02, a total of \$34 million will be available from NOAA to continue coral reef initiatives on U.S. coral reef ecosystems and to initiate related efforts for reefs off the Pacific Freely Associated States.

!

--- SENTENCE 2045 ---
Assessment of a coral reef in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (Photo: Donna Turgeon).

--- SENTENCE 2046 ---
The information used to prepare the biennial reports mandated by the Coral Reef Conservation Act of 2000 has to be based on reliable monitoring data and ecological assessments.

--- SENTENCE 2047 ---
NOAA and DoI are helping local agencies build their scientific capacity to assure that information will be available for those reports.

#### **Map All U.S. Coral Reefs

--- SENTENCE 2048 ---
All U.S. Reefs**

As discussed before, most U.S. coral reefs have never been adequately mapped.

--- SENTENCE 2049 ---
The agencies of the USCRTF are undertaking a major effort to develop comprehensive and consistent coral reef ecosystem maps for all U.S. reefs (Fig. 103).

--- SENTENCE 2050 ---
This is led by NOAA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the USGS (MISWG 1999).

!

--- SENTENCE 2051 ---
[](_page_81_Figure_14.jpeg)

<sup>115</sup> Puerto Rico, the USVI, Hawai'i, American Samoa, Guam, and the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 2052 ---
**7373**

**AGENCY RESPONSES AGENCY RESPONSES**

The USCRTF National Action Plan committed to delineating and digitally mapping all U.S. shallow coral reefs by 2009 using airborne and satellite photography.

--- SENTENCE 2053 ---
Mapping and habitat characterization of selected deep reef and bank areas has also begun using multi-beam sonar, submersibles, and remotely-operated vehicles.

--- SENTENCE 2054 ---
This information will support more effective fish and coastal zone management, disaster mitigation, research, and restoration efforts.

--- SENTENCE 2055 ---
Detailed and spatially accurate digital benthic habitat maps can be used to design monitoring programs, organize data, and conduct assessments.

--- SENTENCE 2056 ---
Digital data and the associated maps delineate major habitat types – seagrass, coral reefs, and mangroves – and can provide a framework for tracking changes in those habitats (Monaco *et al.*  2001).

--- SENTENCE 2057 ---
Other measurements of the ecosystem that correlate with habitat change116 can be layered onto these maps and perhaps ultimately used to help predict habitat change.

--- SENTENCE 2058 ---
Completed maps and related information (discussed in the following subsections) are available on a NOAA web site (Coral Reef Mapping and Monitoring 2002).

Volunteer Monitoring Programs – A variety of volunteer monitoring programs collect information on coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2138 ---
These provide data and related information to the National Coral Reef Monitoring Network and enhance the monitoring being conducted by agency and non-governmental scientists.

--- SENTENCE 2139 ---

--- SENTENCE 2140 ---

Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) –

--- SENTENCE 2142 ---

--- SENTENCE 2143 ---

--- SENTENCE 2144 ---

--- SENTENCE 2145 ---
Reef Check – Initiated in 1997, Reef Check is a protocol for rapid assessment of reefs specifically designed for non-professionals and volunteers (Reef Check 2002).

--- SENTENCE 2146 ---
It evaluates the effects of human impacts on coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2147 ---
Annually it engages a large cadre of volunteer SCUBA and free divers in over 50 countries to survey selected harvested species, classify benthic substrates using the point-

intercept method, and report coral reef damage from bleaching and other stresses.

--- SENTENCE 2148 ---
The GCRMN designated Reef Check as its community-based monitoring protocol (Westmacott *et al.* 2000).

#### **Understand Social and Economic Economic Factors – The Human Dimension – The Dimension**

Coral reef management has traditionally focused on the biophysical aspects of coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2203 ---
Since reefs are coming under increasing pressure from human activities, better understanding the human dimension must play an important role in management programs.

--- SENTENCE 2204 ---
To ensure long-term success, programs must also involve the local community and create cooperative management.

--- SENTENCE 2205 ---
Human activities and their resulting impacts are woven into the social, cultural, and economic fabric of regional coastal communities.

--- SENTENCE 2206 ---
This is particularly important among many of the U.S. Islands, where traditional management of coral reef resources, including subsistence fishing, have been an integral part of local government (Fig. 115).

--- SENTENCE 2207 ---
The human dimension has become a significant component of USCRTF coral reef conservation activities.

--- SENTENCE 2208 ---
In FY00, NOAA shifted its priorities toward a more interdisciplinary approach, and began to diversify its focus, sponsor human

dimension data collection, and help build capacity for long-term coral reef conservation by State, Territorial, and Pacific Freely Associated State agencies.

--- SENTENCE 2209 ---

#### **Expand and Strengthen Marine Protected Protected Areas (MPAs) (MPAs)**

The USCRTF National Action Plan considers MPAs and areas with no-take provisions a key tool for protecting coral reef ecosystems and assuring

**NATIONAL SUMMARY NATIONAL SUMMARY**

the sustainable use of reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 2218 ---
Used nationally and internationally, MPAs conserve biodiversity, protect endangered species, reduce user conflicts, and enhance commercial and recreational activities (Salm *et al.* 2000).

--- SENTENCE 2219 ---
Enforcement determines the effectiveness of this (or any) conservation measure.

--- SENTENCE 2220 ---
**Strengthen Current MPAs MPAs –** Much has been done over the past few years by USCRTF agencies to strengthen MPAs, but most have been incremental and relatively unheralded.

--- SENTENCE 2221 ---
The following are examples of what some of the island governments have undertaken since 1999.

- •

--- SENTENCE 2222 ---

- • Hawai'i has begun to inventory and assess its MPA system and is designing a new structure for designation and management.

--- SENTENCE 2224 ---
It is increasing the size of the Pupukea MPA on O'ahu and creating a no-take zone within this MPA.

In 2001, the islets of Palmyra Atoll were purchased from the Nature Conservancy by the DoI for inclusion in the Palmyra Atoll National Wildlife Refuge (Federal Register 2002a).

--- SENTENCE 2245 ---
This Refuge allows limited recreational fishing and wildlife observation activities.

--- SENTENCE 2246 ---
In 2001, the new National Wildlife Refuge at Kingman Reef was established (Federal Register 2002b).

--- SENTENCE 2247 ---
The entire refuge is protected by no-

take provisions – a total of about 756 mi<sup>2</sup> (1,957 km<sup>2</sup>) of coral reef and other habitats are closed to access except for innocent passage through its waters.

--- SENTENCE 2248 ---
Hawai'i – In 2000, the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve was established by Executive Order (E.O. 13178).

--- SENTENCE 2249 ---
It is the largest U.S. marine protected area, covering approximately 130,900 mi² (339,900 km²) (NWHI Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve 2002).

--- SENTENCE 2250 ---
About 21.4% of the Reserve is within the established Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge, and protected by no-take provisions.

--- SENTENCE 2251 ---
CNMI – Currently, the CNMI has seven established MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 2252 ---
The Sasanhaya Fish Reserve in Rota is a no-take reserve.

--- SENTENCE 2253 ---
In 2001, three new MPAs on Saipan<sup>123</sup> were created but these have yet to be enacted into law.

--- SENTENCE 2254 ---
Overall, MPAs with no-take provisions protect about 3.7 mi<sup>2</sup> (9.6 km<sup>2</sup>), for a total of 1.7% of the shallow-water coral reef ecosystem.

#### **Reduce Impacts of Coastal Impacts of Coastal Uses**

Rapid growth of both population and tourism in coastal areas poses increasing threats to the conservation of nearby coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2287 ---
Coastal activities such as dredging for navigation or marinas, construction of shoreline protection structures, beach renourishment, sand mining, pipeline and cable installation, and destructive land-use practices125 decrease water quality around reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2288 ---
Increased tourism has increased pressure on coral reef resources, either through direct impacts on the reefs or indirectly through increased levels of coastal development, sewage discharge, and vessel traffic.

--- SENTENCE 2289 ---
As the number of people using and transiting coral reefs increases, so does the frequency of vessel groundings on reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2290 ---
A number of actions have been taken by the USCRTF to reduce these impacts.

#### **Recreational Vessels and Water Sports Vessels and Sports –**

Prohibitions on recreational vessels, especially jet skis, were implemented in sensitive areas in Puerto Rico using its revised Coastal Zone Management Program Federal Consistency Guidelines.

--- SENTENCE 2291 ---

--- SENTENCE 2292 ---

--- SENTENCE 2295 ---
Commissioners concluded any practice that modifies natural feeding habits is unacceptable, and practices that teach marine life to associate people with food are unhealthy for both.

#### **Create an Informed Public Public**

The USCRTF strives to increase public understanding of coral reef conservation issues and engage the general public as well as local communities in conservation efforts.

--- SENTENCE 2467 ---
In FY00-01, USCRTF agencies expanded their education and outreach efforts, focusing on coral reef conservation and protection (Coral Reef 2002, Fig. 130).

--- SENTENCE 2468 ---
Most of these efforts are being done by State and Territorial agencies, although many have been assisted by Federal grants.

--- SENTENCE 2469 ---
**Coral Reef Conservation Fund Reef Conservation Fund –**

--- SENTENCE 2470 ---
The Coral Reef Conservation Act of 2000 (CRCA) authorized NOAA to enter into an agreement with a nonprofit organization to establish and administer a Coral Reef Conservation Fund (the Fund).

--- SENTENCE 2471 ---
NOAA established the agreement with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF).

--- SENTENCE 2472 ---
Grants under the Fund support local-level public and private partnerships to conserve coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2473 ---
One of the major focus areas is increasing community awareness through education and stewardship activities.

--- SENTENCE 2474 ---
In 2001, the Fund provided approximately \$2 million in grants for education and public outreach projects.

NATIONAL SUMMARY: NATIONAL SUMMARY: RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS**

Managers of coral reef ecosystems in the United States and the Pacific Freely Associated States assessed and prioritized management needs at a Coral Reef Managers' Workshop held on O'ahu, HI in February 2000.

--- SENTENCE 2519 ---
The managers' table of priorities was updated and the USCRTF Points of Contact have assured that the resulting set of recommendations met local priority needs for FY02.

--- SENTENCE 2520 ---
The priorities in this table are similar to those in the National Coral Reef Action Strategy.

--- SENTENCE 2521 ---
The table should be read as follows.

--- SENTENCE 2522 ---
If work had recently been completed, was underway, or planned and adequately supported, the item was not listed as a priority, although it may be of local importance.

--- SENTENCE 2523 ---
This was also true for mapping priorities, as deep-reef mapping resources were limited by the need to complete shallow-reef mapping first.

--- SENTENCE 2524 ---
At the time this report was being finalized, NOAA and DoI were entertaining FY02 proposals for grant support for projects based on the following priorities.

--- SENTENCE 2525 ---
**Complete Mapping and Establish a Monitoring Establish Monitoring Network Network –** To fill identified information gaps, managers consider mapping, assessing, and monitoring U.S. coral reef ecosystems top priorities for 2002 (Fig. 133).

--- SENTENCE 2526 ---
While Puerto Rico and USVI reefs have been mapped, areas with poor water quality need still need final spatial information.

--- SENTENCE 2527 ---
Therefore, they are still listed even though mapping activities are well underway to fill those gaps.

--- SENTENCE 2528 ---
To provide the more sophisticated monitoring needed to develop coral reef health indicators136 for the next biennial report, the level of funding previously allocated for assessing and monitoring was moderately increased.

--- SENTENCE 2529 ---
For 2001, about \$100,000 was available to each jurisdiction.

--- SENTENCE 2530 ---
For all jurisdictions, training in coral reef monitoring and assessment, and support for assessment and monitoring activities is needed so local capacity can be developed.

--- SENTENCE 2531 ---
This is especially true in the Pacific Freely Associated States.

--- SENTENCE 2532 ---
Local expertise for assessment and monitoring has been increasing, but funds are a limiting factor, especially as finanis decreasing.

--- SENTENCE 2533 ---
Since they are now members of the USCRTF, the Freely Associated States are included in the Mapping, Assessment, and Monitoring Program.

--- SENTENCE 2534 ---
Plans are to initiate assessment and monitoring activities there in FY02.

--- SENTENCE 2535 ---
**Strengthen MPAs MPAs –**

--- SENTENCE 2536 ---
This will continue to be a high priority for all but the U.S. remote insular reefs, Federated States of Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands.

--- SENTENCE 2537 ---
It follows what was accomplished by USCRTF members in 1999 and 2000 to expand and strengthen marine protected areas.

--- SENTENCE 2538 ---
And, except for the remote insular reefs where the considerable transit distances and the generally pristine condition of the reefs makes it a lower priority at this time, improved enforcement is a high priority for MPAs.

!

--- SENTENCE 2539 ---
Mapping, monitoring, and assessment are top priorities, especially for reefs located in more remote and less studied areas (Photo: James Maragos).

--- SENTENCE 2540 ---
Except for Guam who already has 20% of its reef resources protected by no-take provisions, managers are calling for broad-scale strengthening of MPAs to protect shallow-water resources.

--- SENTENCE 2541 ---
**Reduce Overfishing Reduce Overfishing –** Most managers considered conservation measures related to fisheries a high priority.

--- SENTENCE 2542 ---
Fisheries impacts on coral reefs and other benthic habitats are either a high or medium priority for all but the U.S. remote insular reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2543 ---

--- SENTENCE 2640 ---
**Build a Better System of Enforcement Enforcement –**

--- SENTENCE 2641 ---
The managers with responsibility for coral reef resources who helped prepare this report and the USCRTF Points of Contact all made enforcement a high priority.

--- SENTENCE 2642 ---
Except for remote insular refuges, measures to conserve coral reef resources (e.g., notake closures, harvest limits) within most MPAs need adequate enforcement to assure success (Fig. 134).

--- SENTENCE 2643 ---
More effective enforcement is needed both within and outside MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 2644 ---
Difficulties in patrolling and enforcing regulations are almost insurmountable because of the vast distances covered by many jurisdictions, especially the recently-created Northwestern Hawaiian Island Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve and the remaining remote Pacific National Wildlife Refuges.

--- SENTENCE 2645 ---
**Increase Community Involvement Involvement –** Community outreach is a high priority for all areas except the mostly uninhabited Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and the U.S. remote insular reefs (Fig. 135).

--- SENTENCE 2646 ---
**Increase Cooperation Among Agencies Among Agencies –** Interagency coordination is either a medium or high priority for all but Guam and the U.S. remote insular reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2647 ---
Additionally, participants at the 2001 Pacific managers workshop agreed 1) a coherent national and international policy for coral reefs is needed, and 2) a Federal law that provides protection for reef ecosystems is the best way to attain this.

#### **CONCLUSIONS CONCLUSIONS**

There is good news and bad news about U.S. coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2648 ---
The good news is the tremendous headway made so far to begin filling gaps in information, mapping, establishing a consistent monitoring program, making the public aware of the importance of preserving reefs, and getting their active participation in the program.

--- SENTENCE 2649 ---
The new U.S. legislation, congressional funding, and leadership provided by the USCRTF have resulted in new resources that have already made a difference in understanding and conserving reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2650 ---
The concerted efforts to initiate mapping, assessment, monitoring, research, and restoration will provide a consistent basis for assessing the status and trends of and tracking changes in coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 2651 ---
Also, MPAs and the no-take areas are being strengthened and expanded, further protecting critical resources.

--- SENTENCE 2652 ---
The bad news is that current enforcement is inadequate to protect MPAs, particularly remote coral reefs where ships and enforcement personnel are seldom available.

--- SENTENCE 2653 ---
In general, a lot more quantitative, comparable information is needed.

--- SENTENCE 2654 ---
Basic mapping has yet to be done for over 85% of the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2655 ---
Except where mapped, the available data are just estimates.

--- SENTENCE 2656 ---
This is especially true for areas covered by no-take provisions.

--- SENTENCE 2657 ---
Many reef areas need basic assessments and biotic inventories to fill significant gaps limiting the ability of managers to determine the condition of jurisdictional coral reefs, including overall biological diversity, popu-

Elkhorn coral, once abundant throughout the Caribbean has been heavily impacted by (A) disease, bleaching, hurricanes, turbidity, and (B) siltation (Photos: Matt Kendall and E.C. Peters)

lation abundance, species recruitment, and the incidence of disease.

--- SENTENCE 2663 ---
Comparable long-term monitoring needs to be sponsored and integrated across regions.

--- SENTENCE 2664 ---
To track changes in ecosystem health and evaluate the effectiveness of measures to conserve and protect coral reef ecosystems, grants to State and Territorial agencies need to be continued for at least the next 5-10 years, ideally beyond that.

--- SENTENCE 2665 ---
Only a nationally-coordinated program can provide reef managers the advice, support, and resources needed to 1) initiate the bold conservation measures necessary to reverse the downward trends of degraded reefs, and 2) maintain the quality of healthy reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2666 ---
On degraded reefs, water and substrate quality must be improved, overfishing and the gear damage reduced, invasive species controlled, and other human stresses minimized.

--- SENTENCE 2667 ---
Finally, public awareness and education activities need to be enhanced and expanded to develop cooperation.

--- SENTENCE 2668 ---
Renewed citizen awareness and a collective ethic for the sustained use of coral reef ecosystems in the United States and Freely Associated States need to be generated.

--- SENTENCE 2669 ---
Every U.S. reef system has suffered varying degrees of impact from natural or human disturbance.

--- SENTENCE 2670 ---
For example, from the combined impacts of hurricanes, reduced urchin and fish herbivory, high nutrient input, coral diseases, and bleaching in the Caribbean, there has been a measured decrease in coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 2671 ---
The FKNMS recorded a 37% decline in coral cover over the past five years, and reported that other severe impacts predated their monitoring of the Florida Keys coral reef ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 2672 ---
A series of earlier disasters were responsible

for the near elimination of dense stands of elkhorn and staghorn coral from areas in the Florida Keys, Puerto Rico, and the USVI (Fig. 136).

--- SENTENCE 2673 ---
At the extreme end, the eight hurricanes that have struck the USVI over the past two decades, reduced live *Acropora* corals at the Buck Island National Park, USVI by 85%.

--- SENTENCE 2674 ---
In their place are coral rubble and abundant macroalgae.

--- SENTENCE 2675 ---
Caribbean coral reef ecosystems also have yet to recover from a die-off of the longspined sea urchin about 20 years ago.

--- SENTENCE 2676 ---
There is evidence that the loss of this key algal grazer coupled with over-nutrification and overfishing of herbivores may have

contributed to the shift from a coral-dominated ecosystem to a macroalgae-dominated system on many reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2677 ---
Like the Caribbean, the U.S. Pacific island shallow-water coral reefs are currently recovering from natural disturbances occurring over the past two decades – first a crown-of-thorns starfish invasion of several island groups139 in 1979, then several periods of warm temperatures that caused coral bleaching, with the worst in 1997-1998.

--- SENTENCE 2678 ---
Chronic human impacts on coral reefs located near populated areas140 add to these sources of stress.

--- SENTENCE 2679 ---
Human impacts play a large role in the condition of most reefs, particularly those near population centers.

--- SENTENCE 2680 ---
Coral reefs in the Main Hawaiian Islands, American Samoa, Guam, and the CNMI suffer from degradation related to population growth, urbanization, and development.

#### **This report finds:**

- • U.S. coral reef areas are extensive.
- • Healthy reef ecosystems are critical for local and regional economies.
- • All jurisdictions still have some reefs in good-to-excellent health.

--- SENTENCE 2748 ---
These need conservation.
- • All shallow reefs near urbanized coasts are degraded to some extent.

--- SENTENCE 2749 ---
These need restoration.
- • Areas next to densely-populated shorelines generally have poorer water quality than those far from human habitation.

--- SENTENCE 2750 ---
Where water quality is fair to poor, reef ecosystems are degraded.

--- SENTENCE 2751 ---
Water quality needs to be improved in those areas, and measures taken to maintain the water quality of areas where reef condition is now deemed good-toexcellent.
- • Coastal development, runoff, and sedimentation have impacted reefs around most high islands.

--- SENTENCE 2752 ---
These impacts need to be minimized.
- • Fishing pressure has been a primary factor impacting reef ecosystems for decades.

--- SENTENCE 2753 ---
There is evidence that overfishing has changed ecosystem structure and function.

--- SENTENCE 2754 ---
Different and effective methods of management need to be implemented.
- • Remote reefs with little coastal development, good water quality, and low fishing pressure are in excellent health, as characterized by many large fish and generally high species diversity within the reef community.

--- SENTENCE 2755 ---
These need to be studied and preserved.
- • Marine refuges with no-take provisions produce more and larger fish.

--- SENTENCE 2756 ---
With enough time, they can conserve reef communities and long-lived species, producing trophy-sized apex predators.

--- SENTENCE 2757 ---
More no-take areas need to be implemented within MPAs in order to reach the USCRTF goal of 20% protection.
- • Some existing marine protected areas are not protecting reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2758 ---
Regulations within these need to be strengthened and adequately enforced.

--- SENTENCE 2759 ---

#### **Introduction Introduction**

There are three main areas of coral reefs and banks in Florida – the Florida Keys, the southeastern coast from northern Monroe County to Palm Beach County, and the Florida Middle Grounds in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, south of Apalachicola and northwest of Tarpon Springs.

--- SENTENCE 2764 ---
Numerous coral habitats are also scattered from the Florida Middle Grounds to the Florida Keys along Florida's west coast shelf at varying locations.

--- SENTENCE 2765 ---
New communities are constantly being discovered, such as those recently documented along Pulley's Ridge in 45-60 m (150-200 ft) of water.

--- SENTENCE 2766 ---
**The Florida Keys Keys –** The Florida Keys have the only emergent coral reefs off the continental United States.

--- SENTENCE 2767 ---
Arching southwest 356 km from south of Miami to the Dry Tortugas, the Florida reef tract comprises one of the largest reef communities in the world.

--- SENTENCE 2768 ---
Except between Rebecca Shoal and the Dry Tortugas, it is almost continuous.

--- SENTENCE 2769 ---
The majority of the reef tract lies within the boundaries of the 9800 km2 Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (FKNMS or Sanctuary).

--- SENTENCE 2770 ---
Over half of the Sanctuary is located in State of Florida territorial waters (less than 4.8 km from shore in the Atlantic waters and less than 16.5 km from shore in the Gulf of Mexico); the rest of the Sanctuary (42%) is in Federal waters.

--- SENTENCE 2771 ---
Designated in 1990, the Sanctuary is managed jointly between NOAA and the

Figure 143.

--- SENTENCE 2772 ---
A. Staghorn coral (Photo: NCRI); B. elkhorn coral (Photo: Paige Gill, FKNMS).

!

--- SENTENCE 2773 ---
A comprehensive management plan adopted in 1997 guides Sanctuary management.

--- SENTENCE 2774 ---
One management component has been establishing and implementing five types of marine zones, which include 24 individual, fully protected zones designed to offer added protection to some of the over 1,400 km2 of coral reef habitat located within the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2775 ---
Two additional marine protected areas managed by the National Park Service encompass reefs in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2776 ---
Located on the northern boundary of the Sanctuary just south of Miami, Biscayne National Park has 683 km2 of coastal waters.

--- SENTENCE 2777 ---
At the western-most end of the reef tract lies Dry Tortugas National Park, covering 262 km2 .

--- SENTENCE 2778 ---
The Florida Reef Tract has been described as a bank reef system comprised of an almost continuous reef community with elongated reef habitats paralleling one another.

--- SENTENCE 2779 ---
The reef ecosystems consist of distinct habitat types: nearshore patch reefs, mid-channel reefs, offshore patch reefs, seagrass beds, back reefs/reef flats, bank or transitional reefs, intermediate reefs, deep reefs, outlier reefs, and sand/soft bottom areas.

--- SENTENCE 2780 ---
In addition to the bank reefs, over 6000 circular to oval patch reefs lie along the Florida Reef Tract in 2 to 9 m of water.

--- SENTENCE 2781 ---
An outer reef tract lies 4.8 to 11.3 km east and south of the Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2782 ---
The seaward-facing spur and groove formations of the Florida Reef Tract are constructional features, formed partly by wave energy (Shinn 1963, Shinn *et al.* 1981, DoC 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2783 ---
They extend 1 to 2 km off the main reef, from 1 to 10 m. Historically, the tops of the spurs were composed mainly of elkhorn coral (*Acropora palmata*, Fig.

--- SENTENCE 2784 ---
143), especially at depths less than 5 m, while grooves contained carbonate sands and reef rubble (Hendler *et al.*  1995).

--- SENTENCE 2785 ---
These features are typically no more than 200 m long from offshore to onshore.

--- SENTENCE 2786 ---
Primary corals found in this area include the star corals (*Montastrea annularis* complex and *the*  great star coral (*Montastrea cavernosa*), masssive starlet coral (*Siderastrea siderea*), and fire corals

--- SENTENCE 2793 ---
The First Reef has a very low profile with conspicuous small octocoral and algal cover.

--- SENTENCE 2794 ---
The substrate is relict reef of Anastasia Formation limestone and worm reef (*Phragmatopoma*), with breaks and sediment pockets within the reef.

--- SENTENCE 2795 ---
Typical sessile organisms are lesser starlet coral (*Siderastrea radians*) and colonial zoanthids ( *thoa mammalosa caribaeorum* ).

#### **The Middle Grounds Grounds –**

This is a 1,193 km2 area in the eastern Gulf of Mexico (Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission 2001), 137 km south of Apalachicola and 129 km northwest of Tarpon Springs.

--- SENTENCE 2807 ---
Its banks are two parallel ridgelines separated by a valley lying in a northnorthwesterly direction.

--- SENTENCE 2808 ---
Individual banks are 12 to 15 m high with shallow crests 21 m below sea level.

--- SENTENCE 2809 ---
The reef structures are late Pleistocene to early Holocene (Brooks and Doyle 1991).

--- SENTENCE 2810 ---
Winter temperatures reach 16˚ C, limiting many tropical species from occupying these banks.

--- SENTENCE 2811 ---
However, there are 23 species of stony corals (Grimm and Hopkins 1977).

--- SENTENCE 2812 ---
Environmental studies in the 1970s documented 103

species of algae, about 40 sponges, 75 mollusks, 56 decapod crustaceans, 41 polychaetes, 23 echinoderms, and 170 species of fish (Hopkins *et al.*  1977).

--- SENTENCE 2813 ---
Elliptical star coral, yellow pencil coral (*Madracis decactis*), and branching fire coral (*Millepora alcicornis*) are the most abundant stony coral species.

--- SENTENCE 2814 ---
Coral cover may be as high as 30% on some pinnacles.

--- SENTENCE 2815 ---
Overall, the biotic characteristics of this area are very different from either the Florida Keys or the Flower Garden Banks, located off Texas.

#### **Condition of Coral Reef Ecosystems Ecosystems**

Historical fluctuations in sea level have influenced the reefs of Florida, with the last significant rise in sea level starting about 6,000 years ago.

--- SENTENCE 2818 ---
Since that time, the reefs off Southeast Florida and the Florida Keys have been building.

--- SENTENCE 2819 ---
Greater reef development in those areas generally occurs in the Upper and Lower Keys, where the Keys protect reefs from direct water flows from the Gulf of Mexico and Florida Bay (DoC 1996, Robbin 1981, Shinn *et al.* 1989).

--- SENTENCE 2820 ---
Although the reefs of Florida have existed for the past several thousands years, they have only recently become the focus of scientific research and monitoring in an attempt to fully understand changes over time.

--- SENTENCE 2821 ---
Since the creation of the FKNMS, the reefs and associated marine habitats of the Florida Keys have become the subject of a broad research and monitoring program that seeks to establish baseline data on ecosystem condition and ascertain cause-and-effect linkages.

--- SENTENCE 2822 ---
The reefs and banks of Florida's southeastern coast and the Middle Grounds are not as well studied as those of the Florida Keys, though they are beginning to be mapped and estimates of cover are available from some monitoring programs.

--- SENTENCE 2823 ---
As a result, the condition of Florida's coral ecosystems can be best determined for Florida Keys reefs at this time; comprehensive, long-term monitoring of various ecosystem components is critical for the southeastern coast and Middle Grounds.

--- SENTENCE 2824 ---
In the Florida Keys, Sanctuary-wide monitoring of water quality, seagrasses, and coral and hardbottom communities began in 1994 under a Water Quality Protection Program that was jointly undertaken by

NOAA and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA).

--- SENTENCE 2825 ---
In 1997, when a network of fully protected zones, or marine reserves were implemented, a Zone Monitoring Program was initiated to determine whether the zones meet their objectives of reducing pressure on heavily used reefs, preserving biodiversity, facilitating research, and reducing use conflicts, among others.

--- SENTENCE 2826 ---
Each of these monitoring programs and their methods are described in the Current Conservation Management section of this report.

--- SENTENCE 2827 ---
To date, over five years of data from the Water Quality Protection Program and three years of data from the Zone Monitoring Program have provided Sanctuary managers with emerging trends in coral reef ecosystem health throughout the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2828 ---
**Coral–** Early surveys of Florida Keys coral reefs have documented two species of fire coral, 55 species of octocoral, and 64 taxa of stony corals (DoC 1996, Levy *et al.* 1996).

--- SENTENCE 2829 ---
Under the Zone Monitoring Program, scientists from the University of North Carolina at Wilmington's National Undersea Research Center (UNCW/NURC) have more recently conducted rapid, large-scale assessments of coral reefs and hardbottom communities in the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2830 ---
In their 1999 assessment, the UNCW/NURC rapid assessment and rmonitoring program found coral cover highly variable by both habitat type and region (Miller *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2831 ---
Jaap *et al.* (2001) confirmed that gains and losses of coral cover in the Florida Keys fluctuate among habitat types with patch reef habitats suffering the fewest losses and exhibiting the highest average percent cover over time.

--- SENTENCE 2832 ---
Since 1996, over 66% of 160 stations in the Coral Reef/Hardbottom Monitoring Project of the Water Quality Protection Program exhibited losses in stony coral diversity.

--- SENTENCE 2833 ---
From 1996 to 2000, stony coral cover Sanctuary-wide decreased by 36.6% to a low of 6.6% in 2000, with the greatest relative change occurring in the Upper Keys (Jaap *et al.*  2001, Fig. 145).

--- SENTENCE 2834 ---
During this time, 67% of monitoring stations had reduced stony coral species richness, 20% gained species, and 13% had unchanged species richness (Jaap *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2835 ---
However, positive trends were noted in the 1999 2000 survey period, when 69 stations had greater numbers of stony coral species, 56 stations had

fewer species, and 35 stations remained unchanged (Jaap *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2838 ---
In addition to coral cover, recruitment of stony corals to the Florida Keys ecosystem is a basic measure of overall community health.

--- SENTENCE 2839 ---
Relationships between coral cover, recruitment, and juvenile mortality are assessed at six sites in both fully protected Sanctuary zones and in reference areas (Aronson *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2840 ---
Differences in coral recruitment have been seen among all sites over two years.

--- SENTENCE 2841 ---
More important, perhaps, is that juvenile mortality was greatest at shallow stations in the first year (1998) which coincided with a direct strike from Hurricane Georges in the Lower Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2842 ---
UNCW/NURC rapid assessment monitoring of benthic communities indicated no significant differences in juvenile coral density by habitat type and region in 2000 (Miller *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2843 ---
Increasingly, coral diseases threaten the overall health and vitality of reef systems in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2844 ---
However, only three of ten presumptive or purported pathogens have been positively identified (Richardson 1998).

--- SENTENCE 2845 ---
The Coral Reef/Hardbottom Monitoring Project documented increases in the number of stations with diseased coral, the number of coral species with disease, and the number of presumptive diseases (Jaap *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2846 ---
In 1998, a second ongoing coral disease etiology and monitoring program documented regional differences in the incidence of disease, with the highest concentration of coral diseases near Key West and in the Lower Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2847 ---
Significant seasonal increases in diseases were also noted in these

regions (Mueller *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2848 ---
Back reef areas showed the highest prevalence of disease.

--- SENTENCE 2849 ---
These areas are dominated by elkhorn coral, which is susceptible to specific disease conditions (Mueller *et al.* 2001, Fig. 146).

--- SENTENCE 2850 ---
Aspergillosis, a fungal disease that targets the sea fan ( *talina* Sanctuary-wide during these surveys (Mueller ), was the most commonly reported disease *Gorgonia venet al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2851 ---
In addition to confirmed and purported coral diseases, coral bleaching impacts the Sanctuary's reefs (Fig. 147).

--- SENTENCE 2852 ---
Over the past 20 years, bleaching events have increased in both frequency and duration (Hoegh-Guldberg 1999, Jaap 1990).

--- SENTENCE 2853 ---
Massive coral bleaching was first recorded in 1983 along the outer reef tract of the Lower Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2854 ---
Shallow fore reef habitats were most affected (Causey in press).

--- SENTENCE 2855 ---
This event was preceded by periods of low wind and high air temperature, contributing to localized increased water temperature.

--- SENTENCE 2856 ---
Massive bleaching occurred again in July 1987 following doldrum-like weather conditions.

--- SENTENCE 2857 ---
This time, the outer reefs throughout the Florida Keys were afflicted, and secondary impacts such as coral disease were observed.

--- SENTENCE 2858 ---
Then in July 1990, a massive bleaching event occurred Keys-wide.

--- SENTENCE 2859 ---
Inshore reefs bleached for the first time, and mortality of blade fire corals (*Millepora complanata*) reached over 65% on the shallow crest of Looe Key Reef in the Lower Keys (Causey in press).

--- SENTENCE 2860 ---
Bleaching has both expanded and intensified in the last decade.

--- SENTENCE 2861 ---
Another massive episode in 1997 targeted both the inshore and offshore reefs.

--- SENTENCE 2862 ---
Before the reefs could adequately recover, lingering high water temperatures and a particularly strong El Niño event caused yet another bleaching in 1998.

**Water Quality Quality –** Reduced salinity, agricultural and industrial chemical contamination, turbidity, and high nutrients possibly from sewage, upwelling, or groundwater have all impacted water quality to some degree in Southeast Florida, Florida Bay, and the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2945 ---
Ocean outfalls along the coast introduce millions of gallons of secondary sewage to coastal waters, adding nutrients.

--- SENTENCE 2946 ---
Eutrophication of nearshore waters (a result of excess nutrients) is a documented problem in the Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2947 ---
Given these anthropogenic impacts and the importance of also fully understanding natural variability, long-term water quality monitoring is

critical for the entire South Florida region.

--- SENTENCE 2948 ---
Water quality has been monitored at fixed stations in the FKNMS since 1995 as part of the Water Quality Protection Program (FKNMS WQPP 2002).

--- SENTENCE 2949 ---
Results to date indicate dissolved oxygen, total organic nitrogen, and total organic carbon are higher in surface waters, while salinity, turbidity, nitrite, nitrate, ammonium, and total phosphorus are higher in bottom waters.

--- SENTENCE 2950 ---
Geographical differences include higher nutrient concentrations in the Middle and Lower Keys than in the Upper Keys and Dry Tortugas regions.

--- SENTENCE 2951 ---
Generally, declining inshore to offshore trends along transects across Hawk Channel have been noted for nitrate, ammonium, silicate, total organic carbon and nitrogen, and turbidity (Jones and Boyer 2001).

--- SENTENCE 2952 ---
Stations along passes between the Keys had higher nutrient concentrations, phytoplankton biomass, and turbidity than stations located off the Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2953 ---
Although these differences were small, the two shore types support different benthic communities, which may reflect long-term effects of water quality on community composition.

--- SENTENCE 2954 ---
Using a

**FLORIDA FLORIDA FLORIDA FLORIDA**

multivariate statistical approach, these stations were regrouped according to water quality.

--- SENTENCE 2955 ---
This resulted in seven clusters of stations with different water quality characteristics (Fig. 153), giving a functional zonation of Sanctuary water quality.

--- SENTENCE 2956 ---
Probably the most interesting results are temporal trends in concentrations of total phosphorus, nitrate, and total organic nitrogen for much of the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 2957 ---
There have been significant increases in total phosphorus for the Dry Tortugas, Marquesas Keys, Lower Keys, and portions of the Middle and Upper Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2958 ---
No trend in total phosphorus has been observed in Florida Bay or in areas of the Sanctuary most influenced by transport of Bay waters, and there was no concurrent increase in the concentration of chlorophyll *a*, a measure of phytoplankton in the water column.

--- SENTENCE 2959 ---
There were large increases in nitrates, which appeared to be seasonal.

--- SENTENCE 2960 ---
Most of the increases occurred in the Southwest Florida Shelf, Dry Tortugas, Marquesas Keys, and the Lower and Upper Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2961 ---
By contrast, total organic nitrogen decreased modestly at many sites.

--- SENTENCE 2962 ---
Most of the decreases occurred in the Southwest Florida Shelf, the Sluiceway, and the Lower and Upper Keys.

--- SENTENCE 2963 ---
It is possible that these trends are driven by regional circulation patterns arising from the Loop and Florida Currents.

#### **Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs**

**Human Stresses Stresses –** Humans can inadvertently alter physical characteristics of the reef environment, further stressing an ecosystem already combatting the broader stresses of natural variability and global climate change.

--- SENTENCE 2995 ---
Impact from human activities is likely greater in the Keys and along the southeastern coast than in the Middle Grounds.

--- SENTENCE 2996 ---
Due to its offshore location, the Middle Grounds has been somewhat protected, particularly from pollutants.

--- SENTENCE 2997 ---
In the Florida Keys, the greatest immediate pressure is from the three million annual visitors (Leeworthy and Vanasse 1999) and the 80,000 year-round residents.

--- SENTENCE 2998 ---
The population of Monroe County has grown 160% during the past 40 years, a 50,000 resident increase.

--- SENTENCE 2999 ---
Visits to the Florida Keys increased by 15% in the two-year period from 1995-96 to 1997-98, and averages 46,500

58,700 visitors on any given day during the winter tourist season (Leeworthy and Vanasse 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3000 ---
In 1995-1996, over 65% of visitors to the Florida Keys participated in water-based activities, 31% of which were snorkeling and SCUBA diving (Leeworthy and Wiley 1996, Fig. 155).

--- SENTENCE 3001 ---
Since 1965, the number of registered private vessels has increased over six-fold (DoC 1996, Fig. 146).

--- SENTENCE 3002 ---
Damage by humans to hundreds of square kilometers of reef, seagrass, and related habitat over the last 30 years has been documented for some time in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 3003 ---
Boat groundings on coral, seagrasses, and hardbottom areas, propeller scarring of seagrass, accumulation of debris, breaking and damaging corals with ship anchors, using destructive fishing methods, and divers and snorkelers standing on corals have all been documented in various places.

--- SENTENCE 3004 ---
Boat propellers have permanently damaged over 121 km2 of seagrasses.

--- SENTENCE 3005 ---
Over 650 small boat groundings were reported in the Sanctuary in 2000 alone, with 158 of these affecting seagrass and 22 impacting coral reef habitats.

--- SENTENCE 3006 ---
Large ships have been responsible for damaging or destroying over 80,000 m2 of coral reef habitat in the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3007 ---
Wastewater and stormwater treatment and solid waste disposal facilities in the Keys are highly inadequate, having a direct impact on water quality.

--- SENTENCE 3008 ---
However, some solutions to water quality problems are being implemented.

--- SENTENCE 3009 ---
One of the larger ocean outfalls off Key West that delivered approximately seven million gallons a day to the sea was recently replaced with a deep-well injection system (more than 914 m deep and below a containment layer) for treated effluent.

--- SENTENCE 3010 ---
Before injection, the effluent is

--- SENTENCE 3013 ---
Another indirect impact is altered freshwater flow into coastal waters.

--- SENTENCE 3014 ---
The South Florida Water Management District has responsibility for managing the flow and release of freshwater to the ocean through an extensive system of canals and locks.

--- SENTENCE 3015 ---
In Florida Bay, reduced freshwater flow from water management practices in South Florida has been associated with increased plankton blooms (eutrophication), sponge and seagrass die-offs, and fish kills.

--- SENTENCE 3016 ---
Since Florida Bay and nearshore waters provide critical nursery and juvenile habitat for a variety of reef species, the declines seen in these areas indirectly affect the overall health and structure of offshore coral reefs in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 3017 ---
In addition, to control flooding, millions of gallons of fresh water have periodically been released into the canals and near-shore waters of South Florida, creating problems for marine communities.

--- SENTENCE 3018 ---
The highly urbanized coastal region along Florida's southeastern coast puts its coral reefs under varied and chronic stress.

--- SENTENCE 3019 ---
During good weather, both recreational and commercial boating and fishing are very heavy on these reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3020 ---
The nearby Miami, Port Everglades, and Palm Beach ports handle cruise and container ships, oil tankers, and military vessels.

--- SENTENCE 3021 ---
In the past ten years, a number of moderate to severe large vessel groundings in Southeastern Florida have damaged the reef system (Fig. 157).

--- SENTENCE 3022 ---
Signs of anchor damage are also routinely seen.

--- SENTENCE 3023 ---
Four other large-vessel groundings have impacted areas of nearby Biscayne National Park.

--- SENTENCE 3024 ---
Serial overfishing (Ault *et al.* 1998) throughout South Florida has dramatically altered reef fish and other animal populations, contributing to an imbalance in relationships critical to sustaining coral reef diversity.

--- SENTENCE 3025 ---
In Biscayne National Park, 26 of 34 fish species, or 77% of the fish stocks that were examined were overfished (Ault *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3026 ---
In addition, certain types of fishing gear negatively impact reefs in Southeastern Florida.

--- SENTENCE 3027 ---
Reef tracts off Boca Raton and Sunny Isles have been destroyed by dredging for beach renourishment, channel deepening, and channel maintenance.

--- SENTENCE 3028 ---
Chronic turbidity and silt deposition from dredging and similar activities impact water quality, indirectly affecting the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3029 ---
These activities smother sessile invertebrates, resulting in

--- SENTENCE 3030 ---
The M/V Firat grounded offshore of Fort Lauderdale, Florida (Photo: Greg McIntosh).

--- SENTENCE 3031 ---
Fiber optic cables were deployed across reefs in some areas, causing abrasion and detachment of corals and sponges (Jaap 2000).

--- SENTENCE 3032 ---
Introduced, competitive species add additional stress.

--- SENTENCE 3033 ---
Within the past decade, several alien species have been identified on Florida Keys reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3034 ---
At least eight species of marine mollusks have been introduced into South Florida and are expanding their range.

--- SENTENCE 3035 ---
Non-native marine crustaceans are equally diverse and include six crab species, five shrimp species, three barnacles, four isopods, and one tanaid.

--- SENTENCE 3036 ---
Most of these species are foreign to North American waters and were introduced through ship hull fouling or ballast water dumping (USGS 2002).

--- SENTENCE 3037 ---
The majority of Florida's marine fish introductions have come from released aquarium fish, with occasional reports from divers of various exotic species living among native reef fish.

--- SENTENCE 3038 ---
For example, the Indo-Pacific lionfish (*Pterois volitans*) has been sighted on South Florida reefs (Courtney 1995).

--- SENTENCE 3039 ---
Another popular aquarium fish, the Pacific batfish (*Platax orbicularus*), was observed off the Upper Keys; two specimens were removed and delivered to the New England Aquarium (B. Keller pers.

--- SENTENCE 3040 ---
In addition to the myriad of human impacts affecting coral reef health in Florida, natural environmental variability affects these habitats.

Under normal conditions, corals and associated reef organisms tolerate a certain level of environmental stress and recover or acclimatize to sporadic events such as temperature variation or storms.

--- SENTENCE 3045 ---
The added human impacts and stresses may be prolonging the time needed as well as the ability of these organisms and systems to recover from large-scale climate fluctuations and other global changes.

#### **Current Conservation Management Management**

**Mapping Mapping –** Only about 50% of Florida's coral reef and associated benthic habitats have been mapped.

--- SENTENCE 3046 ---
As a result, reliable estimates of the percentage of coral reef and related habitats, as well as the area protected by no-take provisions, cannot be accurately computed state-wide.

--- SENTENCE 3047 ---
Mapping efforts were undertaken in the Sanctuary in the 1990s.

--- SENTENCE 3048 ---
FWC/FMRI and NOAA published digital benthic habitat maps for the Florida Keys in 1998 (FMRI/NOAA 1998, Fig. 159).

--- SENTENCE 3049 ---
Recently, the Dry Tortugas region was characterized (Schmidt *et al.*1999).

--- SENTENCE 3050 ---
Also, Agassiz (1882) produced a remarkable baseline map of Dry Tortugas benthic habitats, which suggest a 0.4 km2 loss of elkhorn coral in a 100-year period (Davis 1982).

--- SENTENCE 3051 ---
Mapping gaps exist for deeper regions of the Tortugas.

--- SENTENCE 3052 ---
The reefs along the Southeastern Florida coast are not as well studied.

--- SENTENCE 3053 ---
In 1999, Nova Southeastern University's National Coral Reef Institute (NSU/ NCRI) and the Broward County Department of Planning and Environmental Protection initiated

mapping of Broward County reefs**.

--- SENTENCE 3054 ---
At this time, there is no comparable mapping program in Palm Beach and Miami-Dade Counties.

--- SENTENCE 3055 ---
Improved mapping has resulted from aerial photos of near-shore areas and laser-based bathymetry of the three reef tracts off Southeastern Florida for specific projects.

--- SENTENCE 3056 ---
For example, detailed LADS (laser depth sounding) bathymetry is complete for all of Broward County, offshore to 36 m. A smaller amount of the area is also mapped with multibeam bathymetry and side-scan sonar.

--- SENTENCE 3057 ---
Estimates of benthic cover are available from some monitoring programs.

--- SENTENCE 3058 ---
There is a general reef distribution map in Jaap and Hallock (1990).

--- SENTENCE 3059 ---
No mapping of the Florida Middle Grounds has been conducted to date.

**Monitoring, Assessments, and Research –**

--- SENTENCE 3061 ---
In the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a comprehensive research and monitoring program has been implemented to establish baseline information on the various components of the ecosystem and help ascertain possible causes and effects of changes.

--- SENTENCE 3062 ---
This way, research and monitoring can ensure the effective implementation of management strategies using the best available scientific information.

--- SENTENCE 3063 ---
Research and monitoring are conducted by many groups, including Local, State, and Federal agencies, public and private universities, private re-

--- SENTENCE 3065 ---
[](_page_121_Figure_14.jpeg)

**FLORIDA FLORIDA FLORIDA FLORIDA**

search foundations, environmental organizations, and independent researchers.

--- SENTENCE 3066 ---
The Sanctuary facilitates and coordinates research by registering researchers through a permitting system, recruiting institutions for priority research activities, overseeing data management, and disseminating findings to the scientific community and the public.

--- SENTENCE 3067 ---
The Water Quality Protection Program (WQPP), funded by the USEPA and recently, NOAA, is the most comprehensive, long-term monitoring program in the Florida Keys.

--- SENTENCE 3068 ---
Begun in 1994, it monitors three components: water quality, seagrasses, and corals/hardbottom communities.

--- SENTENCE 3069 ---
Reef fishes, spiny lobster, queen conch, and benthic cover are also monitored throughout the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3070 ---
Water quality has been monitored at 154 fixed stations since 1995.

--- SENTENCE 3071 ---
Water samples are collected for measuring salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, relative fluorescence, and light attenuation.

--- SENTENCE 3072 ---
Water chemistry includes nitrate, nitrite, ammonium, dissolved inorganic nitrogen, and soluble reactive phosphate.

--- SENTENCE 3073 ---
Concentrations of total organic nitrogen, total organic carbon, total phosphorus, and silicate are also measured, along with chlorophyll *a* and alkaline phosphatase activity (Jones and Boyer 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3074 ---
Seagrass monitoring under the WQPP identifies the distribution and abundance of seagrasses within the Sanctuary and tracks changes over time.

--- SENTENCE 3075 ---
Quarterly monitoring is conducted at 30 fixed stations and annual monitoring occurs at 206 to 336 randomlyselected sites (Fourqurean *et al.* 2001, WQPP 2002).

--- SENTENCE 3076 ---
Permanent stations are co-located at 30 of the water quality monitoring sites to help discern relationships between seagrass health and water quality.

--- SENTENCE 3077 ---
This long-term monitoring is also invaluable for determining human impacts on the Sanctuary's seagrass communities.

--- SENTENCE 3078 ---
The Coral Reef/Hardbottom Monitoring Project (CRMP 2002) tracks the status and trends of coral and hardbottom communities throughout the Sanctuary (Jaap *et al.* 2001, Fig 160).

--- SENTENCE 3079 ---
The project's 43 permanent sites include hardbottom, patch reef, shallow offshore reef, and deep offshore reef communities.

--- SENTENCE 3080 ---
Biodiversity, coral condition, and coral cover are recorded annually at four stations within each site, for a total of 172 stations.

--- SENTENCE 3081 ---
In addition to the WQPP, a Zone Monitoring Program monitors the 24 discrete marine reserves located within the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3082 ---
Implemented in 1997, the goal of the program is to determine whether these fully protected zones effectively protect marine biodiversity and enhance human values related to the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3083 ---
Parameters measured include the abundance and size of fish, invertebrates, and algae, as well as economic and aesthetic values of the Sanctuary and compliance with regulations.

--- SENTENCE 3084 ---
This program monitors changes in ecosystem structure (size and number of invertebrates, fish, corals, and other organisms) and function (coral recruitment, herbivory, predation).

--- SENTENCE 3085 ---
Human uses of zoned areas are also tracked.

!

--- SENTENCE 3086 ---
Photo-monitoring of corals within the FKNMS (Photo: Mike White).

--- SENTENCE 3087 ---
Lastly, continuous monitoring of certain physical parameters of seawater and ocean condition is recorded by instruments (C-MAN stations) installed along the Florida Reef Tract as part of the SEAKEYS program (SEAKEYS 2002).

--- SENTENCE 3088 ---
There are six C-MAN stations from Fowey Rocks to the Dry Tortugas, and one in Florida Bay.

--- SENTENCE 3089 ---
These stations gather data and periodically transmit it to satellites, where it is converted to near real-time reports available on the Internet.

--- SENTENCE 3090 ---
For the past ten years the Sanctuary has maintained a network of 27 thermographs that record water temperature every two hours, located both inshore and offshore throughout the Keys.

--- SENTENCE 3091 ---
As baselines are being documented, Sanctuary managers are developing a comprehensive science plan outlining specific management objectives and their associated monitoring and research needs.

--- SENTENCE 3092 ---
This is an evolving, adaptive management approach to help ensure management decisions are supported by the best available science.

Biscayne National Park encompasses 683 km2 of waters just south of Miami, including the majority of Biscayne Bay and a substantial portion of the northern reef tract with 291 km2 of coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3135 ---

#### **Gaps in Monitoring and Conservation Conservation Capacity CapacityCapacity**

Current monitoring in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary has largely focused on detecting changes within the fully protected zones and determining Sanctuary-wide status and trends of water quality, seagrasses, and corals.

--- SENTENCE 3160 ---
Some trends are beginning to show, providing a source of hypotheses to be tested.

--- SENTENCE 3161 ---
Continued monitoring is critical.

--- SENTENCE 3162 ---
These data will facilitate detecting longterm changes in communities both locally and ecosystem-wide.

--- SENTENCE 3163 ---
Reef monitoring programs in southeastern Florida are limited by a near total lack of comprehensive inventories and assessments of marine communities in this area.

--- SENTENCE 3164 ---
Baseline assessments with monitoring programs at sites located off each of the counties in the region are needed.

--- SENTENCE 3165 ---
The first step should be to develop a functional classification of the reef habitats.

--- SENTENCE 3166 ---
For effective selection of monitoring sites, this classification should incorporate criteria to ensure that both representative habitats and unique sites receive attention.

--- SENTENCE 3167 ---
The databases of reef fish in Broward, Miami-Dade, and Palm Beach Counties are based on visual survey techniques that can overlook a substantial number of cryptic species (as many as 37% in a recent Caribbean survey, Collette *et al.*  2001).

--- SENTENCE 3168 ---
Thus, intensive and broad-scale monitoring needs to be done to obtain a complete picture of the resident ichthyofauna.

--- SENTENCE 3169 ---
In addition, the fish below 30 m are poorly characterized and exploited by recreational fishers.

--- SENTENCE 3170 ---
Likewise, the reef fish communities from seagrass and mangrove habitats of Port Everglades and the Intracoastal Waterway (ICW) remain a mystery.

--- SENTENCE 3171 ---
Given the high level of human activity in the area and since these are potentially important nursery sites (Leis 1991, Fig. 164), there is need for immediate clarification.

--- SENTENCE 3172 ---
A formal monitoring program should also be instituted in the Florida Middle Grounds.

--- SENTENCE 3173 ---
Ideally, stations would be established based on the sites surveyed by Hopkins *et al.* in 1977.

--- SENTENCE 3174 ---
The ability to compare the area's current status with previous data would be helpful in detecting changes over time.

--- SENTENCE 3175 ---
To that end, video transects and methods comparable to the 1977 work should be employed.

--- SENTENCE 3176 ---
The reefs along the southeast coast and the Middle Grounds banks should be fully mapped.

--- SENTENCE 3177 ---
The data should be consistent with state, national, and international programs, and should be rapidly disseminated for public consumption.

--- SENTENCE 3178 ---
A regional archive should be established.

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and and Legislation Legislation**

When President George Bush signed the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary and Protection Act into law in 1990, the FKNMS became the first national marine sanctuary designated by Congress.

--- SENTENCE 3179 ---
Its authority, along with the 12 other national marine sanctuaries, is established under the National Marine Sanctuaries Act (NMSA) of 1972, 16 U.S.C. 1431 *et seq*., as amended.

--- SENTENCE 3180 ---
The Sanctuary is administered by NOAA under the Department of Commerce, and is managed jointly with the State of Florida under a co-trustee agreement because over half of the waters of the Sanctuary are state territorial waters.

--- SENTENCE 3181 ---
The co-trustee agreement commits the Sanctuary to a periodic review of the management plan; the first review will be in 2002.

--- SENTENCE 3182 ---
In 1997, a comprehensive management plan for the Sanctuary was implemented.

--- SENTENCE 3183 ---
It contains ten action plans and associated strategies for conserving, protecting, and managing the significant natural and cultural resources of the Florida Keys marine environment.

--- SENTENCE 3184 ---
Largely non-regulatory, the strategies educate citizens and visitors, use volunteers to build stewardship for local marine resources, appropriately mark channels and waterways, install and maintain mooring buoys for vessel use, survey submerged cultural resources, and protect water quality.

--- SENTENCE 3185 ---
As described previously, the Sanctuary management plan also designated five types of marine zones to reduce pressures in heavily used areas, protect critical habitats and species, and separate use conflicts.

--- SENTENCE 3186 ---
**FLORIDA FLORIDA FLORIDA**

A total of 24 fully protected zones were implemented in 1997 and 2001, covering approximately 6% of the Sanctuary, but protect 65% of shallow bank reef habitats and about 10% of coral resources.

--- SENTENCE 3187 ---
Most of the smaller zones (sanctuary preservation areas) are located along the offshore reef tracts and encompass the most heavily used spur and groove coral formations.

--- SENTENCE 3188 ---
In these areas, all consumptive activities are prohibited.

--- SENTENCE 3189 ---
The effectiveness of these zones and other biological and chemical parameters are monitored under the Research and Monitoring Action Plan of the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3190 ---
Commercial fishing remains one of the largest industries in the Florida Keys (Fig. 165), but it is regulated heavily by State and Federal fishery management councils.

--- SENTENCE 3191 ---
Regulations for most commercial invertebrates and finfish include annual catch quotas, closed seasons, gear catch size restrictions.

--- SENTENCE 3192 ---
The State also collects landing information on approximately 400 kinds of fish, invertebrates, and plants to track trends in catch and to evaluate regulations (DoC 1996).

--- SENTENCE 3193 ---
The reefs of southeastern Florida are in State territorial waters and protected from some impacts by State statutes and regulations.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Recommendations**

Overall, immediate action is needed to curtail alarming declines in coral reef condition throughout Florida.

--- SENTENCE 3199 ---
Local communities that are culturally and economically supported by coral reefs must employ management strategies and focus on alleviating controllable human impacts.

--- SENTENCE 3200 ---
For example, in southeastern Florida, the environmental impacts of fisheries, dredging, vessel anchorages, freshwater management, and nutrient input should receive attention to maximize protection to the reefs in this area.

--- SENTENCE 3201 ---
In the Florida Keys, solutions that address wastewater and stormwater problems, habitat degradation, and overfishing must be pursued.

--- SENTENCE 3202 ---
At the regional level, elected officials and policymakers should work to conserve and protect watersheds, reduce emissions, and decrease energy use.

--- SENTENCE 3203 ---
Citizens, elected officials, and MPA managers must work together to improve water quality,

> minimize physical impacts to corals and save energy.

--- SENTENCE 3204 ---
Globally, strict air pollution standards must be adopted, carbon dioxide emissions reduced, and renewable energy technologies employed to curb global warming trends.

--- SENTENCE 3205 ---
International policies on global climate change should be adopted and implemented.

--- SENTENCE 3206 ---
Comprehensive coral reef protection will ultimately require both proactive local steps and engaging leaders regionally and globally on climate **AB**change issues.
