#### **Introduction Introduction**

The Commonwealth of Puerto Rico is approximately 1,600 km from Miami and lies between the island of Hispaniola and the US Virgin Islands.

--- SENTENCE 3208 ---
These islands – the main island of Puerto Rico and five smaller islands – are the smallest and easternmost in the Greater Antilles.

--- SENTENCE 3209 ---
They have a combined land area of about 8,897 km2 and a linear coastline of 620 km.

--- SENTENCE 3210 ---
Two of the small islands off the eastern coast of the main island are inhabited (Culebra and Vieques); the three islands off the western coast are not (Mona, Monito, Desecheo).

--- SENTENCE 3211 ---
The island of Puerto Rico is almost rectangular (56.3 km by 161 km) with a mountainous interior formed by a central mountain chain (covering 60%), extending east to west across the island.

--- SENTENCE 3212 ---
The main island has coral growth along much of the insular shelf, but reef development is mostly restricted to the eastern, southern, and western coasts as a result of physical, climatic, and oceanic conditions.

--- SENTENCE 3213 ---
With the exception of Monito Island, NOAA recently mapped Puerto Rico's coral reef ecosystem and associated habitats (e.g., sand, hardbottom, algae, mangroves) to a depth of about 20 m, and delineated a total coral reef ecosystem area of 5,009.6 km2 (Kendall *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3214 ---
Coral reef and colonized hardbottom habitat comprised 756.2 km2 (15.1%) of the total area, seagrass habitat covered

Figure 166.

--- SENTENCE 3215 ---
Detail of a spur-and-groove formation (Photo: Matt Kendall).

!

--- SENTENCE 3216 ---
[](_page_128_Picture_6.jpeg)

624.8 km2 (12.5%), macro-algal dominated areas covered 96.7 km2 (1.9%), and the mangrove fringe covered 72.6 km2 (1.4%).

Puerto Rico, Culebra, and Vieques are nearly completely ringed with reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3217 ---
Submerged hardsubstrate rock reefs are found on the northwestern and western coast of Puerto Rico with moderate to high topographic relief and high cover of turf algae and patchy coral growth.

--- SENTENCE 3218 ---
Flat eolianite reefs (rock formed on land by cementation of calcareous dune sands), are mostly along the northern coast of Puerto Rico with high cover of turf algae, sponges, and isolated encrusting corals.

--- SENTENCE 3219 ---
Fringing reefs are found mainly in the eastern, southern, and western coasts of Puerto Rico, Culebra, and Vieques.

--- SENTENCE 3220 ---
Northern fringing reefs are characterized by shallow (1-3 m) back-reef communities dominated by finger coral *Porites porites* and scattered coral colonies of different species.

--- SENTENCE 3221 ---
Shelf-edge reefs are the best-developed but least studied coral reef ecosystems in Puerto Rico.

--- SENTENCE 3222 ---
An extensive reef formation is found at the shelf-edge off the southern coast, from Guayanilla to Cabo Rojo.

--- SENTENCE 3223 ---
This displays a typical spur-and-groove pattern with sand channels cutting through the shelf perpendicular to the coastline (Fig. 166).

--- SENTENCE 3224 ---
Off La Parguera, the reef starts at 18 m and continues down the shelf slope to at least 35 m. Optimal reef development can be found at 20 m at the shelfbreak.

--- SENTENCE 3225 ---
Some of Puerto Rico's best developed shelf-edge reefs are found off the western and southwestern sections of Desecheo and Mona Islands.

--- SENTENCE 3226 ---
Both of these systems are perhaps fringing reefs that extend all the way to the shelf-edge due to the small extension of the insular shelf in these oceanic islands.

--- SENTENCE 3227 ---
The waters that surround these oceanic reefs receive minimal terrigenous inputs.

--- SENTENCE 3228 ---
Patch reefs are relatively small, submerged coral reef systems surrounded by soft sediments.

--- SENTENCE 3229 ---
These are poorly known due to their small size and thus, are excluded from nautical charts.

--- SENTENCE 3230 ---
Nevertheless, these small patch reefs may be significant due to their high abundance in some places (Fig. 167),

such as La Parguera, Cordillera de Fajardo, Mayagüez Bay, Guayanilla Bay, Mona Island, Rincon, and Aguadilla.

--- SENTENCE 3231 ---
Coral cover generally increases with distance from shore with 10-50% live coral at shelf-edge reefs (Morelock et al. 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3232 ---
At shelf-edge sites on the reef platform, boulder star corals dominate at 3-15 m, with colonies up to 5 m in height; living coral extends to at least 40 m (Bruckner 1999, J. Morelock pers.

--- SENTENCE 3243 ---

#### **Environmental Pressures on Coral Environmental Pressures on Coral Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs**

**Human Stresses Stresses –** Reefs off the urbanized island of Puerto Rico are subject to the usual problems generated by pollution/nutrients from urban, agricultural, and industrial sources, sediment runoff (Fig. 178), coastal development, and oil and chemical spills.

--- SENTENCE 3349 ---
These problems are slowly being brought under control, but a lot remains to be done.

--- SENTENCE 3350 ---
In the 1950s, human activities such as the massive deforestation of mangroves, dredging rivers for sand and of the principal bays for ocean cargo, runoff from large scale agricultural developments in the coastal plain, the building of thermoelectric power plants on the northern and southern shores have degraded the coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3351 ---
Ship groundings have damaged reefs over the years.

--- SENTENCE 3352 ---
Vessels removed over the past decade give some indication of the number of vessels that have been grounded (Fig. 179).

--- SENTENCE 3353 ---
Some have extensively damaged reef structure and associated seagrass habitats (Glynn 1973).

--- SENTENCE 3354 ---
The *A. Regina*, a 109.7 m 3,000-ton car-passenger ferry was removed in 1990 after five years of intensive effort to remove the wreck in an environmentally safe way (G. Cintrón pers.

--- SENTENCE 3355 ---
In 1997, when the *Fortuna Reefer* was removed from a site near where the *A. Regina* ran aground, it compounded the damage done by the grounding.

--- SENTENCE 3356 ---
In an old-growth elkhorn coral thicket off Mona Island, it sheared off huge elkhorn coral branches and colonies, and fractured massive brain corals.

--- SENTENCE 3357 ---
Damage extended over 30,000 m2 .

--- SENTENCE 3358 ---
In the early 1990s, the U.S. Navy completed removing and disposing of a 6,700-ton former target ship (*Ex Brookings*) stranded during Hurricane Hugo in 1988 on a seagrass bed in the Vieques Passage (G. Cintrón pers.

--- SENTENCE 3359 ---
In 1991, the Russian 129 m 2,400-ton *Larissa Reysner* ran aground and was removed from a spur-and-groove reef formation off western Puerto Rico.

--- SENTENCE 3360 ---
That same year, the Zapata oceangoing tug *Independence Service* was raised from a 30-foot deep seagrass bed where it had sunk while being towed after grounding and subsequent removal from a nearby reef in the Vieques Passage (G. Cintrón pers comm.).

--- SENTENCE 3361 ---
Other major activities associated with reef degradation include 1) oil spills (Cerame-Vivas 1969); 2) anchoring of large oil cargo vessels (Hernández-Delgado pers.

--- SENTENCE 3362 ---
; 3) overfishing (Appledoorn *et al*. 1992), 4) uncontrolled recreational activities (Hernández-Delgado 1992, 1994), 5) eutrophication (Goenaga and Boulon 1991a), 6) thermal pollution (Hernández-Delgado 1992), and 7) military activities particularly at Vieques and Culebra Islands.

--- SENTENCE 3363 ---
The Navy operates a training facility on Vieques Island.

--- SENTENCE 3364 ---
Since 1941, a portion of the easternmost end of the island has been used for military training.

--- SENTENCE 3365 ---
Since 2001, the Navy has used nonexplosive ordnance.

--- SENTENCE 3366 ---
Scientific assessments report historical bombing off Puerto Rico's Culebra and Vieques Islands during strategic training activities has caused local destruction of reef structure (Antonnius and Weiner 1982).

--- SENTENCE 3372 ---

--- SENTENCE 3373 ---
Hurricane Georges (September 1998) was the worst hurricane since San Ciprian in 1932.

--- SENTENCE 3374 ---

--- SENTENCE 3375 ---
Other storms impacted shallow reefs with weaker winds but heavier rains (e.g., hurricanes Hortense in 1996, Marilyn in 1995, and Hugo in 1989).

--- SENTENCE 3376 ---
Physical damage to reefs from hurricanes and tropical storms over the past two decades has been most severe on the eastern coast near Culebra and Vieques (Hugo and Marilyn) and the southwestern coast near La Parguera (Hortense and Georges).

--- SENTENCE 3377 ---
Hurricane Georges devastated most of the remaining elkhorn corals scoured other shallow reef environments, blew out seagrass habitats, knocked down mangroves near La Parguera (Morelock *et al.*  2001).

--- SENTENCE 3378 ---
Other notable storms impacted shallow reefs with weaker winds but heavier rains (e.g., hurricane Hortense in 1996).

--- SENTENCE 3379 ---
The storm's biggest impact is when the surface wave action fragments the branching corals.

--- SENTENCE 3380 ---
The accompanying rains generate run-off, increasing turbidity.

--- SENTENCE 3381 ---
But hurricanes may also be beneficial because they fragment the fast growing branching corals that monopolize the substrate and create space for the slower growing, massive species.

--- SENTENCE 3382 ---
**Climate Change and Coral Bleaching Change and Bleaching –** Massive coral bleaching occurred in the late 1980s (Buckley-Williams and Williams, Jr. 1987, Goenaga *et al*. 1989, Buckley-Williams and Williams 1988 and 1989) along with elevated sea surface temperatures.

--- SENTENCE 3383 ---
The bleaching created permanent damage.

--- SENTENCE 3384 ---
More recently, Desecheo Island reefs experienced a bleaching event.

--- SENTENCE 3385 ---
ReefKeeper International reported a high incidence of bleaching (13-29%) on Desecheo Island nearshore reefs during its January 1999 survey.

**Research and Monitoring Research Monitoring** – Research on Puerto Rican coral reefs started in the 1960s and has proceeded at a slow pace until present.

--- SENTENCE 3397 ---
Initial qualitative surveys by Almy and Carrión Torres (1963).

--- SENTENCE 3398 ---
Glynn *et al*. (1964) and Glynn (1968) provided taxonomic accounts of corals and guidelines for their identification, which stimulated research on aspects of ecology during the 1970s.

--- SENTENCE 3399 ---
The first geographical inventory of reefs of the area was prepared by Goenaga and Cintrón (1979).

--- SENTENCE 3400 ---
This work, along with subsequent qualitative surveys of reef geomorphology and community structure (Cintrón *et al*. 1975, Colin 1978, Canals and Ferrer

1980, Canals *et al.* 1983) established criteria for designation of marine areas with coral reef development as Natural Reserves by the government of Puerto Rico.

--- SENTENCE 3401 ---
Intensified utilization of the coastal zone stimulated problem-oriented research involving coral reef communities, which allowed further quantitative characterizations during the late 1970s through the 1990s.

--- SENTENCE 3402 ---
Rogers *et al.* (1978) evaluated the impacts of military operations on the coral reefs of Vieques and Culebra on the northeast coast.

--- SENTENCE 3450 ---

--- SENTENCE 3451 ---
Two new Territorial no-take zones prohibit fishing and anchoring.

--- SENTENCE 3452 ---

--- SENTENCE 3453 ---

--- SENTENCE 3454 ---

--- SENTENCE 3455 ---

--- SENTENCE 3458 ---

--- SENTENCE 3459 ---
The Jobos Bay NERR is home to several federally-protected endangered species, such as the brown pelican, the peregrine falcon, the hawksbill turtle, and the West Indian Manatee (Fig. 185).

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and Legislation Laws, Legislation**

Puerto Rico's maritime jurisdiction extends offshore 16.7 km from its coastline.

--- SENTENCE 3460 ---
Recently, there have been new and revised laws and regulations for the protection of coral reefs, fisheries, and related habitats, the approval of the Non-Point Source Implementation Plan, the Mapping of Coral reefs in Puerto Rico, and an increase in Island's NGOs outreach programs.

--- SENTENCE 3461 ---
Developing regulations in the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico is different from that in the United States where control of development is a local responsibility and coastal management programs are at the state level.

--- SENTENCE 3462 ---
Because of its limited size, land use policies in Puerto Rico (including coastal management), are proposed by the Planning Board and approved by the Governor.

--- SENTENCE 3463 ---
With input from the DNER and the EQB, the Planning Board (the Board) has responsibility for overall policymaking and development control.

--- SENTENCE 3464 ---
The Board adopted and established a general policy regarding the "...avoidance of urban sprawl" and to "... concentrate industrial development to avoid potential conflicts between uses and protect the environment and natural systems."

--- SENTENCE 3465 ---
Agricultural development has a general policy to "...protect

--- SENTENCE 3468 ---

--- SENTENCE 3469 ---

The government agencies responsible for coral reef and marine resources include the DNER, the EQB, the Planning Board, the Regulations and Permits Administration (RPA), and the National Marine Fisheries Service.

--- SENTENCE 3470 ---
The DNER manages the coastal zone.

--- SENTENCE 3471 ---
The EQB establishes and monitors water quality.

--- SENTENCE 3472 ---
The RPA administers the land-use regulations adopted by the Planning Board island-wide.

--- SENTENCE 3473 ---
By statute, the RPA works closely with the EQB and DNER.

--- SENTENCE 3474 ---
Guidelines and funding under Section 6217 of the CZMA enabled DNER to prepare the Coastal Non-Point Sources of Pollution Control Plan, approved October 2000 by the NOAA and the USEPA.

--- SENTENCE 3475 ---
A Natural Protected Areas Strategy has been prepared and includes a Marine Protected Areas Subsystem, providing guidelines for important coastal area and resource identification, management and protection.

--- SENTENCE 3476 ---
In 1997, a Coral Reef Working Group was formed in the DNER to update the Coral Reef Action Plan.

--- SENTENCE 3477 ---
The members are from all government divisions and programs with responsibilities for coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3478 ---
Together, they produced the DNER five-year Coral Reef Action Plan (1999-2004) with input from U.S. Islands Coral Reef Initiative, the Puerto Rico

Costal Zone Management Program, and the University of Puerto Rico Sea Grant Program.

--- SENTENCE 3479 ---
The Action Plan focuses on gathering the necessary information needed to support science, education, monitoring, management, and enforcement, but retains the original objective of addressing the lack of information and adequate management of coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3480 ---
These have become key points in further developing a more detailed awareness, outreach, and enforcement plan.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Recommendations**

The present human pressures on Puerto Rican coral reefs are some of the most critical in the Caribbean (Goenaga and Boulon 1991b).

--- SENTENCE 3481 ---
Three of these islands currently support a resident population of over 428 people/km2 .

--- SENTENCE 3482 ---
Largely due to accelerated urban and industrial coastal development over the last four decades and the lack of effective implementation of policies to protect the ecological integrity of these resources, many of Puerto Rico's nearshore reefs are degraded.

--- SENTENCE 3483 ---
Between the 1960s and the 1980s, there was only intermittent interest in the reefs and their health.

--- SENTENCE 3484 ---
Environmental Impact Statements, required by local law for development along the shoreline, have also generated quantitative and qualitative studies of reef communities, but these mostly relate to underwater outfalls from regional wastewater treatment plants and discharges from conventional thermoelectric power plants.

--- SENTENCE 3485 ---
Since the late 1990s, however, scientists and the Government have made a concerted effort to better understand, protect, and manage the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3486 ---
## **STATUS OF CORAL REEFS IN THE U.S. VIRGIN ISLANDS STATUS OF CORAL REEFS IN THE U.S. VIRGIN ISLANDS Don Catanzaro, Caroline Rogers, Zandy Hillis-Starr, Catanzaro, Caroline Hillis-Starr, Don Catanzaro, Caroline Rogers, Zandy Hillis-Starr, Don Catanzaro, Caroline Rogers, Zandy Hillis-Starr, Rick Nemeth, and Marcia Taylor Rick Nemeth, and Marcia Taylor Rick Nemeth, and Marcia Taylor Rick Nemeth, and Marcia Taylor**

#### **THE STATUS OF THE CORAL THE CORAL REEFS OF THE U.S. VIRGIN VIRGIN ISLANDS ISLANDS**

By D. Catanzaro, C. Rogers, Z. Hillis-Starr, R. Nemeth, M. Taylor

#### **Introduction Introduction**

The U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI) is a U.S. territory located approximately 1,000 nmi southeast of Miami and 45 nmi east of Puerto Rico.

--- SENTENCE 3487 ---
Coral reefs are found around the three main islands of St. Croix, St. John, and St. Thomas, as well as most offshore cays.

--- SENTENCE 3488 ---
Fringing reefs, deep reefs (wall and shelf-edge), patch reefs, and spur and groove formations are present on all three islands although only St. Croix has well developed barrier reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3489 ---
Bank reefs and scattered patch reefs with high coral

diversity occur on geological features offshore at greater depths.

!

--- SENTENCE 3490 ---
Shallow-water reef communities cover 61% of the region (Photo: William Harrigan).

--- SENTENCE 3491 ---
Together the USVI total roughly 347 km2 of land area.

--- SENTENCE 3492 ---
St. Croix is the largest of the three USVI islands at 207 km2 (34 km by 10 km) with a relatively high western mountainous tip.

--- SENTENCE 3493 ---
This island has coral growth along much of the insular shelf with a well-developed barrier reef on the eastern end, and deep coral walls on the north shore.

--- SENTENCE 3494 ---
St. Croix is the only island with a permanent source of freshwater.

--- SENTENCE 3495 ---
St. Thomas is the second largest at 83 km2 (22 km by 5 km) and St.

John is the smallest of the three USVI islands at 52 km2 (14 by 5 km).

--- SENTENCE 3496 ---
#### Recently NOAA mapped USVI coral reefs

--- SENTENCE 3499 ---
Deeper water reef habitats off the USVI islands have yet to be mapped.

--- SENTENCE 3500 ---
Coral reef and colonized hardbottom habitats comprised 297.9

km2 and accounted for 61% of the mapped area; submerged aquatic vegetation covered 160 km2 or 33% of the mapped total, and unconsolidated sediments and uncolonized hard-bottom habitat comprised 23 km2 or the remaining 4%.

#### **Condition of Coral Reefs Reefs**

The long-term datasets for the USVI represent some of the best temporal data available for the Caribbean (Connell 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3502 ---
Although monitoring and research has occurred on all three USVI islands, consistent long-term datasets exist only for St. John and Buck Island, St. Croix (e.g. 1988 to present) and have been collected primarily by the Department of the Interior, National Park Service (NPS) and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

--- SENTENCE 3503 ---
Most of these studies are targeted in individual bays that might not be representative of conditions within the entire USVI (Table 1).

#### **Corals and Other Invertebrates Invertebrates –** NPS has conducted and supported

long-term monitoring on St. John (site of Virgin Islands National Park, VINP) and Buck Island, St Croix (site of Buck Island Reef National Monument, BINM) since 1988.

--- SENTENCE 3504 ---
Over time, statistical rigor has significantly increased due to improvements in technology and sample design.

--- SENTENCE 3505 ---
For the last three years USGS and NPS scientists have collaborated on long-term monitoring of coral reefs using a comprehensive protocol based on use of a digital video camera along randomly chosen transects (Miller and Rogers 2001, Rogers *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 3506 ---
This protocol is one of the most statistically rigorous methods to monitor coral reefs in the world.

--- SENTENCE 3507 ---
A total of 79 randomly located transects at four sites (three in St. John and one at Buck Island, St. Croix) have been repeatedly sampled for two or more years.

--- SENTENCE 3508 ---
An additional site at Buck Island, St. Croix (20 transects) has been sampled for one year and one

additional site on St. John has eight nonrandomly located transects which have been sampled for three years.

--- SENTENCE 3509 ---
Live scleractinian coral cover varies at these sites from a low of 5.8% (Buck Island, St. Croix) to a high of 22.8% (Mennebeck, St. John). .

--- SENTENCE 3510 ---
It should be noted that the site with non-randomly located transects has a live scleractinian coral cover of 45.3% (Tektite, St. John).

--- SENTENCE 3511 ---
Results of the repeated sampling are varied but overall, 76% of transects showed declines in the amount of live coral cover when the first year is compared to the third year.

--- SENTENCE 3512 ---
Percent of transects exhibiting declines at individual sites are as follows: 40% (Yawzi, St. John), 65% (Buck Island,

St. Croix), 75% (Mennebeck, St. John), 95% (Newfound, St. John), and 62% (Tektite, St. John).

--- SENTENCE 3513 ---
NOAA monitoring funds were received by the USVI Territorial Government in 2001 and University of Virgin Islands conducted the study.

--- SENTENCE 3514 ---
The first year of this project supported six sites on St. Croix (six transects each) where coral, sea urchin (*Diadema antillarum*), and reef fish have been monitored.

--- SENTENCE 3515 ---
Live scleractinian coral cover varied from a low of 6% (Lang Bank) to

25% (Sprat Hole) (Nemeth *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 3516 ---
Monitoring will be repeated in 2002.

--- SENTENCE 3517 ---
White-band Disease – Branching acroporid species are most susceptible to White-band Disease.

--- SENTENCE 3518 ---
At BINM, elkhorn coral (*Acropora palmata*) cover fell from 85% in 1976 to 5% in 1988 because of mortality from the combination of storms and disease (Rogers *et al*. 1982, Gladfelter 1991).

--- SENTENCE 3519 ---
White-band Disease is still occasionally seen throughout the USVI and shallow reef areas are now graveyards of dead elkhorn coral, with branches and fragments interspersed among algal

--- SENTENCE 3523 ---
Recruitment of elkhorn coral colonies may be increasing and biologists from NPS, USGS, and UVI are now monitoring and mapping this species at several USVI sites.

--- SENTENCE 3524 ---
Plague – In July 1997, conspicuous white patches of necrotic tissue began to appear on scleractinian corals in several bays around St. John.

--- SENTENCE 3525 ---
Tissue samples have confirmed that Plague is affecting these corals.

--- SENTENCE 3526 ---
It has now been observed on 14 coral species.

--- SENTENCE 3527 ---
The disease can progress up to 0.5 cm/day but does not always result in total colony mortality, however diseased portions never recover.

--- SENTENCE 3528 ---
Monthly surveys on one St. John reef have documented new incidence of disease every month from 1997 to present (Miller *et al.* in press) making this the most destructive disease active on St. John.

--- SENTENCE 3529 ---
Black-band Disease – This disease primarily infects major reef-building corals such as *Montastraea annularis* and *Diploria strigosa* (Edmunds 1991, Richardson *et al*. 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3530 ---
In 1988, Edmunds (1991) found very low incidence of Blackband Disease (0.2%) on corals in seven sites in the U.S. and British Virgin Islands.

--- SENTENCE 3531 ---
Nemeth reported 1.2% on St. John and

none on St. Thomas or St. Croix (Nemeth *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 3532 ---
At Buck Island, Blackband Disease is seen on *Diploria* colonies but typically on fewer than 10 colonies a year (Zandy Hillis-Starr pers.

--- SENTENCE 3533 ---
A limited, recent assessment across the USVI found 3.4% (St. Thomas), 7.6% (St. John), and 2.0% (St. Croix) of coral colonies over 25 cm in diameter showing signs of disease (Nemeth *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 3534 ---
Other Diseases – Small USVI patch reefs of *Porites porites* have died from an unknown disease (Rogers 1999, J. Miller pers.

--- SENTENCE 3537 ---
*Porites porites* is not known to be susceptible to either White-band or Blackband Disease.

--- SENTENCE 3538 ---
Sea fan disease, caused by the fungus *Aspergillis syndowii*, occurs in sea fans on St. John reefs (G. Smith pers.

--- SENTENCE 3539 ---
This pathogenic strain has been isolated from air samples taken during African dust events, suggesting a possible link between air quality and sea fan condition.

Conchs – Queen conchs used to be very abundant around St. John (Randall 1964, Schroeder 1965).

--- SENTENCE 3552 ---

--- SENTENCE 3553 ---
Conchs were surveyed along transects

--- SENTENCE 3558 ---

--- SENTENCE 3559 ---
Marine algae and Other Plants – Long term data (e.g. 1990 to present) exists only for St. John.

St. John's previously large, dense seagrass beds are no longer present.

--- SENTENCE 3561 ---
Comparison of aerial photographs (1962 and 1983) showed a decline in areal extent and/or apparent density, especially within popular anchorages.

Digital analysis of photographs of Great Lameshur Bay from 1971 to 1991 indicated a decrease in total seagrass area by 68,000 m² and the

Thousands of boats anchor in these bays each year,

--- SENTENCE 3568 ---

#### **Fish and Fisheries and Fisheries** – Reef fish

assemblages have changed markedly in the USVI (Rogers and Beets 2001), but it is difficult to separate out the causal factors.

--- SENTENCE 3569 ---
Over-fishing, deterioration of coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds all have undoubtedly contributed to significant changes in reef fish assemblages.

--- SENTENCE 3570 ---
However, many of the characteristics of the USVI fishery provide clear evidence of heavy fishing pressure.

--- SENTENCE 3571 ---
Up through the 1960s, groupers and snappers were abundant and dominated the landings in the USVI fishery.

--- SENTENCE 3572 ---
Following the tourism boom and technological changes in the fishery (larger boats, engines, improved gear), fishers began to set more traps and to target species like groupers and snappers, especially their spawning aggregations.

--- SENTENCE 3573 ---
By the 1970s, several spawning aggregations of Nassau grouper had been decimated and local abundance of this species crashed (Olsen and LaPlace 1978).

--- SENTENCE 3574 ---
The Nassau grouper is still particularly scarce today (Wolff 1996, Garrison *et al.* 1998, USGS and NPS,

unpub.

--- SENTENCE 3575 ---
After depleting the larger species of groupers, fishers began targeting smaller aggregating species such as the red hind.

--- SENTENCE 3576 ---
On St. Croix there is active targeting of the mutton snapper aggregations on the southwest side of the island.

--- SENTENCE 3577 ---
Herbivorous species have increased in relative abundance in the catch while groupers and snappers have decreased.

--- SENTENCE 3578 ---
Several studies document the failure of existing territorial regulations to protect reef fishes or reverse the declines in abundance of preferred species such as the large groupers and snappers (Beets 1996, Garrison *et al.* 1998, Wolff 1996, Beets and Rogers in press).

--- SENTENCE 3579 ---
Lack of enforcement has no doubt played a role; in one study of traps set by fishers,

over 50% had no functioning biodegradable panels to allow fish to escape if traps were lost (Garrison *et al.* 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3580 ---
However, it is unlikely that even full compliance with existing regulations would be adequate to reverse the alarming trends.

!

--- SENTENCE 3581 ---
Erosion from unpaved roads are a major source of reef sediment

#### **Water Quality Water Quality**

**–**

--- SENTENCE 3582 ---
In general, increases in point and nonpoint source discharges are causing declines in the water quality in the USVI.

--- SENTENCE 3583 ---
Wastewater disposal has been a chronic problem in the USVI.

--- SENTENCE 3584 ---
There are eight sewage treatment facilities on St. Thomas, seven secondary plants, and an anaerobic pond at the airport.

--- SENTENCE 3585 ---
The plants do not always attain secondary treatment discharge requirements (OAI 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3586 ---
A new secondary treatment plant opened in 2000 serving the 2,000 residents of Cruz Bay and surrounding areas of St. John.

--- SENTENCE 3587 ---
This secondary treatment replaced an overloaded facility that did not meet interim effluent limits and discharged into

a salt pond.

--- SENTENCE 3588 ---
The 50,000 residents of St. Croix are served by one primary wastewater treatment facility.

--- SENTENCE 3589 ---
The sewage collection system consists of 87 miles of gravity and force mains, 3 major sewage lift stations, and 12 feeder pump stations.

--- SENTENCE 3590 ---
Because of long detention time for flows arriving at the wastewater treatment plant, hydrogen sulfide is sometimes generated and deteriorates concrete sewer mains.

--- SENTENCE 3591 ---
Sewer mains have frequently and repeatedly failed, requiring raw sewage bypass during repairs (OIA 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3592 ---
Raw sewage bypasses have lasted close to a year.

--- SENTENCE 3593 ---
Untreated rum-effluent from a St. Croix distillery is discharged on St Croix's south shore resulting in a 5-mile long benthic "dead zone" caused by the high toxin level, high Biological Oxygen Demand, and the high temperature of the effluent.

--- SENTENCE 3594 ---
Each year the VI Government requests and has been granted an exemption from the U.S. Clean Water Act for this discharge.

--- SENTENCE 3595 ---
Poor land management practices associated with accelerating development on St. John pose an increasing threat.

--- SENTENCE 3596 ---

Recent studies suggest that excess sedimentation can exacerbate the effects of natural bleaching events.

--- SENTENCE 3604 ---

At reef sites exposed to sedimentation rates between 10 to 14 mg/cm2 /d, 38% of the coral colonies examined exhibited pigment loss compared to 23% of the corals observed at sites exposed to sedimentation rates between 4 to 8 mg/cm2 /d.

--- SENTENCE 3611 ---
**Socioeconomics Socioeconomics –** Fishing is an important recreational and commercial aspect of the economy of the USVI.

--- SENTENCE 3612 ---
It is important to note that no fish are exported from the USVI; in fact, during peak demand fish are imported into the USVI (Downs and Petterson 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3613 ---
USVI fisheries are small-scale, using several gear types to harvest over 180 species of reef fish (Caribbean Fisheries Management Council 1985, Beets 1997, Garrison

*et al*. 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3614 ---
The primary fishing gear in the USVI fishery (traps, followed by hook and line, and nets) has not changed greatly since the 1930s (Fiedler and Jarvis 1932), although the fishing effort has greatly increased and catch composition has changed (Appeldoorn *et al*. 1992, Beets 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3615 ---
The level of fishing effort varies greatly, some fishers use little gear nearshore and others set long trap lines across the insular shelf (B. Smith unpub.

--- SENTENCE 3616 ---
rept., Garrison *et al*. 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3617 ---
Reef fish harvesting equipment has become more sophisticated, allowing fishers to access more areas; set and retrieve more traps in a day; use longer lasting, less degradable traps; and subsequently severely impact many

species of reef fishes.

--- SENTENCE 3618 ---
Average number of traps fished per full-time fishermen has increased from 4 in 1930, to 8 in 1967, to >100 in 1997 (Fiedler and Jarvis 1932, Dammann 1969, W. Tobias pers.

--- SENTENCE 3619 ---
Maximum number of pots fished by a single fisherman in 1930 was 30 traps whereas in 1997 the maximum was 3000 traps (Fiedler and Jarvis 1932, Downs and Petterson 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3620 ---
Larger scale net fishing has been recently reported occurring in the reef areas adjacent to and east of Buck Island, St. Croix.

--- SENTENCE 3621 ---
Large nylon fishing nets are set directly off the barrier reef in the evenings to catch species of fish during nocturnal migrations off the reef.

--- SENTENCE 3622 ---

#### **Environmental Pressures on Coral Coral Pressures on Reefs**

A diverse array of stresses has caused degradation of USVI coral reefs, associated marine ecosystems, and the fishery resources dependent on them.

--- SENTENCE 3626 ---
Some natural stresses such as hurricanes have had dramatic and acute effects, while

!

--- SENTENCE 3627 ---
Prior to 1979, extensive thickets of elkhorn coral were dominant elements of USVI shallow-water reefs (Photo: Andy Bruckner).

--- SENTENCE 3628 ---
other stresses are considered chronic conditions such as strong swells, sea temperature fluctuation, sedimentation, and pollution.

--- SENTENCE 3629 ---
Human activities are superimposed on these natural stresses.

--- SENTENCE 3630 ---
Anchoring and ship groundings on coral reefs and seagrass beds are examples of acute stresses with immediate, obvious, and sometimes longterm effects (Rogers and Garrison 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3631 ---
Other acute human caused stresses affecting reefs, especially in St. Thomas and St. Croix, are dredging, sand extraction, groin construction, and sewage effluent (Goenaga and Boulon 1992).

--- SENTENCE 3632 ---
**Human Stresses –** Chronic stresses like over-fishing (commercial, hand-line, pot fishing, spear fishing, net, long-line, trolling, driftnet), point and non-point source water pollution, and sedimentation

Figure 200.

--- SENTENCE 3633 ---
This diver is surveying off Buck Island, St. Croix the extent of elkhorn coral rubble left after Hurricane Hugo (Photo: Caroline Rogers).

!

--- SENTENCE 3634 ---
[](_page_147_Picture_6.jpeg)

generally cause changes that are difficult to quantify and track but are particularly damaging.

--- SENTENCE 3635 ---
Moreover, stressors can act synergistically with natural disturbances to accelerate damage to reefs or slow their rate of recovery (Rogers and Beets 2001, Nemeth and Nowlis 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3636 ---
Fishing Pressure – Over-fishing throughout the USVI has had profound effects on the resources, including those within federally protected areas such as VINP and BINM.

--- SENTENCE 3637 ---
Reports and observations from more than 20 years ago suggested that fishing was already changing the reef-associated fishes (J. Randall's field notes 1958-1961, Olsen and LaPlace 1978).

--- SENTENCE 3638 ---
Fisheries are close to collapse, and even those ecosystems within the boundaries of "marine protected areas" are deteriorating (e.g., Beets 1996, Beets and Rogers in press).

--- SENTENCE 3639 ---
Existing zoning, erosion control, and fishing regulations are not providing sufficient protection.

--- SENTENCE 3640 ---
The present combination of natural and human stresses and the magnitude of their effects may be unprecedented.

--- SENTENCE 3641 ---
Recreational Uses – Destruction from boats running aground on reefs has been severe.

--- SENTENCE 3642 ---
Large vessels (greater than 65 ft) run aground with surprising regularity on USVI reefs (more than twice a year) and vessels abandoned after recent hurricanes still litter several harbor and reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 3643 ---
Small boats run aground on shallow reefs, destroying corals, particularly elkhorn coral.

--- SENTENCE 3644 ---
For example, within VINP, an average of four boats per week ran aground on Windswept Reef (R. Boulon pers.

--- SENTENCE 3645 ---
After the installation of resource protection buoys in 1985, groundings to this reef have decreased to an average of one a year (NPS records).

--- SENTENCE 3646 ---
Surveys off St. John make it clear that benthic resources have been damaged by anchoring (Link 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3647 ---
A dramatic case of anchor damage involved the cruise ship "Windspirit" which destroyed a 283-m2

section of reef within VINP in 1988.

--- SENTENCE 3648 ---
Ten years later, no significant recovery of coral had occurred (Rogers and Garrison 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3649 ---
VINP has installed 211 moorings and over 111 resource protection buoys around St. John to help prevent anchor damage to benthic habitats and the entire southern section of VINP is a no-anchor zone.

--- SENTENCE 3650 ---
NPS has been monitoring benthic recovery surrounding moorings in several bays for the last three years.

--- SENTENCE 3651 ---
All three USVI islands have popular snorkel and dive sites experiencing heavy visitor use (>200 visitors/site/day) (St. Croix Cane Bay Dive Shop instructors pers.

--- SENTENCE 3652 ---
comm., NPS records) that may be damaging coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3653 ---
BINM remains the number one tourist destination for St. Croix.

--- SENTENCE 3654 ---
Over 150 people per day visit the underwater interpretive snorkel trail and visits can peak over 200.

--- SENTENCE 3655 ---
BINM has a mooring system at the underwater trail that limits boats and snorkelers, but intensive use has resulted in some coral damage (Z Hillis-Starr pers.

--- SENTENCE 3656 ---
comm).

#### **Natural Stresses Natural Stresses**

Hurricanes – Since 1979, eight hurricanes have affected USVI reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3657 ---
Damage varied with storm path, strength and velocity, wave height and direction, the dominant coral species, and reef depth (e.g., Rogers *et al.* 1997, Bythell *et al.* 2000).

--- SENTENCE 3658 ---
Hurricanes David (1979) and Hugo (1989) were the most destructive and it appears that these acute incidents have pushed percent live coral cover to a relatively stable, albeit lower, equilibrium.

--- SENTENCE 3659 ---
In some shallow zones at BINM, *A. palmata* cover, already reduced from 85 to 5% by White-band Disease, fell to 0.8% after Hurricane Hugo (Gladfelter 1991).

--- SENTENCE 3660 ---
Structural recovery from Hugo has been very slow due to several subsequent hurricanes in 1995, 1998, and most recently in late 1999.

!

--- SENTENCE 3661 ---
In 2001, Buck Island National Marine Monument off the island of St. Croix became the USVI's first substantial no-take area (Photo: NOAA Ocean Service).

--- SENTENCE 3662 ---
Bythell *et al.* (1993) recorded partial and total mortality of coral colonies of three common species at 15 BINM sites over a 26-month period (1989-1991) that included Hurricane Hugo.

--- SENTENCE 3663 ---
The dominant species, *M. annularis*, suffered greater mortality from chronic factors such as predation and tissue necrosis than from the hurricane.

--- SENTENCE 3664 ---
*D. strigosa* suffered more tissue loss from the storm than from chronic factors, while *P*.

--- SENTENCE 3665 ---
*astreoides* had substantial mortality from all factors.

--- SENTENCE 3666 ---
Hurricane Hugo also caused a 40% decline in the living coral in transects surveyed on a reef in Lameshur Bay, St. John which has failed to show any significant recovery in terms of an increase in live coral cover (Rogers *et al.* 1997, NPS and USGS and NPS, unpub.

--- SENTENCE 3706 ---

--- SENTENCE 3707 ---
**Climate Change and Coral Climate Coral Coral Bleaching BleachingBleaching –** Global warming is thought to contribute to an increased frequency and strength of hurricanes in the Caribbean and coral bleaching is often associated with higher water temperatures.

--- SENTENCE 3708 ---
The worst episode of coral bleaching to date occurred worldwide in 1998 (Pomerance 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3709 ---
Extensive coral colony mortality was not associated with 1987, 1998, and 1990 USVI bleaching episodes.

--- SENTENCE 3710 ---
At two St. John sites, bleaching of coral tissues was estimated in the fall of 1998 at 43% and 47% (Rogers and Miller 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3711 ---
The 1998 bleaching episode coincided with the hottest seawater temperatures on record (four sites, NPS records).

--- SENTENCE 3712 ---
At Caret Bay reef, St. Thomas, maximum bleaching recorded was 41% but most colonies had recovered within six months (Nemeth and Nowlis 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3713 ---
Extensive bleaching (but not mortality) was observed at BINM in the fall of 1998 where an estimated 20% of *D. strigosa* at one site and 53% at a second site exhibited bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 3714 ---
During the fall of 1999, when sea temperatures reached 28.8 C,

<sup>\*\*</sup> CMES – Center for Marine and Environmental Service

mild bleaching was observed on 16%, 26%, and 48% of the coral colonies greater than 25 cm in diameter on St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, respectively (Nemeth *et al*. in press).

#### **Current Conservation Management Conservation Management**

The U.S. Department of the Interior (DoI), U.S. Department of Commerce (DoC), and the Virgin Islands Territorial Government all have jurisdiction over submerged lands within the USVI (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 3715 ---
**Mapping Mapping –** Benthic habitat types found throughout the USVI have been digitally mapped to a depth of 20 m (Kendall et al. 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3716 ---
These habitat maps will be the basis for establishing a number of permanent sites as part of a new USVI-wide longterm monitoring program.

#### **Assessments, Research, and Research, and Monitoring Monitoring**

**–**

--- SENTENCE 3717 ---
The NPS and USGS in the USVI have collected some of the longest time-series data sets on coral reefs in the Caribbean, some dating back decades (Table 2).

--- SENTENCE 3718 ---
Several innovative marine research and monitoring projects have been conducted in the USVI.

--- SENTENCE 3719 ---
The Tektite I and II underwater habitat projects took place on the south side of St. John from 1969-1971 (Collette and Earle 1972, Earle and Lavenberg 1975), and approximately 80

Figure 202.

--- SENTENCE 3720 ---
Long-term monitoring is needed to track trends and predict change in the USVI reef ecosystem (Photo: Matt Kendall).

!

--- SENTENCE 3721 ---
Little is known about the roles that deeper reef (A) and mangrove (B) habitats play in the life histories of shallow-water reef species, particularly those that have been overfished (Photo Matt Kendall).

--- SENTENCE 3722 ---
Hydrolab (1977-1985) and 13 Aquarius (1987-1989) underwater habitat missions were conducted in St. Croix.

--- SENTENCE 3723 ---
Much of the baseline information for the VINP comes from a series of reports produced by the Virgin Islands Resource Management Cooperative from 1983 1988.

--- SENTENCE 3724 ---
Fairleigh Dickinson University's West Indies Laboratory, located on St. Croix, conducted nearly 20 years of ecological studies that established a baseline for BINM (Hubbard 1991, Bythell *et al.* 1992, Gladfelter 1992).

--- SENTENCE 3725 ---
BINM and VINP have formal monitoring programs dating to the early 1980s focusing on coral reef condition, reef fish, sea turtle populations, and seagrass beds (only VINP).

--- SENTENCE 3726 ---
USGS and NPS scientists have collaborated on long-term monitoring of coral reefs using a comprehensive protocol based on use of a digital video camera along randomly chosen transects (Miller and Rogers 2001, Rogers *et al.* in press).

--- SENTENCE 3727 ---
Each year three coral reef sites (20 transects each) at VINP and two at BINM are monitored using this protocol.

--- SENTENCE 3728 ---
For the past 14 years, reef fish in VINP have been monitored at between 4 and 16 reef sites (15-18 censuses are conducted at each site) and fish censuses were recently re-established at BINM (130 censuses).

--- SENTENCE 3729 ---
Research and monitoring on

both nesting and juvenile sea turtles at BINM has been summarized in Hillis-Starr and Phillips (1997).

--- SENTENCE 3730 ---
In 2001, the USVI Territorial government initiated a long-term monitoring program with financial support from NOAA.

MPAs and No-Take Reserves – The USVI Territorial Government has designated Marine Reserves and Wildlife Sanctuaries (Salt River, Cas Cay and St. James) where fishing is allowed only with hand lines or for baitfish with a permit.

--- SENTENCE 3731 ---
Federal MPAs provide varying levels of protection and enforcement for USVI coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 3732 ---
**St.** Croix – A total of six federal MPAs protect aspects of coral reef ecosystems off this island.

--- SENTENCE 3733 ---
Buck Island Reef National Monument – The NPS manages the BINM, established on St. Croix, USVI in 1962 (Presidential Proclamation No. 3443) to protect one of the finest coral reef ecosystems in the Caribbean.

## **STATUS OF THE FLOWER GARDEN BANKS OF THE STATUS OF THE STATUS OF THE FLOWER GARDEN BANKS OF THE NORTHWESTERN GULF OF MEXICO NORTHWESTERN GULF OF MEXICO NORTHWESTERN GULF OF MEXICO George P. Schmahl George P. Schmahl Schmahl George P. Schmahl George P. SchmahlGeorge P. Schmahl**

#### **Introduction Introduction**

The Flower Garden Banks are two prominent geological features on the edge of the outer continental shelf in the northwest Gulf of Mexico, approximately 192 km southeast of Galveston, Texas.

--- SENTENCE 3745 ---
Created by the uplift of underlying salt domes of Jurassic origin, they rise from surrounding water depths of over 100 m to within 17 m of the surface (Fig. 205).

--- SENTENCE 3746 ---
Stetson Bank, 48 km to the northwest of the Flower Gardern Banks, is a separate claystone/ siltstone feature that harbors a low diversity coral community.

--- SENTENCE 3747 ---
Fishermen gave the Flower Garden Banks their name because they could see the bright colors of the reef from the surface and pulled the brightly colored corals and sponges up on their lines and in their nets.

--- SENTENCE 3748 ---
These are the northernmost coral reefs on the continental shelf of North America, located between 27˚ 52' and 27˚ 56' North.

--- SENTENCE 3749 ---
They are isolated from other Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico reefs, being over 690 km from the nearest reefs of the Campeche Bank off the Mexican Yucatan Peninsula.

--- SENTENCE 3750 ---
The East Flower Garden Bank, located at 27˚ 54.5' N, 93˚ 36.0' W, comprises about 65.8 km2 and contains about 1.02 km2 of coral reef.

--- SENTENCE 3751 ---
About 19.3 km to the west, the West Flower Garden Bank, (27˚ 52.5' N, 93˚ 49.0' W) comprises about 77.2 km2 , of

which about 0.4 km2 is coral reef (Gardner *et al*. 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3752 ---
Structurally, the Flower Garden Banks coral reefs are composed of large, closely spaced heads up to three or more meters in diameter and height.

--- SENTENCE 3753 ---
Reef topography is relatively rough, with many vertical and inclined surfaces.

--- SENTENCE 3754 ---
If the relief of individual coral heads is ignored, the top of the reef is relatively flat between the reef surface and about 30 m. It slopes steeply between 30 m and the reef base.

--- SENTENCE 3755 ---
Between groups of coral heads, there are sand patches and channels from 1-100 m long.

--- SENTENCE 3756 ---
Sand areas are typically small patches or linear channels.

--- SENTENCE 3757 ---
Probably due to its geographic isolation and other factors, there are only about 28 species of reefbuilding corals, a relatively low diversity.

--- SENTENCE 3758 ---
Interestingly, the Flower Garden Banks contain no elkhorn or staghorn corals and no shallow-water sea whips or sea fans (gorgonians) which are common in the Caribbean.

--- SENTENCE 3759 ---
Coral growth is relatively uniform over the entire top of both banks, occupying the bank crests down to about 50 m. As the reef slopes in the deeper regions, corals grow flatter and individual heads can cover large areas.

--- SENTENCE 3760 ---
The East and West Flower Garden Banks were designated as the Flower Garden Banks National

>

--- SENTENCE 3761 ---
Marine Sanctuary (the Sanctuary or FGBNMS) in January 1992.

--- SENTENCE 3762 ---
In 1996, Stetson Bank was added.

--- SENTENCE 3763 ---
The Sanctuary encompasses 145.8 km2 and includes all of the shallow coral reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 3764 ---
#### **Condition of the the Coral Reefs Reefs**

The Flower Garden Banks are two of the least disturbed coral reefs in the Caribbean and western

--- SENTENCE 3767 ---
The ocean water bathing the reefs is clear with visibility usually 25-30 m. Salinity and temperature variations are well within the range required for active coral growth.

--- SENTENCE 3768 ---
When first studied in the early 1970s, coral communities in the Flower Garden Banks appeared stable and in excellent general health and have remained so.

--- SENTENCE 3769 ---
Some isolated injury caused by anchoring vessels, illegal fishing gear, tow cables, and seismic arrays was observed.

--- SENTENCE 3785 ---
The current status provided by Dokken et al. (1999) is based on data from the 1996 and 1997 monitoring effort (Table 19).

--- SENTENCE 3786 ---
Live coral cover above 30 m averages 51.8% (53.8% on the East Bank and 49.8% on the West Bank).

--- SENTENCE 3787 ---
The coral heads are frequently very cavernous, showing evidence of substantial internal bioerosion (Fig. 207).

--- SENTENCE 3788 ---
Other prominent benthic components include coralline algae-covered rock (45.4%), leafy and filamentous algae (2.7%), sponge (1.5%), and patches of sand (less than 0.1%) may cover 10% of the bottom.

--- SENTENCE 3789 ---
Since sites were chosen to monitor reef habitat and avoid sand, sand channels and patches

probably account for around 10% of the Bank benthos.

--- SENTENCE 3790 ---
By percentage cover, the dominant coral species are the boulder star coral (*Montastrea annularis* complex, 28.8%), symmetrical brain coral (*Diploria strigosa*, 9%), mustard hill coral (*Porites astreoides*, 4.6%), and the great star coral (*Montastrea cavernosa*, 4.4%).

--- SENTENCE 3791 ---
Diversity (H') averaged 1.727 for all monitoring years since 1992,

and Evenness (E) averaged 0.853.

--- SENTENCE 3792 ---
Coral bleaching is routinely observed most years when water temperatures exceed 30° C, but is generally low and does not result in significant mortality (Dokken et al. 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3793 ---
Based on repetitive quadrat photography, no bleaching was observed in 1996 at either the East or West Flower Garden Bank.

--- SENTENCE 3794 ---
In 1997, bleaching was observed in 1.9% of the coral colonies on the East Bank, and in 1.2% of the colonies on the West Bank.

--- SENTENCE 3795 ---
Bleaching during the summer of 1998 was slightly higher than previous years, but was still less than

5%, with mortality less than 1% (Q. Dokken pers.

--- SENTENCE 3796 ---
Coral disease was relatively rare, with only 23 incidents of disease or other unexplained mortality observed in over 3700 colonies.

--- SENTENCE 3797 ---
Data from the 1998 and 1999 monitoring effort have been compiled and are now under review.

--- SENTENCE 3798 ---
Predation of living coral by parrotfish (Bruckner *et al.* 2000) is commonly observed, but the long-term effect of this phenomenon is not known at this time (Fig. 208).

--- SENTENCE 3799 ---
**Algae–** Only recently has the coral reef algal community been well documented.

--- SENTENCE 3800 ---
Crustose coralline and calcareous green algae are common.

--- SENTENCE 3801 ---
Collections obtained in 1999 show a community of at least 44 species of algae in depths above 30 m (S. Fredericq pers.

--- SENTENCE 3802 ---
Benthic macroalgae are a minor, yet important component of the reef community in terms of potential competitors for space (Fredericq *et al.* 2000), growing mostly in crevices and sandy interfaces.

--- SENTENCE 3803 ---
Solitary foliose algae are rarely encountered; most of the algal community is composed of turf species.

--- SENTENCE 3804 ---
Algae are a primary

component of the deeper portions of the banks (below 30 m).

--- SENTENCE 3805 ---
The region between 46 and 88 m is known as the 'algal-sponge zone' (Rezak *et al*. 1985).

--- SENTENCE 3806 ---
Algal populations have historically been low, with percent cover estimates generally less than 5% between 1989 and 1996.

--- SENTENCE 3807 ---
The algal community increased to over 13% after the long-spined sea urchin die-off in 1983-84, but returned to predieoff levels after two years (Gittings and Bright 1986), perhaps due to an increase of other herbivores.

--- SENTENCE 3808 ---
Blue-green algae are abundant and invading open space on coral heads (S. Fredericq pers.

--- SENTENCE 3809 ---
This could be in response to elevated nutrient levels, and therefore, may be an important indicator of water quality degradation and a potential concern for the condition of the entire ecosystem (S. Fredericq pers.

--- SENTENCE 3810 ---
In 1997, a slight increase in a red or blue-green turf algal mat was observed on both banks, averaging about 5% cover (Dokken *et al.* 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3811 ---
Algal cover declined slightly to about 3.2% in 1998, but then underwent a dramatic increase in 1999 (27.6% on the East Bank, 20.7% on the West Bank)

--- SENTENCE 3812 ---
This increase occurred as algae colonized the bare reef rock, and may signal that environmental factors are changing to favor algae.

--- SENTENCE 3813 ---
The mushroom-like shape of this brain coral is a product of bioerosion (Photo: Frank and Joyce Burek).

--- SENTENCE 3814 ---
**Water Quality Water Quality –**

--- SENTENCE 3815 ---
In the vicinity of the Sanctuary, water quality is generally very good.

--- SENTENCE 3816 ---
Being on the outer edge of the Texas-Louisiana continental shelf, the Banks are directly influenced by the circulation patterns of the Gulf of Mexico.

--- SENTENCE 3817 ---
The most prominent current is the Loop Current which brings warm, clear water from the Caribbean through the Yucatan channel into the Gulf of Mexico basin, where it travels in a clockwise direction moving towards the western shelf of Florida.

--- SENTENCE 3818 ---
Moving inshore on the shelf, there is a significant onshore-offshore current component influenced by Loop Current rings and

spin-off eddies.

--- SENTENCE 3819 ---
Close to shore there is a counterclockwise (east to west) shelf current off western Louisiana and Texas.

--- SENTENCE 3820 ---
This current is strongest in

Figure 208.

--- SENTENCE 3821 ---
A stoplight parrotfish at the East Flower Garden Bank (Photo: Dick Zingula).

!

--- SENTENCE 3822 ---
[](_page_154_Picture_14.jpeg)

winter and almost absent in summer (Lugo-Fernandez 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3823 ---
Water temperature near the Sanctuary varies seasonally and with depth.

--- SENTENCE 3824 ---
Average temperature over seven years varied at the reef surface at 24 m from a minimum of 19-20° C in February to a maximum of 29-30° C in July/August, with an annual range of 9-11° C (Lugo-Fernandez 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3825 ---
Interannual variations occur and temperatures over 30° C have been observed (Gittings *et al.* 1992), generally accompanied by varying levels of coral bleaching (Hagman and Gittings 1992).

--- SENTENCE 3826 ---
Salinity ranges between 35 and 36.5 ppt near the reef surface.

--- SENTENCE 3827 ---
Visibility averages 25-30 m. Turbidity is generally very low, but periods of discoloration have been observed, primarily in June or July, and may be associated with the Mississippi and Atchafalaya River outflows and coastal waters moving onto the shelf (Deslarzes 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3828 ---
Surface waters are affected by freshwater flows when wind patterns reverse, changing nearshore currents.

--- SENTENCE 3829 ---
Large Mobile Invertebrates – The Flower Garden Banks are home to at least 27 species of sponges, 20 species of polychaetes, 62 species of crustaceans, 667 species of mollusks, and 36 species of echinoderms.

--- SENTENCE 3830 ---
As in the case of mollusks, when invertebrate taxonomic experts inventory the biota of the Sanctuary, the total number of resident and transient species should increase substantially.

--- SENTENCE 3831 ---
The Flower Garden Banks had an almost complete die-off of the long-spined sea urchin in 1983-84.

--- SENTENCE 3832 ---
There has been very little, if any, sustained recovery, even though individual sea urchins are found (Schmahl pers.

--- SENTENCE 3837 ---
Fish diversity is low compared with other Caribbean and South Atlantic reefs (266 species) and abundance is high (Pattengill-Semmens 1999).

--- SENTENCE 3838 ---
Based on abundance, planktivores and invertebrate feeders are the most dominant trophic groups (Pattengill *et al.* 1997).

--- SENTENCE 3839 ---
Some of the most abundant species at all three banks were reef butterflyfish (Chaetodon sedentarius), Spanish hogfish (Bodianus rufus), bluehead wrasse (Thalassoma bifasciatum), brown chromis (Chromis multilineata), bicolor damselfish (Stegastes partitus), creolefish (Paranthias furcifer), and sharpnose puffer (Canthigaster rostrata).

--- SENTENCE 3840 ---
A unique gold color phase of the smooth trunkfish (Lactophrys triqueter) has been documented (Pattengill 1998, Fig. 209).

--- SENTENCE 3841 ---
Fish families and groups notably absent or only represented by one or few species in low numbers include grunts (Haemulidae), snappers (Lutjanidae), and hamlets (*Hypoplectrus* spp.).

--- SENTENCE 3842 ---
There is also evidence that these reefs may serve as an important spawning and aggregation area for certain species of grouper.

--- SENTENCE 3843 ---
The banks are year-round habitat for devil rays and manta rays (*Mobula hypostoma* and *Manta birostris*, Fig. 210), and whale sharks (*Rhincodon typus*).

--- SENTENCE 3844 ---
They serve as a winter habitat for several species of schooling sharks, including hammerhead (*Sphyrna lewini*) and silky sharks (*Carcharhinus falciformis*), and spotted eagle rays (*Aetobatus narinari*) (J. Childs 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3845 ---
Fishing pressure on the Sanctuary does not appear to be intense, but fishermen have used longline fishing gear in the vicinity of the banks and along the entire continental shelf since the late 1800s.

--- SENTENCE 3846 ---
Commercial snapper and grouper fishing occurs along the continental shelf edge, including the Flower Garden Banks.

--- SENTENCE 3847 ---
Target areas for this activity

are typically the deeper portions of the Bank structure, away from the shallower coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 3848 ---
Anecdotal information suggests that snapper, jewfish, and other grouper populations have declined over time.

--- SENTENCE 3849 ---
These are present but do not occur in abundance.

--- SENTENCE 3850 ---
There is no data prior to the late 1970s.

--- SENTENCE 3851 ---
Fish population estimates were not made at the same time as observations of algal populations, but by 1990, a significant increase in the abundance of queen and stoplight parrotfish (*Scarus vetula* and *Sparisoma viride*, respectively) was reported.

--- SENTENCE 3852 ---
Gittings *et al.* (1992) suggested that this increase may be due to greater availability of algae following the demise of long-spined sea urchins in the mid-1980s.

--- SENTENCE 3853 ---
**Other Marine Life Other Life –** Juvenile loggerhead sea turtles (50-100 kg) are resident at the East and West Flower Garden Banks (Fig. 211).

--- SENTENCE 3854 ---
Based on satellite tracking studies, these turtles have a range of approximately 130 square kilometers, tightly centered on the Banks (Hickerson 2000).

--- SENTENCE 3855 ---
Hawksbill and leatherback turtles (*Dermochelys coriacea*) have also been reported.

--- SENTENCE 3856 ---
Atlantic spotted and pan-tropical spotted dolphins (*Stenella plagiodon* and *S. attenuatus* respectively), and bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*) are commonly seen.

--- SENTENCE 3857 ---
Recently an unidentified species of beaked whale was reported.

#### **Coastal Populations and Reef Economics Economics**

Recreational SCUBA diving is popular and the demand appears to be increasing.

--- SENTENCE 3858 ---
There are currently three live-aboard charter dive vessels which can carry up to 35 divers each.

--- SENTENCE 3859 ---
In 1997, from a survey of charter dive operations, it was estimated that 2,350 divers annually visit the Flower Garden Banks.

--- SENTENCE 3860 ---
These divers spent \$870,000 in Texas.

--- SENTENCE 3861 ---
About \$636,000 was spent in the local economy of Free-port Texas where it generated \$1.1 million in sales/output, \$477,000 in income, and 24 full and part-time jobs.

--- SENTENCE 3862 ---
An additional \$234,000 was spent in other areas of Texas with \$559,000 in sales/output, \$228 thousand in income, and 11 more jobs (Ditton and Thailing 2001).

#### **Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs Reefs**

**Human Pressures Pressures –** Since they are relatively far from both Texas and Louisiana, the Flower Garden Banks are well buffered from urban pressures.

--- SENTENCE 3863 ---
There are four primary threats to these reefs: 1) physical injury from vessel anchoring, 2) potential water quality degradation, 3) impacts of fishing and fishing-related activities, and 4) impacts from oil and gas exploration and development.

--- SENTENCE 3864 ---
Over the last 20 years, a number of large industry vessels, freighters, and fishing vessels have anchored at the Flower Garden Banks and caused significant damage (Gittings *et al*. 1992).

--- SENTENCE 3865 ---
Since 1994 there have been at least three large vesselanchoring incidents.

--- SENTENCE 3866 ---
Foreign-flagged cargo vessels have occasionally anchored, unaware of the anchoring restrictions.

!

--- SENTENCE 3867 ---
A loggerhead turtle (Photo: Frank and Joyce Burek).

--- SENTENCE 3868 ---
Primary sources of potential degradation of water quality include coastal runoff, and river and effluent discharges from offshore activities such as oil/gas development and marine transportation (Deslarzes 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3869 ---
Oxygen-depleted (hypoxic) near-bottom waters have been found in a large area of the northern Gulf.

--- SENTENCE 3870 ---
Although relatively far from the Flower Garden Banks, there is concern that this area could grow and move, impacting the outer continental shelf.

--- SENTENCE 3871 ---
Often called the 'dead zone', this area has included up to 16,500 km2 on the continental shelf from the Mississippi delta to the Texas coast.

--- SENTENCE 3872 ---
General coastal runoff and degraded nearshore water quality can potentially impact the banks through cross-shelf transport processes, which brings turbid, nutrient-rich water offshore.

--- SENTENCE 3873 ---
Deslarzes (in press) postulates the fluorescent bands observed in the carbonate skeletons of some corals come from the seasonal transport of

nearshore water onto the Sanctuary, which may be tainted by urban, agricultural, and biological contaminants.

--- SENTENCE 3874 ---
Research using nitrogen isotopes suggests a pathway for direct primary nitrogen input from coastal river sources a considerable distance away.

--- SENTENCE 3875 ---
Benthic algae from Stetson Bank have a distinct nitrogen isotope signature similar to plants found in coastal estuarine systems, suggesting coastal influences on water quality are reaching only as far as Stetson Bank.

--- SENTENCE 3876 ---
Nitrogen isotopes from the Flower Garden Banks have signatures of oceanic origin (K. Dunton pers.

--- SENTENCE 3877 ---
The impacts of fishing and associated activities are not well known.

--- SENTENCE 3878 ---
At this time, only traditional hook and line fishing is allowed in the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3879 ---
However, illegal fishing by both commercial longliners and recreational spearfishers has been reported.

--- SENTENCE 3880 ---
Targeted fishing efforts, which are allowed under current regulations, could have a significant detrimental impact on snapper and grouper populations.

--- SENTENCE 3881 ---
Lost and discarded fishing gear has been observed at both the Sanctuary and Stetson Banks (Fig. 212).

--- SENTENCE 3882 ---
These can cause localized physical injury to coral reefs and can entangle and injure loggerhead sea turtles and other animals.

--- SENTENCE 3883 ---
The High Island 389A gas production platform within the Sanctuary (Photo: Frank and Joyce Burek).

!

--- SENTENCE 3884 ---
The two primary groups using reef resources are fishers and SCUBA divers.

--- SENTENCE 3885 ---
Recreational hook-and-line fishers frequently use the area.

--- SENTENCE 3886 ---
Commercial snapper and grouper long-line fishers fish along the edges of the banks and sometimes illegally within the borders, or lose gear

!

--- SENTENCE 3887 ---
Hook-and-line fishing gear snagged on a coral (Photo: Frank and Joyce Burek).

that drifts into the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3888 ---
However, these activities are typically in the deeper portions of the bank structure.

--- SENTENCE 3889 ---
The northern Gulf of Mexico is one of the most active areas for oil and gas exploration and development.

--- SENTENCE 3890 ---
By the end of 1995, approximately 5,000 production platforms had been installed (approximately 1,000 were subsequently removed), 32,000 wells had been drilled and 80,000 km of pipeline installed (Deslarzes 1998, A. Alvarado pers.

--- SENTENCE 3891 ---
The Gulf of Mexico accounts for more than 72% of the oil and 97% of the natural gas produced in offshore U.S. waters.

--- SENTENCE 3892 ---
Within a four-mile radius of the Flower Garden Banks, there are currently 10 production platforms and around 161 km of pipeline, half of which are dedicated oil pipelines (Deslarzes 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3893 ---
There is one gas production platform (High Island 389A) within the East Sanctuary boundary (Fig. 213).

--- SENTENCE 3894 ---
Potential impacts from offshore oil and gas exploration and development include accidental spills, contamination by drilling related effluents and discharge, anchoring of vessels involved in placing pipelines, drilling rigs and production platforms, seismic exploration, use of dispersants in oil spill mitigation, and platform removal.

--- SENTENCE 3895 ---
In spite of the intense industrial activity, long-term monitoring studies indicate no significant detrimental impact to the coral reefs of the Sanctuary from nearby oil and gas development (Gittings 1998).

--- SENTENCE 3896 ---
Fortunately, there have been no major oil spills or impacts from these activities.

--- SENTENCE 3897 ---
**Climate Change and Bleaching Change and Bleaching –**

--- SENTENCE 3898 ---
The location and depth of these coral reefs buffer them some-

what from the short-term effects of global warming and climate change.

--- SENTENCE 3899 ---
Even though the effects of coral bleaching are relatively low to date, some bleaching is routinely observed, mostly when the water temperature approaches 30˚ C. As global ocean temperatures increase, this will no doubt increase.

#### **Current Conservation Management Current Conservation Management**

**Mapping Mapping –** Using high-resolution multi-beam sonar coupled with an extremely accurate vehicle motion sensor and very precise navigation, the USGS, the University of New Brunswick, and C & C Technologies, Inc. mapped the East and West Flower Gardens and Stetson Banks (Gardner *et al.* 1998).

####

--- SENTENCE 3900 ---
**Monitoring, Assessments, and Research Monitoring, and Research –**

Since 1989, there has been a consistent, long-term monitoring program at the East and West Flower Garden Banks.

--- SENTENCE 3901 ---
NOAA and the Minerals Management Service (MMS) share the funding for this program.

--- SENTENCE 3902 ---
While not all, much of the monitoring has been related to concerns about the potential impact of oil and gas development.

--- SENTENCE 3903 ---
This program includes analysis of coral cover, relative abundance, diversity, and coral growth rates.

--- SENTENCE 3904 ---
Coral cover, abundance and vitality (disease, bleaching) are measured along random transects and at permanently marked, repeatedly sampled photo-quadrat stations.

--- SENTENCE 3905 ---
Coral growth data are collected using photography and growth-ring measurements from coral cores.

--- SENTENCE 3906 ---
Continuous-recording instruments have been installed to measure temperature and light at the reef surface.

--- SENTENCE 3907 ---
Results of the long-term monitoring efforts are published periodically (Gittings *et al.* 1992, Continental Shelf Associates 1996, Dokken *et al.* 1999, Dokken *et al.* 2001).

--- SENTENCE 3908 ---
Prior to the development of the long-term monitoring program, there had been other quantitative studies of the benthic community at FGBNMS since 1972 (Bright and Pequegnat 1974, Viada 1980, Continental Shelf Associates 1985).

--- SENTENCE 3909 ---
Additional studies include periodic reef fish censuses and trophic studies (Pattengill *et al*. 1997), elasmobranch surveys (sharks and rays), sea turtle tagging and tracking, coral recruitment research, annual observations and experiments relating to mass coral spawning (Fig. 214), and

studies on historical water quality and paleoclimate (using coral cores).

--- SENTENCE 3910 ---
Enhanced water-quality instruments were installed in 2001, and are now collecting data on temperature, salinity, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, pH, and light intensity.

--- SENTENCE 3911 ---
**MPAs–** The Flower Garden Banks were designated as a National Marine Sanctuary in January 1992, and are administered by NOAA.

--- SENTENCE 3912 ---
In cooperation with appropriate partners, the Sanctuary staff directs resource protection, education, research, and enforcement efforts.

--- SENTENCE 3913 ---
MMS provides additional protection through requirements imposed on industry operators in what is known as the 'Topographic Features Stipulation' for the Sanctuary.

!

--- SENTENCE 3914 ---
Researchers from the University of Texas lay tiles out on a reef during a study of coral spawning (Photo credit: Ed Enns).

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and and Legislation Legislation**

Regulations governing the Flower Garden Banks are authorized under the National Marine Sanctuaries Act, as amended, 16 U.S.C. 1431, and are contained within the Code of Federal Regulations 15 CFR 922, Subparts A, E, and L, and can be accessed on the web.

--- SENTENCE 3915 ---
They are designed to protect the sensitive coral reef and bank features of the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3916 ---
They prohibit all anchoring, mooring any vessel greater than 100 feet (30.5 m) in registered length on a Sanctuary mooring buoy, oil and gas exploration and development within a designated no activity zone (almost the entire sanctuary), injuring or taking coral and other marine organisms, using fishing gear other than traditional hook and line, discharging or depositing any substances or materials, altering the seabed, building or

abandoning any structures, and using explosives or electrical charges.

--- SENTENCE 3917 ---
To reduce damage, moring bouys have been installed (Fig. 215).

--- SENTENCE 3918 ---
Effective June 1, 2001, the International Maritime Organization designated the Flower Garden Banks as the world's first international no-anchor zone.

#### Gaps in Current Monitoring and Conservation Capacity

The increased algal abundance highlights the need for more water quality monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 3919 ---
This needs to cover nutrient sampling and more detailed current

and water circulation information.

--- SENTENCE 3920 ---
It also should be expanded to include specific studies on algae population dynamics, the incidence and etiology of coral disease, and the area of the coral reef community in the deeper parts of the Sanctuary.

--- SENTENCE 3921 ---
The frequency of the monitoring program should also be increased to capture the aspects of community ecology that undergo short-term and seasonal

!

--- SENTENCE 3922 ---
Mooring buoys have been installed at FGBNMS to prevent anchor damage to corals (Photo: Joyce and Frank Burek).

--- SENTENCE 3923 ---
fluctuations (algal biomass, coral bleaching, herbivores, etc.).

--- SENTENCE 3924 ---
The distance from shore hampers research and enforcement efforts.

--- SENTENCE 3925 ---
It also hampers monitoring human activity.

--- SENTENCE 3926 ---
While some data on visitor use can be acquired by a variety of remote methods such as overflights, satellite imagery, and remote radar systems, the Sanctuary needs on-site observation, management and enforcement.

--- SENTENCE 3927 ---
In May, 2001, the Sanctuary recently acquired its own vessel, an 82foot cutter, but also relies on charter vessels.

#### Conclusions and Recommendations

Recent data indicating the Flower Garden Banks may be an important spawning area for several species of grouper highlights the importance of considering a marine reserve to protect the biodiversity of this area.
