fishing, boating, diving, snorkeling, and coastal activities.

--- SENTENCE 4679 ---
Concerns have been raised over the impact of the catch-and-release fishery at Midway.

--- SENTENCE 4680 ---
Large jacks have been infrequently encountered on fish surveys at Midway (relative to French Frigate Shoals) since recent surveys began in 1993, and especially since the catch-and-release fishery began in 1996 (NMFS Honolulu Lab in prep.).

--- SENTENCE 4681 ---
Concerns exist over potential commercial SCUBA-based 'live aboard' boats and cruise ships working their way up the NWHI chain.

--- SENTENCE 4682 ---
**Climate Change and Coral Bleaching Change and Coral Bleaching –** Declines in seabirds, monk seals, reef fishes, and phytoplankton in the NWHI from the early 1980s to early 1990s (Polovina *et al*. 1994) are thought to have resulted from regional decreases in oceanic productivity (Polovina *et al*. 1995).

--- SENTENCE 4683 ---
There was little monitoring for bleaching events in the NWHI during the 1997-1998 ENSO bleaching event; remnant evidence of such events was not detected during the NOWRAMP 2000 expedition.

#### **Current Conservation Management Management**

**Mapping Mapping –** The shallow-water (to a depth of approximately 30 m) coral reef ecosystems of the NWHI will be mapped using image analyses of commercially-available, high-resolution satellite imagery.

--- SENTENCE 4684 ---
Imagery has been purchased for 10 NWHI locales.

--- SENTENCE 4685 ---
Unvalidated draft maps have been generated for three of these – Kure Atoll, Midway Atoll, and Laysan Island.

--- SENTENCE 4686 ---
Similar maps are expected to be generated for the remaining seven areas by July 2002.

--- SENTENCE 4687 ---
At that time, an extensive effort will be initiated to validate all maps of the NWHI shallow

**HAWAI'I HAWAI'I HAWAI'IHAWAI'I**

water coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4688 ---
It is anticipated that final maps will be available by January 2003.

--- SENTENCE 4689 ---
**Assessment and Monitoring Assessment Monitoring –** NOAA, USFWS, Hawai'i DLNR, the Bishop Museum, the Oceanic Institute, the University of Hawai'i, the University of California at Santa Cruz (UCSC), and private sector companies launched the NOW-RAMP initiative in 2000 to map and assess the status of coral reef shallow-water habitats in the NWHI (Fig. 259).

--- SENTENCE 4690 ---
An additional expedition in 2001, sponsored primarily by the NOAA Honolulu Fisheries Laboratory with additional participation by USFWS and UCSC, provided the opportunity to collect additional information and establish data monitoring buoys on reefs at French Frigate Shoals, Maro Reef, Lisianski Island, Pearl and Hermes Atoll, Midway Atoll, and Kure Atoll, and also included limited diver observations on Raita Bank (Maragos and Gulko 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4691 ---
An early baseline assessment of shallow reef fish populations was conducted at French Frigate Shoals and Midway Atoll during 1980-1983 by USFWS fisheries biologists.

--- SENTENCE 4692 ---
Honolulu Laboratory biologists completed new baseline assessments at French Frigate Shoals and Midway in 1992 and 1993, respectively (DeMartini *et al.* 1996) and conducted annual monitoring surveys at both sites during 1995-2000 (DeMartini *et al.* 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4693 ---
Since the early 1980s, NOAA Honolulu Fisheries Laboratory scientists have monitored endangered Hawaiian monk seals and sea turtles off French Frigate Shoals, Laysan, Lisianski, Pearl and Hermes, Midway, and Kure.

--- SENTENCE 4694 ---
Since 1992 NMFS has conducted annual reef fish surveys at French Frigate Shoals and Midway Atoll.

--- SENTENCE 4695 ---
Since 1990, these scientists have also mapped NWHI underwater benthic habitats using towed divers, video cameras, and submersible vehicles.

--- SENTENCE 4696 ---
The NWHI contain a number of examples of species-specific, limited-take MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 4697 ---
The majority of the NWHI is classified as Critical Habitat for the endangered Hawaiian monk seal.

--- SENTENCE 4698 ---
By federal regulation, a 50-mile protected species zone exists around the NWHI islands and atolls restricting longline fishing, and seasonal area closure zones were in effect for the take of NWHI lobster until the entire fishery was recently closed down.

--- SENTENCE 4699 ---
On May 26, 2000, President Clinton directed the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior, in cooperation with the State of Hawai'i, and in consultation with the Western Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Council (WPRFMC), to develop recommendations for a new coordinated management regime to increase protection for the unique coral reef resources of the NWHI.

--- SENTENCE 4700 ---
As a result, discussions have ensued over their trusteeship and jurisdictional authority.

--- SENTENCE 4701 ---
The State of Hawaii holds trusteeship of all reef resources out to three nautical miles from any emerged point of land in the NWHI173.

--- SENTENCE 4702 ---
The USFWS administers a National Wildlife Refuge throughout the NWHI (with the exception of Kure Atoll), the boundaries of which are currently being solidified and may vary in certain portions of the refuge.

--- SENTENCE 4703 ---
NOAA currently has jurisdictional authority over most reef resources outside of three nautical miles primarily through NMFS with the WPRFMC serving in an advisory role.

--- SENTENCE 4704 ---
The result of this effort was Executive Order 13178, which on December 4, 2000 established the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve.

--- SENTENCE 4705 ---
The new NWHI Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve contains provisions for a number of functional notake areas distributed across the entire NWHI (with the exception of Midway) in federal waters and ranging from 25 to 100 fathoms in depth.

--- SENTENCE 4706 ---
Other regulations to be included within these areas include restrictions on anchoring, discharge and non-extractive uses.

--- SENTENCE 4707 ---
This scientist is making a video record of one of the many reefs surveyed during the 2000 NOWRAMP assessment (Photo: James Maragos).

Midway, though geographically located within the NWHI, is the only portion of the Hawaiian Archipelago that is not part of the State of Hawai'i.

--- SENTENCE 4709 ---
It is administered independently by the USFWS as a National Wildlife Refuge.

#### **Gaps in Current Monitoring Gaps Monitoring**

Multiple agency jurisdictional authority over reef resources raises questions about effective stewardship of the NWHI's coral reefs, which is arguably the last major set of reef ecosystems left in the world that have not been heavily affected by human intrusion.

--- SENTENCE 4711 ---
The recent establishment of the NWHI Coral Reef Ecosystem Reserve should help sort out some of these conflicts and provide for a protective umbrella within Federal waters under which the various agencies can partner to effectively manage these unique resources.

--- SENTENCE 4712 ---
Currently State waters are not covered within this reserve and comparable effective State management structure or resources are lacking.

--- SENTENCE 4713 ---
This is of critical importance as many reef scientists feel that the majority of high biodiversity coral reef habitat in the NWHI is located within State waters.

--- SENTENCE 4714 ---
Current lack of regulations controlling extractive activities within NWHI waters pose a particular problem; the proposed State of Hawai'i FMA for the NWHI may not fully close this gaping loophole to protecting this fragile and unique wilderness area.

--- SENTENCE 4715 ---
Difficulties in patrolling and enforcing regulations throughout the 1,600 km (1,000 miles) length of the NWHI poses a problem in encouraging compliance from the various types of vessels (fishing, research, and eco-tourism) currently in the area and the large number of vessels expected to enter the area in the future.

--- SENTENCE 4716 ---
Creation of an automated Vessel Monitoring System (VMS), with a transmitting unit required on all vessels operating in the NWHI, and which automatically notifies both the ship in question and the appropriate enforcement and resource trustees of approach to protected or off-limits174 areas would go a long ways towards effectively solving this problem given the large distances and the extremely limited resources available to the USCG and the resource trustees.

--- SENTENCE 4717 ---
Efforts are currently underway to fund installation of VMS on various types of vessels, though how the vessels will be monitored and which agencies will have access to the data still needs to be worked out.

--- SENTENCE 4718 ---
Management of the NWHI has been shared among agencies with differing missions.

--- SENTENCE 4719 ---
Reliance on the WPRFMC to advise NMFS on management of NWHI fisheries resources at levels that do not impact the sustainability of the fished species, nor

prevent reef ecosystem damage, may have been of limited success.

--- SENTENCE 4720 ---
Federal court litigation has occurred during the last two years relating to NMFS compliance with federal fisheries management and endangered species laws in the NWHI.

--- SENTENCE 4721 ---
The proposed draft WPRFMC Coral Reef Ecosystem Fisheries Management Plan (FMP) proposes to manage the coral reef ecosystems of the NWHI at an ecosystem level, yet excludes all other existing FMPs from the majority of listed management measures.

--- SENTENCE 4722 ---
Since many of the coral reef species are already listed under other existing FMPs (crustaceans, groupers, snappers, sharks)

--- SENTENCE 4723 ---
the ecosystem approach is still subordinate to single-species decision-making.

--- SENTENCE 4724 ---
Mechanisms (such as automated VMS, active zoning, mitigative bonding) that have been successful in other managed coral reef areas of the Pacific have not been incorporated fully into the existing or proposed WPRFMC's FMPs for the NWHI.

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and Legislation Government Policies, Laws, and Legislation**

The majority of the shallow water coral reefs are under the jurisdictional authority of the State of Hawai'i (primarily DLNR).

--- SENTENCE 4725 ---
Direct military control over areas of the NWHI has been phased out over the last 30 years; Midway was turned over to the USFWS, and the USCG abandoned LORAN stations at Kure and Tern Island (French Frigate Shoals) in the 1970s to 1980s.

--- SENTENCE 4726 ---
In 1998, President Clinton signed Executive Order 13089 for Coral Reef Protection which mandated "All Federal agencies whose actions may affect U.S. coral reef ecosystems shall: a) identify their actions that may affect U. S. coral reef ecosystems; b) utilize their programs and authorities to protect and enhance the conditions of such ecosystems; and, to the extent permitted by law, c) ensure that any actions they authorize, fund, or carry out will not degrade the conditions of such ecosystems.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Recommendations**

Coral reefs have always been an important component of human existence in Hawai'i, as they provide habitat and other resources for fish and invertebrates that are popular for human consumption (Fig. 260).

--- SENTENCE 4748 ---
The nearshore reefs once provided the majority of the protein for the Hawaiian people, and today consumptive uses of reef resources include subsistence, commercial, and recreational activities.

--- SENTENCE 4749 ---
Despite their importance, coral reefs in Hawai'i suffer from degradation related to continued human population growth, urbanization and development.

--- SENTENCE 4750 ---
Ocean outfalls, urbanization, and massive coastal recreational development (e.g., hotels, golf courses) are presently focal points for coral reef degradation in Hawai'i (Jokiel and Cox 1996).

--- SENTENCE 4751 ---
New technologies for extraction, offshore aquaculture, and bioprospecting raise concerns about the ability of management agencies to keep up with new impacts to coral reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 4752 ---
Economic and business pressures to allow such

**HAWAI'I HAWAI'I HAWAI'I HAWAI'I HAWAI'I**

impacts may have severe consequences for Hawai'i where coral reefs represent a thin band of habitat directly next to the shore, yet are extremely important to the marine tourism industry which serves as a major lynchpin in the overall Hawaiian economy.

--- SENTENCE 4753 ---
There are strong indications of overfishing for the majority of food fish and invertebrates in the MHI.

--- SENTENCE 4754 ---
Similar concerns are starting to be expressed in regards to the impact of the marine ornamental trade.

--- SENTENCE 4755 ---
These problems are compounded by the realization that the status of fisheries resources in the MHI are considerably under-reported, making proper management of these resources difficult at this time.

--- SENTENCE 4756 ---
The coral reefs of the Hawaiian Archipelago represent not only the majority of U.S. reef area, but also a set of unique ecosystems of unusually high endemism and diversity of reef types, along with a uniquely predator-dominated fish assemblage within the NWHI.

--- SENTENCE 4757 ---
Given this, issues such as alien species introduction and marine ornamental collection175, are of stronger concern here then in many other coral reef areas.

--- SENTENCE 4758 ---
Hawai'i has a wide variety of types of MPAs which protect coral reef habitat to some extent, yet very little of MHI reefs are 'No-take MPAs' where extraction of any type is not allowed.

--- SENTENCE 4759 ---
With only 0.3% of the MHI coral reef habitat protected as 'No-take MPAs,' it's going to be extremely challenging to meet the USCRTF's established goal of setting aside a minimum of 20% of the representative coral reef habitat as 'No-take MPA' by the year 2010.

--- SENTENCE 4760 ---
Even those few areas that are currently 'Notake MPAs' in the MHI are exposed to heavy human usage for recreation and marine tourism potentially undermining their effectiveness in representing 'natural' coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4761 ---
While new efforts and joint partnerships have been initiated by the resource trustee agencies, academia, nongovernmental organizations and the various communities themselves, more support (financial and political) for the existing and proposed efforts is needed in order to effectively sustain the exceptionally wide variety and area of coral reef habitat and resources found in the Hawaiian Archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 4762 ---
**HAWAI'I HAWAI'I HAWAI'IHAWAI'I**

#### **Condition of Coral Coral Reefs**

Due to the steepness of the main islands, shallow water habitats around the islands are limited and consist primarily of fringing coral reefs (85%) with a few offshore banks (12%), and two atolls (3%).

--- SENTENCE 4784 ---
The fringing reefs

have narrow reef flats (50-500 m); depths of 1000 m are reached within 2-8 km from shore.

--- SENTENCE 4785 ---
The coral reefs are currently recovering from a series of natural disturbances over the past two decades: a crown-of-thorns starfish invasion (1979), three hurricanes (1986, 1990, 1991), and a period of warm water temperatures that caused mass coral bleaching (1994) (Fig. 261).

--- SENTENCE 4786 ---
Additionally, there are chronic human-induced impacts in areas like Pago Pago Harbor (Craig *et al*. 2000a).

--- SENTENCE 4787 ---
By 1995, the corals were beginning to recover, as evidenced by an abundance of coral recruits (Mundy 1996, Birkeland *et al*. 1997).

--- SENTENCE 4788 ---
Coral growth has continued through 2000, but a full recovery will take time.

--- SENTENCE 4789 ---
There have also been improvements to reefs in Pago Pago Harbor by the removal of 9 shipwrecks; and another shipwreck was removed at Rose Atoll (Green *et al*. 1998).

--- SENTENCE 4790 ---
Additionally, the export of 'live rock' from coral reefs was banned in June 2000.

--- SENTENCE 4791 ---
**Algae–** Information is limited, but with a few exceptions, the algae found around the islands indicate a low-nutrient environment and/or heavy grazing by herbivores.

--- SENTENCE 4792 ---
Encrusting coralline algae cover (*Porolithon*) is high (40-50%).

--- SENTENCE 4793 ---
These algae help cement and stabilize the loose surface below (Birkeland *et al*. 1997).

--- SENTENCE 4794 ---

--- SENTENCE 4795 ---
Despite the on-going recovery of corals on local reefs, many fish and invertebrates are not recovering as quickly.

--- SENTENCE 4807 ---

--- SENTENCE 4808 ---

**Water Quality Water Quality –** Due to the steepness of the islands and their limited development of shallow water habitats, the continual flushing by ocean currents provide generally good water quality.

--- SENTENCE 4816 ---
There are three exceptions: 1) sedimentation from improper land use practices that pours into coastal waters after heavy rains, 2) nutrient enrichment from human and animal wastes in populated areas, and 3) contamination in Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 4817 ---

#### **Coastal Populations and Reef Reef Economics EconomicsEconomics**

American Samo's population was 57,300 in 2000.

--- SENTENCE 4823 ---
During the past 10 years, the population increased by 10,500 people, an increase of 22%.

--- SENTENCE 4824 ---
The population is increasing at a yearly rate of 2.1%, adding about 1,200 people each year (Fig. 264).

--- SENTENCE 4825 ---
It is expected to continue, given the high birth rate (4.0 children per female), the fact that 50% of the population is younger than age 20, and the high immigration rate.

--- SENTENCE 4826 ---
Adverse human-related impacts will likely increase with rapid population growth.

--- SENTENCE 4827 ---
Population growth in American Samoa.

!

--- SENTENCE 4828 ---
[](_page_193_Figure_15.jpeg)

A recent Governor's Task Force on Population Growth report called for a population ceiling of 115,000.

--- SENTENCE 4829 ---
This ceiling is calculated on resources (particularly drinking water) and the diminishing quality of life.

--- SENTENCE 4830 ---
An action plan for the Territory identifies specific steps to reduce birth and immigration rates (Craig *et al*. 2000b).

--- SENTENCE 4831 ---
More than 18,000 tourists (calculated in 1995) visit the islands annually and expend over \$10 million (calculated on tourist receipts from 1990, United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4832 ---
In 2001, ex-vessel landings from small boats in the domestic commercial fisheries generated \$2 million (NMFS 2001).

--- SENTENCE 4833 ---
However, the actual economic impact of commercial fisheries in American Samoa is far greater when distant-water tuna harvests are included.

--- SENTENCE 4834 ---
These fish are processed in two local canneries in Pago Pago Harbor.

--- SENTENCE 4835 ---
Their ex-vessel value from both foreign and domestic vessels was approximately \$232 million (Western Pacific Fishery Management Council 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4836 ---
American Samoans still rely on local coral reefs for food, and it is estimated that the reefs provide an economic base of \$1 million per year (Fig. 265).

**Natural Stresses Natural Stresses –** American Samoa lies close to a warmer than usual mass of seawater that tends to form south of the territory during La Niña years.

--- SENTENCE 4840 ---
Nearby Fiji and Western Samoa have been hit hard by mass coral bleaching in recent years, so it would seem probable the reefs of American Samoa may be similarly impacted.

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and Legislation Laws, Legislation**

Legislation is in place for water quality standards, land use regulations, waste disposal, fishery management, habitat protection, endangered species, protected areas, ship pollution, and other environmental issues.

--- SENTENCE 4867 ---
Environmental violations are more frequently detected and prosecuted, but enforcement of these regulations is not widespread and many problems persist.

--- SENTENCE 4868 ---
Local environmental agencies have also undertaken aggressive education programs to increase community awareness and understanding of environmental issues.

--- SENTENCE 4869 ---
This effort is commendable, but it is difficult to keep pace with the territory's rapidly growing population and development pressures.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Recommendations**

To date, coral reefs in American Samoa have been resilient to a series of natural perturbations, although full recovery may take another decade.

--- SENTENCE 4881 ---
The message for managers is that the reefs will recover no additional human pressure, but there are several examples where serious harm has already been done, particularly overfishing of reef resources, reduced water quality in populated areas, and loss of turtle nesting beaches to coastal construction.

--- SENTENCE 4882 ---
Climatic change has uncertain consequences for local reefs.

--- SENTENCE 4883 ---
Several areas needing additional work for coral reef conservation in the Territory.

--- SENTENCE 4884 ---
**Expand coral reef monitoring efforts, but focus the objectives.

--- SENTENCE 4885 ---
Most quantitative monitoring efforts in American Samoa might be characterized as ecological monitoring that tracks changes in the ecosystem over time.

--- SENTENCE 4886 ---
These studies have provided valuable insight, highlighting that coral reefs are very dynamic systems.

--- SENTENCE 4887 ---
From another perspective, however, these studies do not address questions commonly faced by coral reef managers.

--- SENTENCE 4888 ---
Such things as "Is overfishing occurring?"

--- SENTENCE 4889 ---
"Is sediment from poor land-use practices harming the reef?"

--- SENTENCE 4890 ---
Consequently, any monitoring program must clearly identify 1) who is the intended user of the data, and 2) what parameters should be measured to provide that information.

--- SENTENCE 4891 ---
In addition to this management-driven approach, a monitoring program in American Samoa should be 1) achievable with local staff, although off-island scientific expertise may be needed to address some issues, 2) stable to rotations of technical staff who are typically hired on 2-year contracts, 3) comparable to other programs as much as possible, and 4) open to community input and management.

--- SENTENCE 4892 ---
**Restart monitoring of coral reef fisheries.

--- SENTENCE 4893 ---
A workshop in American Samoa identified overfishing as the major problem hindering recovery of local reefs (Craig *et al*. 1999).

--- SENTENCE 4894 ---
It is essential to collect basic harvest data to monitor trends in total catch, catch-per-unit-effort, etc.

--- SENTENCE 4895 ---
**Improve land-use practices that impact water quality.

--- SENTENCE 4896 ---
Despite welcome improvements in water quality in Pago Pago Harbor, coral reefs there have not fully recovered nor is there safe swimming or

uncontaminated fish in the harbor.

--- SENTENCE 4897 ---
A phased recovery plan is needed to build on the progress already made.

--- SENTENCE 4898 ---
Harbor fish and sediments also need to be re-tested for toxicity at regular intervals.

--- SENTENCE 4899 ---
Additionally, improvements in land-use and waste disposal practices are needed to reduce sedimentation and pollutants (Fig. 267).

--- SENTENCE 4900 ---
**Create a territorial network of no-take marine protected areas.

--- SENTENCE 4901 ---
** There are two issues here.

--- SENTENCE 4902 ---
First, existing MPAs in the territory are not adequately enforced.

--- SENTENCE 4903 ---
Second, no-take MPAs are needed in the main islands where there is overfishing.

--- SENTENCE 4904 ---
**Create a regional network of MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 4905 ---
A meaningful effort to protect coral reef resources requires a regional approach.

--- SENTENCE 4906 ---
In addition to the issue of larval transport of reef fishes and invertebrates, sea turtles provide an excellent example of a shared resource that binds the islands in the region together.

--- SENTENCE 4907 ---
Tagging data show green sea turtles nest in American Samoa and migrate to both Fiji and Tahiti to feed, so conservation efforts are needed at both ends of their migration routes.

--- SENTENCE 4908 ---
The South Pacific biogeographic region needs a network of MPAs to address these issues.

--- SENTENCE 4909 ---
Land-use practices within nearby watersheds affect coral reef health through their influence on sedimentation and nutrient levels (Photo: Kip Evans).

## **STATUS OF THE CORAL REEFS OF GUAM STATUS OF THE CORAL REEFS OF GUAM STATUS OF THE CORAL REEFS OF GUAM Robert H. Richmond and Gerry W. Davis Robert W. Davis Robert H. Richmond and Gerry W. DavisRobert H. Richmond and Gerry W. Davis Robert H. Richmond and Gerry W. Davis**

#### **Introduction Introduction**

Guam is a U.S. territory located at 13o 28' N, 144o 45' E and is the southernmost island in the Mariana Archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 4911 ---
It is the largest island in Micronesia, with a land mass of 560 km2 and a maximum elevation of approximately 405 m.

--- SENTENCE 4912 ---
The northern portion of the island is relatively flat and consists primarily of uplifted limestone.

--- SENTENCE 4913 ---
The southern half of the island is primarily volcanic, with more topographic relief and large areas of highly erodible lateritic soils.

--- SENTENCE 4914 ---
The island possesses fringing reefs, patch reefs, submerged reefs, offshore banks, and a barrier reef surrounding the southern shores.

--- SENTENCE 4915 ---
The reef margin varies in width, from tens of meters along some of the windward areas, to well over 100 meters.

--- SENTENCE 4916 ---
The combined area of coral reef and lagoon is approximately 69 km2 in nearshore waters between 0-3 nmi, and an additional 110 km2 in federal waters greater than 3 nmi offshore (Hunter 1995).

--- SENTENCE 4917 ---
Guam lies close to the center of coral reef biodiversity.

--- SENTENCE 4918 ---
Sea surface temperatures range from

Figure 268.

--- SENTENCE 4919 ---
Common Acropora species (Photo: Gustav Paulay).

!

--- SENTENCE 4920 ---
[](_page_198_Picture_8.jpeg)

about 27-30OC with higher temperatures measured on the reef flats and in portions of the lagoons.

--- SENTENCE 4921 ---
According to G. Paulay (pers.

--- SENTENCE 4922 ---
comm.), 4 seagrass species, 306 marine macroalgae species, 403 stony and 77 soft coral species, 128 sponge species, 295 foraminiferan species, 53 flatworm species, 1,673 mollusk species, 104 polychaete species, 840 arthropod species, 194 echinoderm species, 117 ascidian species, 3 sea turtle species, and 13 marine mammal species have been

recorded from Guam's coral reef ecosystems.

--- SENTENCE 4923 ---
Myers and Donaldson (in press) list 1019 species of shorefishes (epipelagic and demersal species found down to 200 m) from the islands of the Southern Marianas, making no distinction among Guam, Rota, Tinian, and Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 4924 ---
Coral reef fisheries include both finfish and invertebrates.

--- SENTENCE 4925 ---
These fisheries are both economically and culturally important.

--- SENTENCE 4926 ---
Reef fish have been historically important in the diet of the population, however, westernization and declining stocks have reduced the role of reef fish overall.

--- SENTENCE 4927 ---
Many of the residents from other islands in Micronesia continue to include reef fish as a staple part of their diet.

--- SENTENCE 4928 ---
Sea cucumbers, a variety of crustaceans, molluscs, and marine algae are also eaten locally.

--- SENTENCE 4929 ---
In addition to the cash and subsistence value of edible fish and invertebrates, reef-related fisheries are culturally important as family and group fishing is a common activity in Guam's coastal waters.

#### **Condition of Coral Reef Ecosystems Ecosystems**

The condition of Guam's reefs is variable, ranging from excellent to poor, depending on adjacent land and land-use characteristics, accessibility, location of ocean outfalls and river discharges, recreational pressures and oceanic circulation patterns.

--- SENTENCE 4930 ---
Due to the limestone nature of northern Guam (hence no natural lakes or streams), the northern reefs are generally in better condition than those affected by erosion and sedimentation in the south.

--- SENTENCE 4931 ---
Aquifer discharge and associated eutrophication effects are evident on some northern reefs.

--- SENTENCE 4932 ---
Coral cover and diversity are generally highest on the northeastern (windward) exposures, with a variety of *Acropora*  species dominating the reef crest and slope (Fig. 268).

--- SENTENCE 4933 ---
The eastern reefs along the central and southern portions of the islands are heavily affected by sedimentation and freshwater runoff during the rainy season that occurs from June through November.

--- SENTENCE 4934 ---
During this period, terrigenous sediments often accumulate on the reef flats and reef slope.

--- SENTENCE 4935 ---
During the early 1990s, a road project along the southern shores of the island resulted in particularly heavy sedimentation of a 10 km section of

fringing reef, killing all the coral.

--- SENTENCE 4936 ---
Most of the fringing reefs along the southern part of the island, continuing up along the southwestern shores are in poor to fair condition.

--- SENTENCE 4937 ---
Apra Harbor is off the central part of the island, on the Philippine Sea (western side).

--- SENTENCE 4938 ---
The harbor is home to a large Navy Base and is also the location of the port facilities.

--- SENTENCE 4939 ---
Both fringing reefs and

shoals (patch reefs) are found within the harbor, and those closest to the harbor mouth are in relatively good condition.

--- SENTENCE 4940 ---
Further into the harbor, corals and reefs have been impacted by freshwater runoff, sediment and thermal discharges from the Island's main power generation facilities.

--- SENTENCE 4941 ---
Agana, Tumon, and Piti Bay (also known as Tapungun) Bays have heavy human use.

--- SENTENCE 4942 ---
The inner areas of these bays are in relatively poor condition, affected by discharges from land as well as the impacts of recreational activities.

--- SENTENCE 4943 ---
Agana and Tumon Bays are centers for tourism.

--- SENTENCE 4944 ---
East Agana Bay serves as a main site for commercial watercraft (jet ski) operations.

--- SENTENCE 4945 ---
West Agana has a sewage treatment plant built on the reef flat that had a pipe discharge in 60 ft of water (Fig. 269).

--- SENTENCE 4946 ---
Infrastructure upgrades presently underway are expected to improve water quality within these bays, and limited/experimental restoration activities are planned.

--- SENTENCE 4947 ---
**Coral and other Invertebrates and other Invertebrates –** Coral cover on the good-to-excellent reefs ranges from 35-70%, while the most damaged sites have less than 10%

Figure 270.

--- SENTENCE 4948 ---
Crown-of-thorns starfish (Photo: Donna Turgeon).

!

--- SENTENCE 4949 ---
Sewage from ocean outfalls (A) contributes to euthrophication (B) algae washed up on tourist beaches (Photo: Bob Richmond and Donna Turgeon).

--- SENTENCE 4950 ---
coral cover and fleshy algae and sediment dominate the substratum.

--- SENTENCE 4951 ---
Data compiled by Birkeland (1997b) found transect data taken in the 1960s generally showed reefs with over 50% live coral cover, but only 7 of 113 transects measured in the 1980s-1990s had over 50% live coral cover, while 88 had less than 25% live coral.

--- SENTENCE 4952 ---
In surveys taken off the Northern District sewer outfall in the early 1990s, not only was coral cover below 25%, most of the live coral was restricted to a few species, particularly the rapidly growing, common lobe and plate coral

--- SENTENCE 4953 ---
[*Porites* (*= Synarea) rus*], with indications of an overall reduction in coral species diversity.

--- SENTENCE 4954 ---
Recruitment data also support the observations of an overall decline in coral reef condition.

--- SENTENCE 4955 ---
In 1979, 278 coral recruits were found from 525 fouling plates placed out on reefs around Guam (0.53 corals/plate), while data collected in 1989 and 1992 found only 0.004 and 0.009 recruits/plate respectively (Birkeland pers.

--- SENTENCE 4956 ---
Coral diseases, the competitive black encrusting sponge *Terpios hoshinota*, and coralline algal lethal orange disease (CLOD) have all been observed on Guam's reefs, but none seem to be at a critical level at this time.

--- SENTENCE 4957 ---
While the crown-of-thorns starfish occurred in small to moderate numbers over the past few years, a greater abundance of juveniles now is cause for concern about the potential for a future outbreak (Fig. 270).

--- SENTENCE 4958 ---
**Algae–** Blue-green algae that recently are overgrowing coral have been a concern at some sites.

--- SENTENCE 4959 ---
**Fish** – Fish populations have declined 70% over the past 15 years, as documented by the Guam Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources.

--- SENTENCE 4960 ---
Total day and night finfish harvest for 1985 was estimated at 151,700 kg.

--- SENTENCE 4961 ---
In 1999, this number had dropped to 62,689 kg.

--- SENTENCE 4962 ---
Acanthurid fishes (surgeons), important reef herbivores, accounted for approximately 23% of the total catch in 1999 (Fig. 271).

--- SENTENCE 4963 ---
Catch-per-unit-effort has dropped by over 50% since

1985, and large reef fish are rare.

--- SENTENCE 4964 ---
Seasonal runs of juvenile rabbitfish (Fig. 272), a local favorite, were considered poor for the 1997-1999 seasons, but numbers increased last year.

--- SENTENCE 4965 ---
Regulations and protected reserves are being enforced to deal with this problem.

--- SENTENCE 4966 ---
SCUBA spear fishing and gill netting are still allowed on Guam, which is contrary to the prevailing conservation ethic.

--- SENTENCE 4967 ---
Legislation is being proposed to regulate these fishing methods.

--- SENTENCE 4968 ---
**Water Quality** – Increased stormwater runoff from an airport expansion project, new roads, hotels, shopping centers and golf courses resulted in reduced coastal water quality, especially in bays and areas of restricted water circulation.

--- SENTENCE 4969 ---
The salinity of waters over coastal reefs was found to drop below 28 ppt after periods of rainfall during summer coral spawning, which results in reproductive failure (Richmond 1996).

--- SENTENCE 4970 ---
Stormwater collection passes into sewer lines, and during heavy rain

the sewage treatment plants divert the wastewater directly into the ocean outfall pipes, often with only primary treatment.

--- SENTENCE 4971 ---
Three of the Island's outfall pipes discharge within 200 m of the shoreline, in depths of 20-25 m and in areas where corals are found.

--- SENTENCE 4972 ---
Extension of the Northern and Central District outfalls into deeper waters further offshore is planned.

--- SENTENCE 4973 ---
A variety of pollutants has been found in the sediments of

!

--- SENTENCE 4974 ---
Two species of Acanthurid fish from Guam (Photo: Gustav Paulay).

--- SENTENCE 4975 ---
Apra Harbor, including PCBs, heavy metals, and PAHs.

--- SENTENCE 4976 ---
A harbor dredging project is in the planning stages and poses a concern for surrounding reefs.

--- SENTENCE 4977 ---
Agrochemicals are also a concern for coastal waters.

## Coastal Populations and Reef Economics

The island underwent a development boom in the late 1980s and early 1990s, resulting in a 15.4% increase in the past ten years to its current population of 154.8 thousand (U.S. Cen-

sus Bureau 2000).

--- SENTENCE 4978 ---
Additionally over 1.4 million tourists visit the island each year (OIA 1997).

--- SENTENCE 4979 ---
Tourism, primarily from Japan and other Asian countries, is the largest industry on island.

--- SENTENCE 4980 ---
In 1990, tourist expenditures contributed \$936 million to Guam's economy (UNESCAP 2002).

--- SENTENCE 4981 ---
Hence, coral reefs and associated marine recreation are of substantial economic value, contributing over \$80 million per year.

--- SENTENCE 4982 ---
Guam's coral reef fisheries, both finfish and invertebrates, are economically and culturally important.

--- SENTENCE 4983 ---
The annual ex-vessel value of commercial fisheries landings on Guam is currently \$1.3 million (NMFS 2001).

--- SENTENCE 4984 ---
Marine algae also are eaten locally.

--- SENTENCE 4988 ---

mented to substantially reduce both coral diversity and abundance (Fig. 273, Randall and Birkeland 1978).

--- SENTENCE 4993 ---
Fish populations and catch-per-unit-effort have measurably declined since data collection began in 1985 (Fig. 274).

--- SENTENCE 4994 ---
Fishing practices, including the use of unattended gill nets, bleach, SCUBA spearfishing, and fish traps have contributed to the problem.

--- SENTENCE 4995 ---
However, habitat loss due to sedimentation, pollution, and physical damage has also been responsible for reduced fish populations.

--- SENTENCE 4996 ---
With over 1 million tourists visiting Guam each year, many from countries where a coral reef conservation ethic is not fully developed, damage to reefs is inevitable.

--- SENTENCE 4997 ---
In addition to impacts from SCUBA divers and snorkellers, underwater walking tours using surface-supplied equipment and a large number of personal watercraft (jet skis) have affected reefs and water quality.

--- SENTENCE 4998 ---
A coastal use zoning law called the Recreational Water Use Master Plan was passed into law to address these problems but it needs enforcement support and updating to cover new activities and areas of concern.

--- SENTENCE 4999 ---
Groundings of fishing vessels, recreational watercraft, and ships carrying cargo and illegal immigrants have resulted in localized damage to reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5000 ---
Guam's main power generation facilities are located on Cabras Island, in the northern portion of Apra Harbor (Fig. 275).

--- SENTENCE 5001 ---
Water that used to cool the generators has killed coral.

--- SENTENCE 5002 ---
Cleaning chemicals have also been discharged, with subsequent impacts on local coral populations.

--- SENTENCE 5003 ---
**Natural Stresses Natural Stresses –** Guam is in the tropical Pacific 'typhoon belt,' and experiences an average of one substantial tropical storm or typhoon each year.

--- SENTENCE 5004 ---
The coral reefs are of major value in providing protection from storm waves and associated coastal erosion.

--- SENTENCE 5005 ---
**Climate Change and Coral Bleaching Change and Bleaching –** Coral bleaching has been documented to coincide with elevated water temperatures associated with El Niño events.

--- SENTENCE 5006 ---
Potential climate change impacts include inundation of low lying coastal areas, and increased sedimentation from drought followed by heavy rains.

--- SENTENCE 5007 ---
Coral bleaching has been observed at a number of sites including within Apra Harbor and in Piti Bay just to the north.

--- SENTENCE 5008 ---
Both scleractinians and alcyonarians have been affected, with a few pockets of high mortality.

--- SENTENCE 5009 ---
However, the 1998 bleaching event in the Pacific did not cause widespread coral mortality in Guam.

#### **Current Conservation Management Management**

**Mapping Mapping –** Guam needs coral reef habitat mapping.

--- SENTENCE 5010 ---
With current funding levels, NOAA habitat mapping of Guam's coral reef ecosystems is planned to begin in 2002.

--- SENTENCE 5011 ---
In FY00, NOAA awarded a grant to the Guam Division of Aquatic and Wildife Resources (DAWR) for water quality monitoring at 30 stations (10 freshwater, and 20 marine) within the Agana and Tumon sub-watersheds.

--- SENTENCE 5012 ---
After reviewing existing data and survey work, sites identified as high risk for altered water quality were sampled for a battery of key microbial, chemical, and physical water quality parameters.

--- SENTENCE 5013 ---
Total fisheries harvest in Guam, 1985-1996 (Modified from Birkeland 1997).

These two watersheds are located in urban-use areas (i.e., the primary hotel area and a major portion of Guam's business district), and are high human-contact zones (recreationally, commercially, and consumptively).

--- SENTENCE 5015 ---
This project will be the basis for the development of future long-term coral reef monitoring strategies and sound management approaches to preserve and restore Guam's coral reef systems.

--- SENTENCE 5016 ---
In FY01, Guam continued its water quality monitoring of urbanized bays and initiated coral cover monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5017 ---
The University of Guam Marine Laboratory has ongoing coral reef monitoring programs, in col-

--- SENTENCE 5019 ---
laboration with the DAWR and the Guam Environmental Protection Agency (GEPA).

--- SENTENCE 5020 ---
The Marine Lab database dates back to 1970, and focuses on the marine biota.

--- SENTENCE 5021 ---
The DAWR collects data on fish catch through creel censuses, while GEPA has routine water quality sampling programs.

--- SENTENCE 5022 ---
A joint educational outreach program exists as a collaboration among the three aforementioned groups as well as the Guam Coastal Management Program.

--- SENTENCE 5023 ---
**MPAs and No-take Reserves Reserves –** There are two Federal (War in the Pacific National Historical Park and Guam National Wildlife Refuge) and 11 territorial MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 5024 ---
Five of the territorial MPAs are no-take marine reserves (Pati Point, Tumon Bay, Piti Bomb Holes, Sasa Bay, and Achang Reef Flat

Preserves) representing approximately 12% of the coastline and 28% of the coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5025 ---
Established in 1998, all five marine reserves are under full enforcement.

--- SENTENCE 5026 ---
In 1986 two ecological no-take reserves were established as mitigation.

--- SENTENCE 5027 ---
These reserves would add 2% more coastline and 5% more reef area to the total but they have not been enforced.

--- SENTENCE 5028 ---
An ocean current assessment is presently underway at the Pati Point Preserve to determine the areas most likely to be seeded by larvae originating from this preserve.

--- SENTENCE 5029 ---
Fish abundance, size, and diversity data are being collected to document the value of the preserves and the success of the program.

#### **Government Policies, Laws, and and Legislation Legislation**

Guam's natural resource legislation protecting coral reef resources is presented in two laws.

--- SENTENCE 5030 ---
The prevailing legal authority is the Guam Legislature or statutory law.

--- SENTENCE 5031 ---
These laws are relatively old and have not been revised in the past 20 years.

--- SENTENCE 5032 ---
For this reason, although it is specifically referenced, coral is considered a fish.

--- SENTENCE 5033 ---
When these laws were created, the only group likely to impact reefs were fishermen.

--- SENTENCE 5034 ---
Guam's statutory laws regulate the taking of coral and have penalties for fishing damage.

--- SENTENCE 5035 ---
Coral can be taken only under a permit issued by the Department of Agriculture.

--- SENTENCE 5036 ---
But no permits have been issued since 1982.

--- SENTENCE 5037 ---
The law has provisions for both personal and commercial take but limits such permits to five days and requires specific collecting locations be identified.

--- SENTENCE 5038 ---
This same title (5 GCA chapter 63) also regulates fishing net mesh sizes used in coastal waters as well as illegal chemical and explosives.

--- SENTENCE 5039 ---
In addition, the legislature also delegated the authority and responsibility of management and oversight for all aquatic and wildlife resources to the Department of Agriculture.

--- SENTENCE 5040 ---
Recently, the Department of Agriculture's DAWR used its regulatory authority to amend and expand the existing fishing regulations.

--- SENTENCE 5041 ---
Title 16 regulates the size restrictions and seasons for aquatic fauna.

--- SENTENCE 5042 ---
Also contained in these regulations is an expanded definition section which now properly defines coral and other freshwater and marine fauna types, with a section preventing transplanting of corals or other aquatic fauna.

--- SENTENCE 5043 ---
A major component of these new regulations are the rules governing the five newly established permanent marine preserves and maps defining their boundaries (Fig. 276).

--- SENTENCE 5044 ---
These areas define nearly 12% of Guam's coastline as no-take fisheries areas.

--- SENTENCE 5045 ---
Statutes have authority over regulations.

--- SENTENCE 5046 ---
The penalty for violating both statutes and regulations is a petty misdemeanor, with a fine of up to \$500.

--- SENTENCE 5047 ---
There are also laws that provide indirect protection to coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5048 ---
GEPA has local water quality standards.

--- SENTENCE 5049 ---
These fines can be charged daily and cumulatively, up to \$10,000 a day.

--- SENTENCE 5050 ---
The Seashore Protection Commission has review and approval authority over construction projects proposed within the area from 10 meters inland of the mean high tide mark out to a depth of 60 ft.

--- SENTENCE 5051 ---
This is a 21-member government review group who look at all the various impacts.

--- SENTENCE 5052 ---
Once this group reviews the proposal for a project, their comments are submitted to a commission made up of appointed members of the public for consideration of approval or rejection.

--- SENTENCE 5053 ---
This commission has not been very successful in upholding their responsibilities.

--- SENTENCE 5054 ---
Guam still needs laws to address ship groundings and ways to assess damage and levy fines for large-scale human induced coral reef damage.

--- SENTENCE 5055 ---
It is also in the process of converting the misdemeanor penalties to a magistrate court system that could be used to issue citations instead of requiring a court hearing to collect penalties.

#### **Gaps in Current Monitoring and and Conservation Capacity Capacity**

Guam is fortunate to have a large number of technical experts in coral reef ecology, management, and policy.

--- SENTENCE 5056 ---
Three government agencies have staff dedicated to dealing with coral reef and coastal resource monitoring and protection – the DAWR, the Guam Coastal Management Program within the Bureau of Planning, and GEPA.

--- SENTENCE 5057 ---
In addition, there are two research units at the University of Guam that focus on coral reef and coastal environmental issues – The University of Guam

!

--- SENTENCE 5058 ---
Pati Point Preserve (a) and Piti Bomb Holes Preserve (b) are two of the newly established MPAs (Photos: Jay Gutierrez and Danko Taborosi/WERI UOG).

--- SENTENCE 5059 ---
Marine Laboratory and the Water and Environmental Research Institute.

--- SENTENCE 5060 ---
Collaboration and cooperation is high among these agencies and institutions.

--- SENTENCE 5061 ---
Funds specifically earmarked for monitoring are limited, especially for water quality monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5062 ---
More stakeholder involvement is needed.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Recommendations**

In general, Guam's coastal reefs continue to decline, primarily as a result of land-based activities.

--- SENTENCE 5063 ---
Data on coral recruitment indicate significant reductions over the past two decades.

--- SENTENCE 5064 ---
Areas impacted by natural disturbances, including typhoons, crown-of-thorns outbreaks, and earthquakes are simply not recovering in specific areas.

--- SENTENCE 5065 ---
Community education initiatives have been paying off in terms of increased awareness and the political will to address reef decline is improving.

--- SENTENCE 5066 ---
However, there is far more to be done in these areas.

--- SENTENCE 5067 ---
Overfishing is still a concern, but establishing five marine reserves that formally received enforcement protection in June 2000 is a very positive step forward.

--- SENTENCE 5068 ---
Enforcement of existing laws and environmental regulations is still a major problem.

--- SENTENCE 5069 ---
More infrastructure improvements and erosion control programs are needed to reduce the land-based stresses on reefs.

## **STATUS OF CORAL REEFS IN THE COMMON- STATUS OF CORAL REEFS IN THE COMMON-WEALTH OF THE NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS WEALTH MARIANA ISLANDS WEALTH OF THE NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS John Starmer, Michael S. Trianni, and Peter Houk Michael S. Trianni, Houk John Starmer, Trianni, and Peter HoukJohn Starmer, Michael S. Trianni, and Peter Houk John Starmer, Michael and Peter Houk**

#### **Introduction Introduction**

The Marianas Archipelago encompasses 15 islands and numerous banks oriented on a north-south axis stretching over 460 nmi from Santa Rosa Reef south of Guam, to Uracas Bank north of the island of Uracas, or Farallon de Pajaros.

--- SENTENCE 5071 ---
Approximately 120 nmi west of the main island chain exists a succession of seamounts also oriented on a northsouth axis, referred to as the west Mariana Ridge.

!

--- SENTENCE 5072 ---
Volcanic activity on Pagan Island (Photo: Americopters, Inc.).

--- SENTENCE 5073 ---
The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is a political subset of the Mariana Archipelago that includes Rota Island in the south, extending northward to Uracas Bank.

--- SENTENCE 5074 ---
The 14 islands of the archipelago are geologically divided into two types; the southern arc characterized as raised limestone plateaus overlying volcanic cores, and the more recent northern islands are basaltic and volcanically active.

--- SENTENCE 5075 ---
The southern arc consists of islands and banks from Rota Island to Sonome Reef north of Farallon de Medinilla.

--- SENTENCE 5076 ---
The oldest and most complex reefs in the CNMI are associated with the western (leeward) sides of these islands.

--- SENTENCE 5077 ---
The majority of the CNMI's residents live on three of these islands: Rota, Tinian, and the Capitol, Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 5078 ---
species, and a species of mangrove have been

The northern arc consists of all islands and banks from Esmeralda Bank to Uracas Bank north of Uracas Island.

--- SENTENCE 5079 ---
The chain of islands north of Saipan are collectively referred to by local CNMI residents as the 'Northern Islands.'

--- SENTENCE 5080 ---
The extent of reefs around these islands is unassessed, however preliminary indications are that there is less reef development in comparison to the southern islands.

--- SENTENCE 5081 ---
Although some of these islands have held small permanent and seasonal communities, all permanent residents were evacuated in 1981 after the eruption of Pagan (Fig. 277).

--- SENTENCE 5082 ---
The banks and seamounts of the western Mariana Ridge are the youngest geologically, with some of the banks rising to nearly 9 m from the surface.

--- SENTENCE 5083 ---
There is currently no good estimate of the total area of coral reefs in the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 5084 ---
The length of total coastline is approximately 417 km (D. Mauro, pers.

--- SENTENCE 5085 ---
Nearly all of this is potential coral habitat, although active reef development may not be occurring in all areas.

--- SENTENCE 5086 ---
This is exclusive of the numerous offshore banks and reefs within CNMI's EEZ, nor does it include the extensive coral platform adjacent to Saipan.

#### **Condition of Coral Reefs Reefs**

The local interagency Marine Monitoring Team (MMT) continues to survey reefs in the southern islands to develop a baseline assessment of reef health.

--- SENTENCE 5087 ---
While the majority of the surveyed reefs are in good condition, there are extensive areas in the populated southern islands where polluted runoff is either preventing recovery or degrading coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5088 ---
Coral bleaching during the summer of 2001 caused extensive shallow water coral mortality, However, areas with good water quality are already showing signs of recovery.

--- SENTENCE 5089 ---
Overfishing is a problem associated with population centers near the southern islands.

--- SENTENCE 5090 ---
The status of coral reefs in the northern islands remains unassessed.

--- SENTENCE 5091 ---
**Marine Macroalgae and Higher Plants Plants –** Over 150 species of algae in 80 genera, three seagrass

--- SENTENCE 5093 ---
Documented algal species diversity continues to grow, due to an ongoing biodiversity survey being conducted by the Coastal Resources Management Office (CRMO).

--- SENTENCE 5094 ---
This project is documenting algal and plant species diversity and distributions within discrete habitats and throughout the archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 5095 ---
It is supported primarily with a NOAA Coral Reef Initiative grant.

--- SENTENCE 5096 ---
Seagrasses are found only within the extensive Saipan Lagoon and in a small area on Rota.

--- SENTENCE 5097 ---
There have been extirpations (localized extinctions) on southern reef flats on both Rota and Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 5098 ---
Mangrove habitat is restricted to two small areas near the commercial port areas in Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 5099 ---
Although these small areas represent the northernmost mangrove communities in the western Pacific and are unique habitat in the CNMI, they have no legal protection.

--- SENTENCE 5100 ---
**Coral Condition Condition –** There have been 256 species of corals from 56 genera and 41 octocorals in 20 genera identified from CNMI coral reef habitats (Randall, 1995, Houk, unpub.

--- SENTENCE 5101 ---

--- SENTENCE 5102 ---
These numbers continue to grow as the MMT continues its surveys.

--- SENTENCE 5103 ---
Diversity is higher in the southern islands where reefs are older, more developed, and have more diverse habitats.

--- SENTENCE 5104 ---
Coral density, species richness, and coral cover on Saipan reefs all tend to increase moving from the shoreline to the outer reef margin (Randall 1991, Fig. 278).

--- SENTENCE 5105 ---
Coral cover in the inner reef zone and on the reef flat of most reef areas on Saipan tends to be patchy with fewer species and less coverage than on the reef fronts and terraces (Randall 1991).

--- SENTENCE 5106 ---
This may be attributed to the low

level of water on many reef flats, resulting in high variations of temperature and salinity.

--- SENTENCE 5107 ---
Fewer coral studies have been conducted on Tinian and Rota.

--- SENTENCE 5108 ---
However, fringing reef communities on these islands are expected to be similar to those on Saipan and Guam.

--- SENTENCE 5109 ---
Of the northern islands, detailed surveys have only been conducted for Maug (Eldredge *et al.* 1977), and indicate that coral diversity is much lower, with only 74 species of scleractinian corals and four species of nonscleractinians in localized coral communities.

--- SENTENCE 5110 ---
The MMT is investigating disease incidences and potential impacts of three common coral reef diseases: coralline algae lethal orange disease, tumors, and black-band disease (Fig. 279).

--- SENTENCE 5111 ---
**Large Mobile Invertebrates Large Invertebrates –**

--- SENTENCE 5120 ---
After initially publicized outbreaks in the late 1960s and early 1970s, the crown-of-thorns starfish briefly reappeared in large numbers on Saipan's reefs in 1984 (Fig. 280).

--- SENTENCE 5121 ---

**Fish and Harvested Species Species –** The ichthyofauna of CNMI belongs to the Indo-West Pacific (Myers 1999).

--- SENTENCE 5124 ---
According to the latest information (Myers and Donaldson in press), there are 1,019 species of shorefishes (epipelagic and demersal species found to 200 m) from the islands of the Southern Marianas, making no distinction between Guam, Rota,

Tinian, and Saipan.

--- SENTENCE 5125 ---
Previously, 946 species of fish had been recorded in the Mariana Islands, with 933 recorded in the southern islands and 427 species in the northern islands (Donaldson 1995).

--- SENTENCE 5126 ---
The bulk of the fish fauna in the Marianas, as in other parts of the region, is comprised of the ten largest fish families: Gobiidae, Labridae, Serranidae, Pomacentridae, Muraenidae, Apogonidae, Blennidae, Carangidae, Acanthuridae, and

Chaetodontidae (Moots *et al.* 2000).

--- SENTENCE 5127 ---
Only three species of shallow-water reef fish are known to be endemic to the Mariana Islands: the yellowcrowned butterflyfish (*Chaetodon flavocoronatus*, Fig. 281) and two species of Guam reef damselfish (*Pomachromis gumaensis, Prealticus poptae*; M. Trianni pers.

--- SENTENCE 5128 ---
There is little data assessing the health of fish resources in the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 5129 ---
The fish resources in the northern islands are perceived as healthier than the populated islands southern because they have the least amount of fishing pressure.

--- SENTENCE 5130 ---

--- SENTENCE 5137 ---
Commercially-harvested in other parts of Micronesia, its shell is used for buttons, and the meat is a popular food source of the local CNMI population.

Marine Reptiles and Mammals – Green and hawksbill sea turtles are known to frequent nearshore waters in the CNMI (Fig. 283).

--- SENTENCE 5154 ---

--- SENTENCE 5155 ---

**Water Quality** – Both point and nonpoint sources of pollutants are responsible for lowering the quality of CNMI's coastal water.

--- SENTENCE 5166 ---
Sewage outfalls, sewage overflows, dredging, and sedimentation from unpaved roads and development are significant factors degrading marine water quality.

--- SENTENCE 5167 ---
Eutrophication and sedimentation are the two biggest stressors.

--- SENTENCE 5168 ---
All three southern islands have unpaved secondary roads that funnel soil and sediment into nearshore waters during heavy rains, increasing turbidity of nearshore waters.

--- SENTENCE 5169 ---
There have been several reports of sedimentation associated with major construction projects (e.g., the Nikko Hotel, Lau Lau Bay Resort, and Bird Island Road) that covered near-

--- SENTENCE 5175 ---

--- SENTENCE 5176 ---

--- SENTENCE 5177 ---
Nutrient loading is also a concern for the reefs adjacent to populated islands.

--- SENTENCE 5178 ---

The DEQ Laboratory recently began collecting data on nutrient levels.

--- SENTENCE 5191 ---
There is concern whether the current readings of nutrients reflect natural or anthropogenic sources (Houk 2002).

--- SENTENCE 5192 ---
A final determination will require monitoring nutrient levels in marine waters surrounding uninhabited islands over a sufficient period of time to establish the natural ambient conditions.

#### Coastal Populations and Reef Economics

Prior to receiving U.S. Commonwealth status in 1978, CNMI was part of the Pacific Trust Territories under the administration of the United States.

--- SENTENCE 5193 ---
along with the Marshall Islands, Palau, and the Federated States of Micronesia.

--- SENTENCE 5194 ---
During the U.S. administration of the islands, economic development was limited, there were few commercial enterprises, and the population relied primarily on subsistence agriculture and fisheries, and Federal aid.

--- SENTENCE 5195 ---
The population in the islands has increased 57.2% over the past ten years to 69,200 in 2000 (U.S. Bureau of Census 2002).

--- SENTENCE 5196 ---
In 1995, about 90% of the CNMI population was in Saipan, 6% was in Rota, 5% was in Tinian, and less than 1% was in the Northern Islands (Stewart 1997).

--- SENTENCE 5197 ---
As with most tropical islands, marine-related tourism is an important part of the island economy (Fig. 285).

--- SENTENCE 5198 ---
In the early 1980s, Japan invested heavily in tourism development, bringing in large numbers of foreign workers for facility construction and operation (Stewart 1992), creating a period of dramatic economic growth.

--- SENTENCE 5199 ---
In 1996, the CNMI received 737,000 visitors who spent over \$587

#### **Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs on Reefs**

**Human Stresses Stresses –**

--- SENTENCE 5202 ---
The nearshore reefs closest to the population centers on Saipan, Tinian, and Rota, as well as reefs surrounding Farallon de Medinilla and offshore banks used for fishing have the greatest potential to be impacted by human activities.

--- SENTENCE 5203 ---
The reefs adjacent to these southern populated islands are of great concern.

--- SENTENCE 5204 ---
They receive most of the human impact from coastal development, population growth, fishing, and tourism.

--- SENTENCE 5205 ---
Tourism and Marine Recreation – Concerns over the potential impacts of marine recreational sports on the nearshore marine environment caused the CRMO to limit the number of permitted motorized marine sports concessions.

--- SENTENCE 5206 ---
CRMO is currently conducting a study to determine the types and extent of impacts being caused by the various marine sports so they can better manage the industry.

--- SENTENCE 5207 ---
Working with the local dive operators association, CRMO is also installing and refurbishing mooring buoys at heavily used dive sites with funds made available through the NOAA Coral Reef Initiative.

--- SENTENCE 5208 ---
Fishing Impacts – The types of fishing and related impacts have been historically varied and continue to change as technology and the islands' demographics change (Fig. 286).

--- SENTENCE 5209 ---
The reef-associated fisheries resources that have been studied have shown impacts from commercial fishery activities.

--- SENTENCE 5210 ---
Evaluation of CNMI-wide fisheries pressures is

complicated by the lack of staff, funding, and complexity of fishery target species and age classes as a result of a growing and diverse contract worker population.

--- SENTENCE 5211 ---
Destructive fishing methods continue to be used.

--- SENTENCE 5212 ---
They are difficult to regulate due to lack of staff and funding for enforcement agencies.

--- SENTENCE 5213 ---
Though dynamite fishing using the remains of WWII ordnance was prevalent in the past, this practice appears to be nonexistent today.

--- SENTENCE 5214 ---
While fishing using poisons (e.g., household bleach) does occur, how common the practice is or the extent of damage caused by poisons has not been documented.

--- SENTENCE 5215 ---
Oil Spills and Ship Groundings – More than 20 vessels have grounded in the CNMI over the past several decades.

--- SENTENCE 5216 ---
The majority of these groundings were typhoon related; two were the result of operator error.

--- SENTENCE 5217 ---
While some of these vessels have since been removed, nearly half remain in the water.

--- SENTENCE 5218 ---
Although most of these vessels were reportedly cleaned of fuel and oil, they still pose a threat to coral reef habitat as they disintegrate and the debris shifts across reefs during storms.

--- SENTENCE 5219 ---
The CRMO recently held an interagency meeting in an attempt to address vessel-grounding issues with a focus on prevention.

--- SENTENCE 5220 ---
The office intends to coordinate the development of a Vessel Grounding Action Plan that will guide CNMI officials in closing communication gaps, creating or revising laws and regulations, strengthening enforcement, developing preventive measures, and addressing funding and resources limitations (B. Lizama pers.

--- SENTENCE 5221 ---
Other Physical Damage to Coral Reefs – The CNMI was a major battlefield during WWII, and there is a significant amount of war debris and unexploded ordnance in the nearshore waters (Fig. 287).

--- SENTENCE 5222 ---
In 1996, through the former CNMI Governor, the former Director of the CNMI Emergency Management Office requested the U.S. Navy detonate depth charges on the wreck of a WWII subchaser at the popular Coral Gardens dive site.

--- SENTENCE 5223 ---
They felt the charges posed a hazard to recreational divers and fishermen (Worthington and Michael 1996).

--- SENTENCE 5224 ---
In response, an assessment of the administrative record of unexploded ordinance operations was conducted on Rota by the U.S. Navy and the CNMI Emergency Management Office.

--- SENTENCE 5225 ---
The force of the

detonation caused significant damage to the nearby Sasanhaya Fish Reserve, one of CNMI's few marine reserves, killing numerous fish, decimating coral, and killing an endangered hawksbill turtle (Trianni 1998).

--- SENTENCE 5226 ---
In addition, secondary damage was caused by an extensive sediment plume resulting from the blast, blanketing a large area in and around the Coral Garden site.

--- SENTENCE 5227 ---
Two typhoons subsequently caused tertiary damage and expanded the impacted area to approximately 29,000 m2 (Richmond 1998).

--- SENTENCE 5228 ---
Estimates based on a value of \$2,833/ m2 put the total economic impact at \$82 million (J. Starmer pers.

--- SENTENCE 5229 ---
Since World War II, the uninhabited island of Farallon de Medinilla (FDM) has been under the control of the U.S. Navy, and since 1971 has been the target site of live-fire military exercises.

--- SENTENCE 5230 ---
In 1981 the Navy signed a 50-year lease with an option to renew after 50 years, to use FDM for live-fire exercises.

--- SENTENCE 5231 ---
In developing an environmental impact statement for military activities in the Marianas, the Navy conducted a preliminary survey of the nearshore marine resources in 1997.

--- SENTENCE 5232 ---
In the completed Environmental Impact Statement the Navy agreed to conduct an annual nearshore marine survey of FDM for three consecutive years (1999-2001).

--- SENTENCE 5233 ---
This survey collected qualitative data on fish abundance and species richness as well as coral species richness, in addition to documenting habitat changes from military exercises.

#### Natural Stresses –

Typhoons are a routine part of the annual seasonal cycles in the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 5253 ---
These storms can affect coral reefs even when they do not pass directly over an island.

--- SENTENCE 5254 ---
Swells can cause coral damage through increased wave action directly and by shifting loose objects (coral, debris, grounded vessels, etc.) around the reef.

--- SENTENCE 5255 ---
The precipitation associated with typhoons also tends to increase sedimentation and nutrient inputs from polluted runoff.

!

--- SENTENCE 5256 ---
Aerial photograph of Saipan Lagoon with an overlay of habitats delineated during the Saipan Lagoon Habitat Assessment Project (Photo: CNMI Marine Monitoring Team).

--- SENTENCE 5257 ---
Climate Change and Coral Bleaching – Bleaching was noted around Saipan in 1994, 1995, and near both Saipan and Pagan in 1997.

--- SENTENCE 5258 ---
There was no quantitative assessment of bleaching for any of these events.

--- SENTENCE 5259 ---
Over the summer of 2001, most shallow-water reefs (less than 3 m) on Saipan, Rota, and Tinian were affected by coral bleaching; bleaching was noted as deep as 18 m. Many encrusting Montipora and Acropora coral colonies died during this event.

--- SENTENCE 5260 ---
The MMT is currently collecting data to assess the effects of this bleaching event on CNMI reefs.

#### Current Conservation Management

**Mapping** – The first habitat and reef map for the CNMI was developed by the USGS for Saipan (Cloud 1959).

--- SENTENCE 5261 ---
These maps are still useful for ecological comparisons.

--- SENTENCE 5262 ---
A beach and reef atlas was commissioned by the CRMO in 1980 (Eldredge and Randall 1980).

--- SENTENCE 5263 ---
It provided information on reef location and some information regarding habitat types for Saipan,

Tinian, Rota, Aguijan, and Farallon de Mendinilla based on aerial photographs.

--- SENTENCE 5264 ---
The MMT's Saipan Lagoon Habitat Assessment Project is currently mapping coral reefs and associated habitats within Saipan's western lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5265 ---
Field surveys are verifying habitats in aerial photographs (Fig. 288).

--- SENTENCE 5266 ---
This will allow comparisons among historical aerial photography to detect ecological changes.

--- SENTENCE 5267 ---
Expanding on this project, CRMO is now working with georectified IKONOS satellite imagery provided through NOAA to create initial coral reef maps for the

entire CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 5268 ---
The MMT is ground-truthing reef habitats in the southern islands for this mapping initiative.

--- SENTENCE 5269 ---
The MMT will collaborate with NOAA Coral Reef Ecosystem Monitoring Program to ground-truth the northern islands imagery in 2003.

--- SENTENCE 5270 ---
**Monitoring** – CNMI DEQ has been testing water quality at a number of sites adjacent to population centers on Saipan since 1980.

--- SENTENCE 5271 ---
More recently, water quality testing has been extended to Tinian and

Figure 289.

--- SENTENCE 5272 ---
Diver measuring the size of a reef fish during a monitoring survey (Photo: Fran Castro).

!

--- SENTENCE 5273 ---
DEQ posts warnings at local beaches when water quality parameters exceed the acceptable limits for public health.

--- SENTENCE 5274 ---
The CNMI also collects data on coral bleaching mortalities.

--- SENTENCE 5275 ---
The Fisheries Section of the DFW has been collecting data on fish diversity and abundance primarily within the existing and proposed conservation areas on Saipan, Tinian, and Rota since 1999 (Fig. 289).

--- SENTENCE 5276 ---
During fish surveys, data are also collected on reef topography (vertical relief) and estimated hard coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 5277 ---
There are three major monitoring activities carried out in the CNMI.

--- SENTENCE 5278 ---
First, site surveys are conducted to satisfy local and regional requirements in EIS work.

--- SENTENCE 5279 ---
These surveys provide snapshots of CNMI reefs and can be very informative, but are usually limited to a single reef area.

--- SENTENCE 5280 ---
These have been and should continue to be used to understand changes over time.

--- SENTENCE 5281 ---
For example, comparison between two sites in Lau Lau Bay (Fig. 290) that were surveyed in 1991 and recently re-surveyed in 2001 by the MMT (Houk 2001) to see how they differ.

--- SENTENCE 5282 ---
Turf algae dominate the benthic cover (46.7% and 52.3% ten years later).

--- SENTENCE 5283 ---
Coral cover was 28.1% then and 42.0% now.

--- SENTENCE 5284 ---
The second site showed a longterm decrease in mean coral diameter and the relative frequencies of large branching corals, attributed to the 1983 crown-of-thorns starfish outbreak.

--- SENTENCE 5285 ---
Between 1991-2001, the abundance of macroinvertebrates such as sea urchins and sea cucumbers decreased at both sites (Houk 2001).

--- SENTENCE 5286 ---
Second, the DFW is monitoring several MPAs on Saipan (Mañagaha Marine Conservation Area, Bird Island Sanctuary, and Forbidden island Sanctuary) and Rota (Sasanhaya Bay Fish Reserve), as well as the proposed Tinian Marine Sanctuary located to the north of Puntan Diablo on Tinian.

--- SENTENCE 5287 ---
Done twice a year, the surveys gather data on the diversity and abundance of fish and commercially-important invertebrates and benthic cover.

--- SENTENCE 5288 ---
Third, the MMT surveys benthic cover, coral communities, invertebrate and fish abundance, and much more as part of its long-term marine monitoring program.

--- SENTENCE 5289 ---
These data are being incorporated into a GIS for local and federal agencies.

--- SENTENCE 5290 ---
The MMT is also monitoring a portion of Saipan lagoon and creating habitat maps.

--- SENTENCE 5291 ---
This includes benthic coverage, invertebrate abundance, biodiversity and water quality.

!

--- SENTENCE 5292 ---
The marine ecosystem within Lau Lau Bay has been surveyed in 1991 and 2001 (Photo: Fran Castro).

--- SENTENCE 5293 ---
With NOAA grant support, the CNMI increased local capacity to conduct long-term monitoring by hiring a manager to coordinate its coral reef program.

--- SENTENCE 5294 ---
Now the MMT monitors 13 sites off Saipan Island, 8 sites off Rota, 7 sites off Tinian, and 1 site off Aguijan.

--- SENTENCE 5295 ---
Parameters monitored include benthic coverage, coral communities, coral biodiversity, fish and macroinvertebrate abundance and diversity, sedimentation rates, and water quality.

--- SENTENCE 5296 ---
This program will provide the CNMI with a comprehensive baseline survey and the ability to track and predict changes in coral reef ecosystem health through time.

--- SENTENCE 5316 ---
Enforcement of these regulations is hampered by a lack of funding and resources.

--- SENTENCE 5319 ---
Local resource management agencies are emphasizing education to increase understanding of and concern for the environment and, hopefully, increase voluntary compliance with regulations.
