# STATUS OF THE CORAL REEFS IN THE PACIFIC FREELY ASSOCIATED STATES

Charles Birkeland, Ahser Edward, Yimnang Golbuu, Jay Gutierrez, Noah Idechong, James Maragos, Gustav Paulay, Robert Richmond, Andrew Tafileichig, and Nancy Vander Velde

From east to west, the Freely Associated States include the Republic of the Marshall Islands (the Marshalls or the RMI), the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), and the Republic of Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5321 ---
The Federated States of Micronesia – Kosrae, Pohnpei, Chuuk, and Yap – along with Palau, are known as the Caroline Islands, which are among the longest island chains in the world at 2,500 km.

--- SENTENCE 5322 ---
All of these Micronesian islands were formerly a part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands administered by the United States after World War II.

--- SENTENCE 5323 ---
All three countries achieved independence within the past 25 years but retain close economic and strategic ties to the United States (Hezel 1995).

--- SENTENCE 5324 ---
Although the process was initiated as early as 1979, the Compacts of Free Association for the RMI and FSM did not go into effect until 1986<sup>176</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 5325 ---
The Palau Compact was approved later 177 but was not effected until a few years after that.

--- SENTENCE 5326 ---
Mostly unmapped, estimates of coral reef habitat for the Freely Associated States range from 11,600 km² (Spalding *et al.* 2001) to 81,500 km² (Holthus *et al.* 1993, Maragos and Holthus 1999).

--- SENTENCE 5327 ---
Throughout the region, there is high diversity of corals and associated organisms.

--- SENTENCE 5328 ---
The human population is heavily dependent on coral reefs and related resources both economically and culturally.

## The Republic of the Marshall Islands<sup>178</sup>

#### Introduction

The Republic of the Marshall Islands encompasses approximately 1,225 individual islands and islets with 29 atolls and 5 solitary low coral islands (Fig. 292).

--- SENTENCE 5329 ---
Situated from 160°-173° E, and between 4°-

14° N, the Marshalls have a total dry land area of only about 181.3 km².

--- SENTENCE 5330 ---
However, when the Exclusive Economic Zone (by statute, from the shoreline to 200 miles offshore) is figured in, the Republic covers 1,942,000 km² of ocean within the larger Micronesia region.

--- SENTENCE 5331 ---
There are 11,670 km² of sea within the lagoons of the atolls.

--- SENTENCE 5332 ---
Land only makes up less than 0.01% of the area of the Marshall Islands.

--- SENTENCE 5333 ---
Most of the country is the broad open ocean with a seafloor that reaches 4.6 km (15,000 ft).

--- SENTENCE 5334 ---
Scattered throughout are nearly a hundred isolated submerged volcanic seamounts; those with flattened tops are called **guyots**<sup>179</sup>.

--- SENTENCE 5335 ---
The average elevation of the Marshall Islands is about 2 m (7 ft) above sea level.

--- SENTENCE 5336 ---
The air is warm and moist; humidity is around 80% with considerable salt spray.

--- SENTENCE 5337 ---
The air temperature averages 27.8° C (82° F) with a range of 24-32° C (76-90° F).

--- SENTENCE 5338 ---
Rainfall tends to be seasonal, ranging from 4 m a year in the south to as little as 0.6 m a year in the

Figure 292.

--- SENTENCE 5339 ---
Satellite imagery of Aur and Maloelap Atolls (Photo: Earth Sciences and Image Analysis Laboratory, NASA Johnson Space Center).

!

--- SENTENCE 5340 ---
Law 99-239, the Compact of Free Association Act of 1985.

--- SENTENCE 5341 ---
<sup>&</sup>lt;sup>178</sup> Much of this information was from a report by the National Biodiversity Team of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (2000).

--- SENTENCE 5342 ---
These were geological masses formed millions of years ago that were not quite able to keep pace with subsidence or reach sea level to become or remain as islands or atolls.

!

--- SENTENCE 5343 ---
As demonstrated by the lush coral garden in this picture, there are still healthy coral reefs on Majuro (Photo: Marshall Islands Visitors Authority).

north.

--- SENTENCE 5344 ---
In extremely dry years, there may be no precipitation on some of the drier atolls.

--- SENTENCE 5345 ---
Tropical storms (typhoons) are relatively rare, but can be devastating.

--- SENTENCE 5346 ---
The atolls vary in size from Kwajalein, the world's largest atoll with 16.4 km2 of dry land and a lagoon of 2,174 km2 , to Bikar with only 0.5 km2 of land, but with 37.4 km2 of lagoon, and Namdrik with more land (2.7 km2 ) but only 8.4 km2 of lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5347 ---
Individual islands range from tiny sand-spits and vegetated islets that are inundated during storms and extreme high tides, to much larger islands such as Kaben Island at Maloelap Atoll, and Wotho Island, the main island at Wotho Atoll; both are over 8 km2 .

--- SENTENCE 5348 ---
Lagoons within the atolls typically have at least one deep-pass access; however, some, such as Namdrik, have no natural passes.

--- SENTENCE 5349 ---
The atolls and islands of the Marshalls formed when fringing reefs began to establish and grow around ancient emergent volcanoes.

--- SENTENCE 5350 ---
After that, the volcanic peaks gradually sank and shrank, leaving lagoons in the vacated spaces and eventually became coral atolls after the volcanoes disappeared entirely beneath the reefs and sediments of coral atolls.

--- SENTENCE 5351 ---
The five solitary islands were formed in much the same way, but the peaks were small enough that no interior lagoon developed.

--- SENTENCE 5352 ---
With seamounts and guyots, the subsidence took those volcanoes and reefs far below the surface of the sea.

--- SENTENCE 5353 ---
Mostly, the atolls of the Marshalls are not circular, nor do they have uniform islets.

--- SENTENCE 5354 ---
They are much larger than those in the Indian Ocean and are surrounded by numerous islets.

--- SENTENCE 5355 ---
The islets are more dominant on the windward side and seemingly sprawl around a deep lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5356 ---
They are also

different from other atolls because they are deeper and have more circulation within their lagoons.

--- SENTENCE 5357 ---
The islets are extremely young geologically and likely formed either when sea level dropped about 2 m to its present level around 4,000 years ago or in the aftermath of large waves that cast large reef blocks, coral rubble, and sand up on top of shallow reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5358 ---
Then vegetation, birds, crabs and other animals colonized the emergent islands, and eventually the Micronesian ancestors of the present day Marshall Islanders arrived.

--- SENTENCE 5359 ---
In contrast, the atoll reefs are 50 million years old or more, and up to a mile thick atop their volcanic foundation.

#### **Condition of Coral Reef Ecosystem Ecosystem**

In general, the reefs of the Marshall Islands are in good condition.

--- SENTENCE 5360 ---
Even those in the former nuclear test sites show remarkable recovery, although many of the larger bomb craters may not fill in for years, if at all.

--- SENTENCE 5361 ---
The reefs near the urban areas of Majuro are stressed, but still have an abundance of fish and invertebrates (Fig. 293).

--- SENTENCE 5362 ---
Recent information on the status of coral reefs of the Marshalls can be found in Maragos and Holthus (1999), Price and Maragos (2000), and the National Biodiversity Team of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (NBTRMI, 2000).

--- SENTENCE 5363 ---

--- SENTENCE 5365 ---
Other members of the mangrove community are found in inland depressions rather than along the coast.

--- SENTENCE 5376 ---
The after-effects of some of the 67 nuclear tests in the northern Marshalls between 1946-1958 on fish have also been studied, but most studies were years after the tests ended.

--- SENTENCE 5377 ---

--- SENTENCE 5378 ---

--- SENTENCE 5379 ---
Over the years, many of those radionuclides have diminished by radioactive decay and natural processes (Noshkin *et al.*  (1997).

--- SENTENCE 5380 ---

--- SENTENCE 5432 ---

--- SENTENCE 5435 ---

--- SENTENCE 5489 ---
The **Coast Conservation Act** protects and preserves the coast from sea erosion or encroachment of sea-related to development activities.

--- SENTENCE 5490 ---

--- SENTENCE 5491 ---
But it does not include fishing within 7.6 m (25 ft) landward of mean high water line and 61 m (200 ft) seaward of the mean low water line.

--- SENTENCE 5492 ---
The **Planning and Zoning Act** requires local governments to establish a Planning Commission and Planning Office to oversee coastal zoning activities and assure compliance.

--- SENTENCE 5493 ---
The United States Army Kwajalein Atoll is under U.S. laws and regulations, including CITES, NEPA, and the Migratory Bird Act.

--- SENTENCE 5494 ---
Relevant RMI laws protecting coral reef resources include the **Republic of the Marshall Island Constitution** (1979, Article X), which preserves traditional land tenure and titles system.

--- SENTENCE 5495 ---
It holds that no person with customary land rights may alienate or dispose of land without approval of traditional landowners, but the government retains the authority to acquire land or aquatic habitats and establish conservation and research programs for resident endangered or threatened species.

--- SENTENCE 5496 ---
Under the **Public Lands and Resources Act** (1988 Title 9, Chapter 1, Section 3), all lands below mean high water mark belong to the government, with exceptions, but no one has the right to abuse, destroy, or damage mangroves or land (Fig. 301).

## Conclusions and Recommendations

At present, the coral reefs of the Marshall Islands are in good condition.

--- SENTENCE 5519 ---
While the two atolls used for the nuclear testing program experienced unique stresses, the reefs of the RMI as a whole have escaped the extensive damage seen in other parts of the world.

--- SENTENCE 5520 ---
The remoteness of many of the atolls and the fact that the country as a whole is relatively isolated has helped to minimize many potential impacts.

--- SENTENCE 5521 ---
However, this isolation also leaves the coral

reefs vulnerable to illegal or semi-legal exploitation.

--- SENTENCE 5522 ---
Moreover, increased globalization and the pressures to change from the traditional subsistence economy could easily alter the present situation and allow at least some of the stresses discussed before to become more serious threats.

--- SENTENCE 5523 ---
The Federated States of Micronesia

#### **Introduction**

The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) is comprised of four states – from east to west, Kosrae, Pohnpei, Chuuk, and Yap.

--- SENTENCE 5524 ---
Along with Palau, these comprise the Caroline Islands.

--- SENTENCE 5525 ---
Each island or group has its own language, customs, local government, and reef tenure system.

--- SENTENCE 5526 ---
Traditional leaders (Chiefs or their equivalent) and community groups are active in traditional governance as well as western-style, democratically elected officials.

--- SENTENCE 5527 ---
This dual system provides opportunities and challenges to reef and marine resource protection.

--- SENTENCE 5528 ---
FSM has high islands and low atolls, and a strong dependence on coral reefs and marine resources, both economically and culturally.

--- SENTENCE 5529 ---
Each state supports population centers on high volcanic islands surrounded by barrier reefs (Pohnpei, Chuuk) or very broad fringing reefs that are nearly barrier reefs (Kosrae, Yap).

--- SENTENCE 5530 ---
All states except Kosrae also include remote clusters of atolls and low coral islands (Maragos and Holthus 1999).

--- SENTENCE 5531 ---
Spalding *et al.* (2001) estimated total shallowwater coral reef area off the FSM to be 5,440 km<sup>2</sup>.

!

--- SENTENCE 5532 ---
Aerial view of two of the islands that make up Yap State (Photo: Ben Mieremet).

--- SENTENCE 5533 ---
Kosrae is a single volcanic island with a landmass of 109 km2 and an elevation of 629 m. It is surrounded by a fringing reef and has a single harbor.

--- SENTENCE 5534 ---
The volcanic island of Pohnpei is the largest island in the FSM and is the FSM capitol (Fig. 303).

--- SENTENCE 5535 ---
It has an area of 345 km2 with a well-developed barrier reef surrounding a narrow lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5536 ---
It and the eight nearby coral islands and atolls make up the state of Pohnpei.

--- SENTENCE 5537 ---
Chuuk State (formerly known as Truk) has 15 inhabited volcanic and coral islands and atolls.

--- SENTENCE 5538 ---
Chuuk Lagoon is the largest atoll in the FSM and serves as the population and political center of Chuuk State.

--- SENTENCE 5539 ---
It is famous for the Japanese wrecks that were sunk in the lagoon during World War II (Fig. 304).

--- SENTENCE 5540 ---
Yap State has a main volcanic island approximately 100 km2 , along with 15 coral islands and atolls (Fig. 305).

--- SENTENCE 5541 ---
The peoples inhabiting the offshore atolls and coral islands in Chuuk, Yap, and Pohnpei states are among the most traditional, with a highly sophisticated marine tenure and associated marine resource management system.

#### **Condition of Coral Reef Ecosystem Ecosystem**

The condition of FSM coral reef ecosystems is generally good to excellent (Fig. 306).

--- SENTENCE 5542 ---
Most of the reefs in the low islands are in excellent condition.

--- SENTENCE 5543 ---
The primary human impacts come from fishing pressure and ship groundings.

--- SENTENCE 5544 ---
Reefs in Kosrae have been impacted by coastal development, specifically the construction of an airport built on top of a broad reef at Okat.

--- SENTENCE 5545 ---
Some dredging and road construction projects have

resulted in the destruction of specific reef areas including much of Okat.

--- SENTENCE 5546 ---
**Marine Algae and Higher Plants Marine Plants –** Crustose coralline algae are abundant on the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5547 ---
FSM has 14 species of mangroves.

--- SENTENCE 5548 ---
**Corals and Benthic Cover Benthic Cover –**

--- SENTENCE 5549 ---
The reefs around the island of Pohnpei vary in condition.

--- SENTENCE 5550 ---
Surveys done after a ship grounding found the average coral cover above 20% adjacent to Sokehs channel, and limited survey information from the barrier reef shows 50-70% at selected sites.

--- SENTENCE 5551 ---
Due to high annual rainfall and steep volcanic topography, erosion and sedimentation can be heavy.

--- SENTENCE 5552 ---
Upland clearing of forested areas to grow sakau (kava) has resulted in landslides and other impacts to coastal villages and resources.

Most reefs in FSM are quite healthy (Photo: James McVey).

--- SENTENCE 5566 ---
**Water Quality** – There are no problems with sedimentation and erosion or coastal pollution in the uninhabited atolls.

#### Coastal Populations and Reef Economics

The population for all FSM inhabited islands has grown by 22.6% over the past ten years to 133,100 in 2000 (U.S. Census Bureau 2002).

--- SENTENCE 5569 ---
The most populated centers occur at Kolonia, the national capitol on the north side of Pohnpei Island, and within Chuuk lagoon on several volcanic islands.

--- SENTENCE 5570 ---
Population growth has been rapid, with Chuuk already considered overcrowded.

--- SENTENCE 5571 ---
In contrast, the neighboring coral islands and atolls retain stable populations.

--- SENTENCE 5572 ---
These islands also have more traditional control over coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5573 ---
Tourism has been growing in the FSM.

## Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs

**Human Stresses** – As with the other high islands, road construction and development projects without adequate erosion control have been responsible for reef damage from sed-

imentation.

--- SENTENCE 5581 ---
Dredging projects associated with airport and harbor construction have destroyed specific reefs (Fig. 306), and subsequent increases in freshwater runoff have limited recovery.

--- SENTENCE 5582 ---
Increased population is a concern for the future of some islands as they come to terms with the need for associated infrastructure, including sewage processing plants and outfalls.

--- SENTENCE 5583 ---
And if not carefully guided, planned tourism development has the potential to impact reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5584 ---
Export fisheries have been a problem for Chuuk and there have been numerous reports of destructive fishing practices in the past.

--- SENTENCE 5585 ---
Ship groundings have been a problem for both the high and low islands.

--- SENTENCE 5586 ---
Foreign long-liners have been abandoned on numerous FSM reefs, with no funds

**Global Warming and Coral Bleaching Global Warming and Coral Bleaching –**

--- SENTENCE 5594 ---
There is concern about potential sea level rise from global warming inundating the low islands and atolls.

--- SENTENCE 5595 ---
Tropical storms and related weather patterns are also an issue.

--- SENTENCE 5596 ---
Marine scientists documented the impact of a destructive 1990 typhoon passing over remote reefs in Pohnpei State (Holthus *et al.* 1993, Fig. 309), including large waves passing over Minto Reef.

--- SENTENCE 5597 ---
These picked up massive coral heads from the lagoon, depositing them on the reef flat and killing a variety of associated wildlife.

--- SENTENCE 5598 ---
FSM reefs have experienced bleaching, but information is limited.

#### **Current Conservation Management Management**

**Mapping Mapping –** Some FSM shallow-water coral reef and associated benthic habitats have been mapped but only off the four high island population centers.

--- SENTENCE 5599 ---
Coastal resource inventories and atlases have been prepared for the islands of Pohnpei, Yap, Kosrae, and Moen Island in Chuuk Lagoon185 and initiated for the rest of Chuuk Lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5600 ---
Consistent with similar initiatives in the Marshalls, the FSM inventories summarized the species, habitats, uses, and conditions of reefs, and the atlas maps portray the location of study sites, coastal uses, protected areas, cultural sites, bathymetry and distribution of reef habitats surrounding these islands.

--- SENTENCE 5601 ---
**Assessments and Monitoring Assessments and Monitoring –**

--- SENTENCE 5602 ---
The College of Micronesia-FSM has faculty and staff trained in marine resource assessment and monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5603 ---
The FSM has regulatory agencies (Environmental and Marine Resource) with trained personnel.

--- SENTENCE 5604 ---
Damage done to a coconut and breadfruit plantation in FSM by a typhoon (Photo: James McVey).

--- SENTENCE 5605 ---
state has a Marine Resources Management office and an Environmental Protection Agency office.

--- SENTENCE 5606 ---
Cooperation among regional institutions formalized under the Marine Resources Pacific Consortium and funded by the DoI is intended to increase local and regional capacity for assessment and monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5607 ---
Non-governmental organizations are active in the FSM, primarily The Nature Conservancy, and offer technical and financial assistance for related programs.

--- SENTENCE 5608 ---
The Peace Corps also has a presence in the FSM, and some of its volunteers have been involved in monitoring programs.

--- SENTENCE 5609 ---
Coral reefs are protected by MPAs in the Trochus Sanctuaries Heritage Reserve and Kosrae Island Heritage Reserve.

--- SENTENCE 5610 ---
Other conservation areas are presently being negotiated in partnership with the FSM National Government.

--- SENTENCE 5611 ---
Chiefs and other traditional leaders usually control protection of specific areas.

--- SENTENCE 5612 ---
In Yap, the villages own the reefs, and have authority over resource use.

--- SENTENCE 5613 ---
A number of the islands have areas set aside for reef protection and limit resource extraction, but currently the FSM lacks the enforcement capacity to protect these MPAs (A. Edward pers.

--- SENTENCE 5614 ---
comm.).

Technical expertise in the FSM has been increasing, with a number of highly trained individuals dispersed among the College of Micronesia-FSM, the regulatory agencies, and local institutions like the Pohnpei Environmental Research Institute.

--- SENTENCE 5615 ---
Funds are a limiting factor, especially as financial support from the Compacts of Free Association is

#### Conclusions and Recommendations

The reefs within the FSM are in relatively good condition.

--- SENTENCE 5622 ---
However, land use practices on the high islands are a concern.

--- SENTENCE 5623 ---
Reef fisheries on some islands have been over-exploited.

--- SENTENCE 5624 ---
Damaging blast fishery practices have been documented in Chuuk Lagoon as late as 1994 (J. Maragos pers.

--- SENTENCE 5625 ---
Integrated watershed management programs need to be developed.

--- SENTENCE 5626 ---
Improved coordination of management activities among the states is recommended.

--- SENTENCE 5627 ---
Education and programs involving the community need to be expanded.

--- SENTENCE 5628 ---
Ship groundings need to be addressed at the State and National level possibly requiring vessels to post bonds to cover any damage to the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5629 ---
Additional support for the resource agencies is necessary if they are to meet their mandates.

### The Republic of Palau

#### **Introduction**

The Republic of Palau is a separate sub-archipelago at the western end of the Caroline Islands.

--- SENTENCE 5631 ---
It is the westernmost archipelago in Oceania, located 741 km east of Mindanao in the southern Philippines and about 1,300 km southwest of Guam.

--- SENTENCE 5632 ---
The islands and reefs of Palau stretch 700 km from Ngaruangel Atoll and Velasco Reef in the north to Helen Atoll in the south.

--- SENTENCE 5633 ---
There are about 20 large and intermediate islands and over 500 small islands (Fig. 311).

--- SENTENCE 5634 ---
The biggest island,

nic.

--- SENTENCE 5635 ---
Koror (the capital) lies on the south of Babeldaob with the other islands in the chain south of it.

--- SENTENCE 5636 ---
Koror and the southern islands are separated from Babeldaob by a deep pass (30-40 m), Toachel El Mid. which cuts in from east to west, separating the reefs of Babeldaob from all the southern reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5637 ---
The southwestern islands

Babeldaob, is volca-

!

--- SENTENCE 5638 ---
Betel nut agriculture on Yap (Photo: FSM Visitors Board and Tim Rock).

of Palau lie about 339-599 km southwest of the main Palau archipelago.

--- SENTENCE 5639 ---
Most of the population resides in Koror and Babeldaob.

--- SENTENCE 5640 ---
Beyond the main islands to the north are two atolls and one submerged atoll reef.

--- SENTENCE 5641 ---
One large atoll (Helen) and five smaller low coral islands are up to 600 km to the south (Maragos and Cook 1995).

--- SENTENCE 5642 ---
The islands exhibit numerous island and reef types.

--- SENTENCE 5643 ---
On the western coast of Palau there is a 144-km, well-developed barrier reef protecting the main cluster of islands from north of Babeldaob to the southern lagoon, then merging into the fringing reef.

--- SENTENCE 5644 ---
Peleliu is at the southern end of the fringing reef.

--- SENTENCE 5645 ---
Off the east coast of Babeldaob, the barrier reef is not well developed.

--- SENTENCE 5646 ---
Only Ngchesar and

Airai have a barrier reef.

--- SENTENCE 5647 ---
Ngerchelong, Ngarard, and Melekeok do not.

--- SENTENCE 5648 ---
Ngiwal has a submerged barrier reef about 5-10 meters below sea level.

--- SENTENCE 5649 ---
The southern lagoon has much more extensive barrier reefs, lacking passage on the west side while the southeast side has numerous gaps and passes extending into the lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5650 ---
Hundreds of rock islands or emergent coral reefs are concentrated in the southern lagoon.

--- SENTENCE 5651 ---
Maragos and Meier (1993) estimated the total area covered by shallowwater coral reefs to be 1,661 km<sup>2</sup>.

#### **Condition of the Coral Reefs the Coral Reefs**

**Marine Higher Plants –** Nine species of seagrass have been reported from Palau (Tsuda *et al*. 1977).

--- SENTENCE 5653 ---
Seagrass is found throughout Palau, from Kayangel Atoll through Babeldaob to Peleliu.

--- SENTENCE 5654 ---
The whole shoreline of Babeldaob, Koror, and Peleliu is covered with seagrass; even the lagoon side of the barrier reef has seagrass.

--- SENTENCE 5655 ---
Also, nine species of mangroves have been confirmed along with several more subspecies on Palauan islands and islets.

--- SENTENCE 5656 ---
**Coral and Benthic Cover and Benthic Cover –**

--- SENTENCE 5657 ---
Within the whole Indo-Pacific region, Palau's coral diversity approaches the highest coral diversity of the Philippines, Indonesia, and Australia (Fig. 312).

--- SENTENCE 5658 ---
When assessments and biotic characterizations are complete, scientists expect diversity to be about 25% higher than that for Guam (R. Richmond pers.

--- SENTENCE 5659 ---
Maragos (1994b) estimates Palau has 425 named species of stony corals belonging to 78 genera, although some of the species names may be synonyms (J. Maragos pers.

--- SENTENCE 5660 ---
There are an additional 120 species of octocorals in 57 genera (J. Starmer unpubl.

--- SENTENCE 5661 ---
For reefs in good condition, coral cover generally ranges from 50-70%.

--- SENTENCE 5662 ---
Coral diversity is moderate to high, ranging from 45-95 species at different sites.

--- SENTENCE 5663 ---
Coral cover at lagoon slopes of the barrier reef is 60% with a diversity of 45 species.

--- SENTENCE 5664 ---
The ocean reef slopes reach a total length of 62.7 km.

--- SENTENCE 5665 ---
Coral cover at the northeast slopes average 10% with an average of 35 species.

--- SENTENCE 5666 ---
The protected bight at the southern end of Ngkesol has higher

coral cover and diversity (45 coral species accounting for about 25% of total cover).

--- SENTENCE 5667 ---
Along western ocean-facing reef slopes, coral cover ranged from 60 to 70% and diversity averaged 35 species.

--- SENTENCE 5668 ---
Northwestern ocean-facing reefs have lower coral cover (10-20%), but had higher diversity, with 50 species encountered during the REA.

--- SENTENCE 5669 ---
The northern reef slopes protected by Ngerael, Ngkesol and Kayangel reef have higher coral abundance and diversity.

--- SENTENCE 5670 ---
The lagoon of Kayangel Atoll generally has low coral cover and diversity, but the Atoll had a total of 126 species of corals belonging to 47 genera.

--- SENTENCE 5671 ---
The Ulach channel along the western rim supports healthy marine communities including corals.

--- SENTENCE 5672 ---
During the REA surveys in 1992, the average coral cover for the outer walls was 70%, 50% inside.

--- SENTENCE 5673 ---
Coral cover at the ocean slopes averaged 20-25% along its 62.7 km length, with 40-50 coral species at different sites along the ocean slopes.

--- SENTENCE 5674 ---
The western Babeldaob lagoon has over 500 patch reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5675 ---
Coral cover on the slope of the patch reefs is around 50%.

--- SENTENCE 5676 ---
Diversity ranges from 45 to 70 species in different sites.

--- SENTENCE 5677 ---
Several rare coral genera are found in these patch reefs including *Cynarina, Zoopilus*, and *Siderastrea*.

--- SENTENCE 5678 ---
The 1992 Ngermeduu Bay Natural Resource Surveys, found 200 species of corals (Maragos, 1992).

--- SENTENCE 5679 ---
Areas away from freshwater and sedimentation stress average 50 species of corals per site, with several sites with as many as 60 species.

--- SENTENCE 5680 ---
The sites with higher diversity also have high coral cover averaging over 50%, sometimes as high as 70%.

--- SENTENCE 5681 ---
Palau's coral reefs exhibit high biodiversity (Photo: Ethan Daniels, Kevin Davidson, and PICRC).

--- SENTENCE 5686 ---
These showed no significant differences in coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 5687 ---

During the survey of the same sites in 1991, coral cover was 55.7% at the reef margin and 82.2% at the slope (Birkeland *et al*. 1976, Birkeland *et al*. 1993).

--- SENTENCE 5689 ---
Before the 1998 bleaching event in Palau, the remote reefs were generally healthy and in good condition.

--- SENTENCE 5690 ---
The reefs closer to population centers or areas where there is development are showing signs of degradation and are not as healthy as the remote reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5691 ---
The bleaching event severely affected most reefs in Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5692 ---
**Other Macroinvertebrates Other Macroinvertebrates –** Over 300 species of sponges have been reported from the Palau Archipelago (Spalding *et al*. 2001).

--- SENTENCE 5693 ---
According to these authors, a total of 144 species of marine invertebrates other than coral were observed around Kayangel atoll alone.

--- SENTENCE 5694 ---
The Ngermeduu Bay Natural Resource surveys identified 170 species of invertebrates other than corals (Richmond 1992).

--- SENTENCE 5695 ---
There, the seagrass beds support numerous species of echinoderms including edible sea cucumbers (Fig. 313), whereas suspension feeders dominate the mouth of the bay.

--- SENTENCE 5696 ---
The crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster planci*) is a problem in areas of Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5697 ---
They target the few remaining *Acropora* corals that survived bleaching.

--- SENTENCE 5698 ---
**Fish and Fisheries –** Palau has the largest number of reef fish species within Micronesia, a total of 1,278 known species.

--- SENTENCE 5699 ---
But based upon gaps of

known distribution of fish, Myers (1999) projects this should be 1,449 (Fig. 233).

--- SENTENCE 5700 ---
Fish populations in the main islands of Palau are showing signs of overfishing when compared to the Southwest islands where fishing is less intense (Donaldson 1993).

--- SENTENCE 5701 ---
Highly desired species of fish are either absent or present in low numbers around the main islands of Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5702 ---
A 1991 REA recorded 467 species of fish from Kayangel, Ngeruangel/Velasco and 495 species from the Northern Lagoon and barrier reef complex (Amesbury 1992).

--- SENTENCE 5703 ---
These were the most diverse regions of Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5704 ---
Ngermeduu Bay had 277 species of fish (Amesbury 1992).

--- SENTENCE 5705 ---
This area is unique in that it has two overlapping types of fish communities.

--- SENTENCE 5706 ---
One is the rich coral reef assemblage typical of other areas in Palau and Micronesia.

--- SENTENCE 5707 ---
The second community is dominated by planktivores, more commonly found in Indonesia.

--- SENTENCE 5708 ---
There were 347 fish species recorded from West Babeldaob during an REA (Maragos *et al*. 1994).

--- SENTENCE 5709 ---
Adding the 277 species from Ngermeduu Bay Natural Resource Surveys (Amesbury 1992) brings the total for West Babledaob to 400 fish species.

--- SENTENCE 5710 ---
Three hundred thirty-seven species of fish were recorded for East Babeldaob during the 1991 REA.

--- SENTENCE 5711 ---
Newly discovered fish species and new range extensions found in Palau during exploration of deep reefs (Photos: Richard Pyle, Bishop Museum).

Channels serve as important pathways for migrating fish.

--- SENTENCE 5713 ---
For example, the Toachel Mlengui channel, located slightly north of the Ngermeduu Bay entrance and 15 km southwest of Daimechesengel pass in Ngardmau, is important to the coral reef ecosystem because it serves as a pathway for fish traveling between the lagoon and ocean reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5714 ---
Located 85 km south, the

Sengelokl pass, however, only offers a subtidal connection between the western ocean and the southern lagoon, so does not play a prominent role.

--- SENTENCE 5715 ---
**Marine Reptiles and Mammals Marine Reptiles and Mammals –** There are four species of sea turtles known to use Palauan reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5716 ---
Historically, the Rock Islands supported large numbers of endangered hawksbill turtle nesting sites.

--- SENTENCE 5717 ---
But in recent years the poaching of eggs and the take of turtle shell for bekko jewelry have drastically reduced nesting activity.

--- SENTENCE 5718 ---
This species and part of its critical habitat is now protected within the Rock Island Reserve.

--- SENTENCE 5719 ---
Elsewhere, on unprotected reefs, hawksbill turtle nesting is diminished or has been eliminated altogether from excessive harvesting (NMFS and USFWS 1998).

--- SENTENCE 5720 ---
According to G. Paulay (pers.

--- SENTENCE 5721 ---
comm.), two species of sea snakes are known from the reefs of Palau – the egg-laying banded sea snake (*Laticauda colubrina*), and the viviparous yellowbellied sea snake (*Pelamis platurus*, Fig. 315).

--- SENTENCE 5722 ---
The latter species is pelagic, ranging from East Africa to the Pacific coast of the Americas (Allen and Steene 1996).

--- SENTENCE 5723 ---
There are reports of two species of marine mammals, including the endangered dugong or sea cow (*Dugong dugon*).

#### **Coastal Populations and and Reef Economics Reef Economics**

Over the past ten years, the Palauan population increased 23.4% to about 18,800 in 2000

(U.S. Bureau of Census 2002).

--- SENTENCE 5731 ---
Tourism is now a major component of the economy.

--- SENTENCE 5732 ---
In 1999, over 78,000 tourists a year visited the islands, contributing around \$78.8 million annually to the local economy (B. Graham pers.

--- SENTENCE 5733 ---
The number of foreign visitors and workers has increased dramatically over the past decade, and the population center is shifting to Babeldaob, by far the largest (volcanic) island in Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5734 ---
As with the FSM, the more remote islands, atolls, and villages retain more traditional population levels and controls over coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5735 ---
Commercial fisheries generate a reported \$6.4 million in gross value output (FAO 1998).

--- SENTENCE 5736 ---

**Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs Environmental Pressures on Coral Reefs**

**Human Pressures Pressures –** Palau has already done a great deal toward limiting the impacts of tourists on reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 5738 ---
Mooring buoys, laws preventing the collection of corals, and diving tour operator education help conserve the culturally and economically important reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 5739 ---
Now the largest direct impact on some reef sites is the volume of divers with varying levels of training.

--- SENTENCE 5740 ---
At the moment, the single greatest concern is the Compact road project for Babeldaob.

--- SENTENCE 5741 ---
It has a number of potential impacts on reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5742 ---
First, acute and dramatic erosion and sedimentation are likely to occur during and after construction.

--- SENTENCE 5743 ---
There are likely to be chronic, long-term impacts from damaged upland habitats.

--- SENTENCE 5744 ---
Second, the road will open large areas to development, increasing both land and reef use with the

**FREELY ASSOCIATED STATES FREELY ASSOCIATED STATES**

resulting impacts on water quality and reef health.

--- SENTENCE 5745 ---
Finally, plans to dredge for fill material needed to build the road base have the potential for reef damage.

--- SENTENCE 5746 ---
Once built, the increased population (both local and visitors) will require additional sewage treatment and other support facilities.

--- SENTENCE 5747 ---
Foreign-based fishing activities are already a problem (Fig. 316).

--- SENTENCE 5748 ---
Poachers from Indonesia and the Philippines are frequently encountered on Helen's Reef.

--- SENTENCE 5749 ---
Ship groundings have also been occurring off the main islands as well as those in the south (Fig. 317).

--- SENTENCE 5750 ---
Foreign fishermen and their catch on Sonsorol Island in Southwest Palau (Photo: James McVey).

#### Natural Stresses – Natural

stress includes outbreaks of crown-of-thorn starfish, typhoons (even though rare), and big waves from storms.

--- SENTENCE 5751 ---
Although the Palau islands generally lie south of the main pathway for typhoons in the northwestern tropical Pacific, infrequent tropical cyclones do pass over the islands.

--- SENTENCE 5752 ---
Climate Change and Coral Bleaching – Palau experienced substantial coral bleaching in 1997, when an estimated 30% of its reefs were heavily impacted.

--- SENTENCE 5753 ---
Acropora corals were especially susceptible, and in many places mortality was high (Figs. 318 and 319).

--- SENTENCE 5754 ---
In 1998 surveys of Ngaruangel, live coral coverage ranged from 10-30% with an average cover of 5-10%.

--- SENTENCE 5755 ---
An estimated 30-50% of these were bleached.

--- SENTENCE 5756 ---
All adult Acropora table-type corals were dead, yet juvenile colonies less that 10 cm in diameter had almost full survival (C. Birkeland pers.

--- SENTENCE 5757 ---
An estimated 75-85% of soft corals in the west and south side of Ngeruangel were also bleached.

--- SENTENCE 5758 ---
On the eastern side of the atoll, coral cover on the slopes ranged from 1-10%, averaging 4%; about 20% of the live coral was bleached and all staghorn coral had died.

--- SENTENCE 5759 ---
Live corals consisted mainly of massive corals.

--- SENTENCE 5760 ---
Dead coral cover averaged 10-25%.

--- SENTENCE 5761 ---
The lagoon patch reefs showed very low live coral coverage.

--- SENTENCE 5762 ---
Only a few blue-colored coral (*Heliopora*) and brain corals (*Porites*) remained on the patch reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5763 ---
All the *Acropora* corals were dead.

--- SENTENCE 5764 ---
The southern side of the main channel was similar to the patch reefs, with most corals dead (PCS unpub.

--- SENTENCE 5765 ---
Moderate coral bleaching was observed at Helen and Tobi Reefs in early December 1996 (P. Colin pers.

--- SENTENCE 5766 ---
During the summer of 1999, most corals at Helen reef died from a bleaching event (P. Colin pers.

--- SENTENCE 5767 ---
Other islands in the Southwest must have also been affected, since offshore reefs in the Palau main islands were impacted the most (C. Birkeland pers.

--- SENTENCE 5768 ---
During a late 1998 survey of Oruaol Libuchel patch reef, a state conservation area for

Ngatpang, live coral cover at the western side of the reef was 17% and dead coral covered 21% of the area (Golbuu, 2001).

--- SENTENCE 5769 ---
The eastern side had a higher coral cover (26%) and lower dead coral covered (11%).

--- SENTENCE 5770 ---
A nearby patch reef was also surveyed as a control for the conservation area monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5771 ---
It had 31% live coral cover and 14% dead coral cover.

--- SENTENCE 5772 ---
Ngchesar in east Babeldoab was seriously hit by bleaching in 1998.

--- SENTENCE 5773 ---
Most of the corals at the barrier reef died.

--- SENTENCE 5774 ---
The fringing reefs at Ngchesar were not as badly affected as the barrier reef.

--- SENTENCE 5775 ---
Some corals survived, mainly *Porites*, but most of the *Acroporas* in the fringing and patch reefs are dead.

--- SENTENCE 5776 ---
Surveys at Ngerumekaol (Ulong Channel) in Koror revealed a high percentage of dead coral.

--- SENTENCE 5777 ---
In the

--- SENTENCE 5786 ---

--- SENTENCE 5789 ---

Fish populations were also affected by the recent bleaching event.

--- SENTENCE 5791 ---
Surveys at the Southwest Islands revealed the abundance of fish that prey on corals, use corals for shelter, or feed on fish that feed on corals decreased dramatically from 1992 levels (T. Donaldson pers.

comm.).

**Assessment and Monitoring Monitoring –**

--- SENTENCE 5795 ---
The Palau International Coral Reef Center (PICRC) was created to enhance the knowledge about coral reefs and related marine environments so they can be effectively managed and conserved within the Republic and the Western Pacific.

--- SENTENCE 5796 ---
PICRC has established 14 permanent sites on shallow reefs to monitor corals, coral recruitment, and fish.

--- SENTENCE 5797 ---
In addition, PICRC has also surveyed close to 200 non-permanent sites around Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5798 ---
The Palau Conservation Society is active in conservation activities in the archipelago, and collaborates on monitoring and assessment programs with the Coral Reef Research Foundation, Palau Community College, the Environmental Quality Protection Board (EQPB) and the Marine Resources Division.

--- SENTENCE 5799 ---
The Nature Conservancy has an office on Palau, and works with the other agencies and organizations on coral reef conservation.

--- SENTENCE 5800 ---
Palau has substantial expertise, but financial resources are somewhat limiting.

--- SENTENCE 5801 ---
**MPAs and No-take Zones Zones –** Currently, Palau has a total of 13 established MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 5802 ---
In 1956, the Rock Island Management and Preservation Act designated certain areas of the Rock Islands as reserves and others as tourist activity areas.

--- SENTENCE 5803 ---
This was Palau's first MPA.

--- SENTENCE 5804 ---
The total area of Palau's coral reef ecosystems protected by no-take reserves is 65.3 km2 , which is equivalent to about 3.9% of the country's coral reef area.

#### **Gaps in Current Monitoring and Gaps in Current Monitoring and Conservation Capacity Capacity**

Palau's PICRC needs funding to continue monitoring of its established long-term coral reef *

changes in structure.

--- SENTENCE 5806 ---
can resource managers effectively implement management plans.

--- SENTENCE 5807 ---
Currently, there are not enough technical personnel to do the required monitoring.

--- SENTENCE 5808 ---
Additional people need to be trained if consistent and robust monitoring is to be done.

--- SENTENCE 5809 ---
**FREELY ASSOCIATED STATES**

So far, most of the training has been for short-term monitoring and is focused on collection techniques that are easy and not timeconsuming.

--- SENTENCE 5810 ---
Coral identification is usually not covered.

--- SENTENCE 5811 ---
Without it, biological diversity surveys cannot be done, and the data that is collected may not truly reflect the actual condition of the coral reef ecosystem.

--- SENTENCE 5812 ---
For example, the Malakal sewer outfall study determined percent coral cover, and found no significant difference between 1976 and 1991.

--- SENTENCE 5813 ---
But species diversity decreased dramatically since 1973.

--- SENTENCE 5814 ---
So without taxonomic information, the conclusion would be that the reefs were doing well when they were not.

--- SENTENCE 5815 ---
Periodically, funds are needed to bring people together for an REA of the entire reef environment from Ngeruangel to the Southwest Islands (Fig. 320).

--- SENTENCE 5816 ---
Reef studies tend to be limited to Koror and selected places in Babeldaob, neglecting unique areas far

Figure 321.

## **Laws, and Legislation Legislation**

Palau National Government policies regarding environmental issues are given in the Palau National Master Development Plan (SAGRIC 1996).

--- SENTENCE 5820 ---
The Plan recommends actions necessary to protect the environment, including formalizing a policy process, insti-

tuting and strengthening education and research programs, protecting habitats and wildlife, managing waste, reducing pollution, and implementing new coral reef conservation legislation.

--- SENTENCE 5821 ---
As a Compact Nation, U.S. laws apply to the conservation of Palau's coral reef resources.

--- SENTENCE 5822 ---
The **Marine Protection Act** regulates taking certain species of marine organisms, prohibits or limits certain fishing methods, and authorizes the Minister of Resources and Development to develop regulations regarding the collection of marine animals for aquaria or research (Fig. 321).

--- SENTENCE 5823 ---
The **Environmental Quality Protection Act** was consolidated into Palau National Code as Title 24.

--- SENTENCE 5824 ---
Division 1 of this Act creates the EQPB and mandates it to protect the environment of Palau.

--- SENTENCE 5825 ---
Division 2 (Chapter 10) deals with wildlife protection.

--- SENTENCE 5826 ---
Protected sea life includes turtles (Fig. 322), sponges, mother-of-pearl, dugong, *topshell* gastropods and clams.

--- SENTENCE 5827 ---
Chapter 13 deals with illegal fishing methods including the use of explosives, poisons, or chemicals.

--- SENTENCE 5828 ---
Division 3 deals with the protected areas of Ngerukewid and Ngerumkaol.

--- SENTENCE 5829 ---
**The Natural Heritage Reserve System** Act mandates a set of reserves, sanctuaries, and refuges to be identified, developed, and strengthened.

--- SENTENCE 5830 ---
The Palau Bureau of Natural Resources and Development is the body responsible for designating and nominating areas for inclusion in the reserve and developing regulations to implement the Act.

--- SENTENCE 5831 ---
State Government legislation is also helping to preserve the reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5832 ---
The Rock Island Management

!

--- SENTENCE 5833 ---
Green sea turtles and their eggs are protected by the Environmental Quality Protection Act (Photo: James McVey).

--- SENTENCE 5834 ---
and Preservation Act designated certain areas of the rock islands as reserves and others as tourist activity areas (Fig. 323).

--- SENTENCE 5835 ---
Koror State Public Law K6 101-99 established the Ngerukewid Islands Wildlife Preserve and prohibited fishing in Ngerumkaol spawning area.

--- SENTENCE 5836 ---
Koror State Public Law (No. K6 119-2201, effective as of January 10, 2001) closed off Ngederrak reef (C. Emaurois pers.

--- SENTENCE 5837 ---
The Fishing Conservation Act 1987 set aside two reef areas in Ngeremlengui State as a fish reserve and prohibited fishing in Toachel Mlengui channel during the summer months when fish are spawning.

--- SENTENCE 5838 ---
The Ngatpang Conservation Act of 1999 established the Ngatpang Reserve which includes three areas and Ngatpang's portion of Ngermeduu Bay.

--- SENTENCE 5839 ---
And the Ngiwal State Conservation Act of 1997 established Ngemai Conservation Area.

#### **Conclusions and Recommendations Conclusions and Recommendations**

For effective coral reef management, regular assessment and monitoring of Palau coral reefs is required.

--- SENTENCE 5840 ---
Regular monitoring programs detect problems earlier, allowing more effective strategies to be developed.

--- SENTENCE 5841 ---
There should also be an emphasis on reports and publications from the monitoring program.

--- SENTENCE 5842 ---
There are many reports dealing with coral reefs buried in government offices and generally inaccessible to the public.

--- SENTENCE 5843 ---
Having this available to the community would increase awareness and support for conservation.

--- SENTENCE 5844 ---
Palau Community College has a public library staffed by one librarian and five full-time staff.

--- SENTENCE 5845 ---
All the materials in the library are cataloged and available for online computer search.

--- SENTENCE 5846 ---
Since the library already has the facility, staff, and resources, it would be wise to designate it as a depository for all documents relating to coral reefs.

--- SENTENCE 5847 ---
Effective management of marine resources requires an informed and supportive public, so education is another important aspect of reef conservation.

--- SENTENCE 5848 ---
School curricula from elementary to secondary and post secondary should incorporate environmental issues and concerns.

--- SENTENCE 5849 ---
Community outreach projects could extend this education and awareness to the communities.

--- SENTENCE 5850 ---
Efforts should focus on raising awareness among policy makers, traditional and political leaders, and villagers.

--- SENTENCE 5851 ---
Catch levels and trends for reef fisheries should be monitored closely and accurately so effective management of coral reef fish resources can be implemented.

--- SENTENCE 5852 ---
Currently, only two fish markets in Koror are providing landings information to the Marine Resources Division.

--- SENTENCE 5853 ---
To have accurate market data, the Marine Resources staff need to have landings and catch data from all fish markets.

--- SENTENCE 5854 ---
Other information such as the type of fishing gear used and the number of hours spent fishing would help in determining the level of exploitation.

--- SENTENCE 5855 ---
Finally, a collaborative program needs to be established between all the agencies and organizations involved with coral reef monitoring and management.

--- SENTENCE 5856 ---
This could be a strategic planning group, setting priorities and areas of focus for each group/ area and focusing on problems that can only be solved with cooperation.

--- SENTENCE 5857 ---
With limited resources (time, money, and people) and a large coral reef area, everyone needs to work together to avoid duplication of effort and competition between the different groups.

--- SENTENCE 5858 ---
With a more coordinated effort, coral reef conservation will no doubt improve.

--- SENTENCE 5859 ---
Palau's rock islands have been zoned to serve as marine reserves or tourism and recreation areas (Photo: William Perryclear/PICRC).

#### **Appendix IV: Federal Protection for U.S. Coral Reef Ecosystems Appendix IV: for U.S. Ecosystems**

A variety of Federal legislation currently authorizes protection for aspects of coral reef ecosystems inside and outside Federal MPAs.

--- SENTENCE 5961 ---
These include the following.

- • National Marine Sanctuaries Act, 16 U.S.C. 1431 et seq.

--- SENTENCE 5962 ---
Authorizes NOAA to designate areas as national marine sanctuaries and promulgates regulations for the conservation and management of those areas.
- • National Park Service Organic Act of 1916, 16 U.S.C. 1 et seq.

--- SENTENCE 5963 ---
Authorizes the creation of National Parks "to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wildlife therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such a manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.

--- SENTENCE 5964 ---
"
- • National Wilderness Preservation System, 16 U.S.C. 1131 et seq.

--- SENTENCE 5965 ---
Authorizes designation of federally owned areas as "wilderness areas" to be administered to preserve their pristine character.
- • National Wildlife Refuge System Improvement Act of 1997, 16 U.S.C. 668dd et seq.

--- SENTENCE 5966 ---
Authorizes National Wildlife Refuges to conserve fish, wildlife, and plants and their habitats; requires all Refuges to complete Comprehensive Conservation Management Plans within 15 years of enactment.
- • Sikes Act, 16 U.S.C. 670a-o. Requires the Department of Defense to provide for conservation and rehabilitation of natural resources on military installations.

- • The Clean Water Act (CWA).

--- SENTENCE 5967 ---
Among other objectives, the CWA regulates the discharge of dredged or fill materials into waters of the United States (marine and freshwater).

--- SENTENCE 5968 ---
It also contains provisions governing the filling or draining of wetlands (which include seagrass beds, mangroves and salt marshes).
- • The Coastal Zone Management Act (CZMA).

--- SENTENCE 5969 ---
Through cooperation between federal and state agencies, the CZMA provides for controlled management and development of shoreline areas.
- • The Endangered Species Act (ESA).

--- SENTENCE 5970 ---
Provides federal resources, including money and institutional support, for monitoring, conserving, and promoting the recovery of species listed as either "endangered" or "threatened".
- • The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

--- SENTENCE 5971 ---
Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) or Statements (EISs) are required by NEPA for proposed projects that involve federal sponsorship or approval.
- • Lacey Act, 16 U.S.C. 3372 et seq., 18 U.S.C. 42.

--- SENTENCE 5972 ---
Makes it unlawful to import, export, sell, receive, posess, or transport wildlife taken in violation of state, federal, tribal, or foreign laws or regulations.
- • Magnuson Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, 16 U.S.C. 1801 et seq.

--- SENTENCE 5973 ---
Conserves and manages fish stocks throughout the 200-mile U.S. Fishery Conservation Zone by developing fishery management plans and designating essential fish habitat.
